News.title: Watch: Clean up begins after French riots but police remain
News.content:
Following a weekend of intense rioting across France, a clean up operation has begun - but tensions remain, with police still in position and a curfew in place in some big cities.

Outside of Paris, Marseille saw some of the worst damage, with shop owners reporting more than 600 premises having been looted.

From the port city in southern France, the BBC's Nick Beake explains some of the factors behind the protests.

Read more about this here.

News.title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
News.content:
Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.

Regulations due to be laid in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to Â£800 a month in universal credit over several years while already having their bed and board funded through the NHS while receiving psychiatric treatment.

The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds annually.

The parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023, welcomed the announcement.

The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to Parliamentary approval.

News.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
News.content:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a Â£1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.

Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".

Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."

The new rules will give drivers:

a guaranteed 5 minute period to decide whether to park

A 10 minute window to leave without facing a penalty

Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parks

Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines

Maximum charges of Â£20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking

A freeze on the maximum parking charge at Â£100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.

With each charge worth up to Â£100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than Â£4.6m each day.

The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.

The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.

The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.

But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament.

The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice".

The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.

Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".

But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.

The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

News.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.

She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.

The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.

She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.

She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine".

"I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."

The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.

From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.

In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".

The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.

Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.

The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.

She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.

Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.

She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.

She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.

The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.

Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Brand denies all the charges he faces.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

News.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
News.content:
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.

If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.

The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.

"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

News.title: US church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
News.content:
America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities.

President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction".

But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq".

While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction.

BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more.

Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis.

News.title: The singles choosing in-person dating events over apps
News.content:
Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive.

Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night.

"It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs.

This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue".

She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on.

According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year.

News.title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
News.content:
This report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms.

Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush.

Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain.

"I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says.

Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy.

She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms.

"Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says.

"But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad."

The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus.

News.title: Four arrested after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Four people have been arrested - including a woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and possessing a firearm - after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The male officer remains in hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

Two women, 27 and 25, and a 24-year-old man were arrested after police stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of Nottingham on Sunday evening, while a 30-year-old man was arrested in Bedfordshire in the early hours of Monday.

The 27-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

The 24-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Separately, after stopping a vehicle in Bedfordshire, the 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Troubles legacy bill is not an amnesty for soldiers - NI secretary
News.content:
The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has rejected claims that planned changes to the government's Troubles legacy bill amount to an "amnesty" for former soldiers.

Sir Chris Bryant said it was "completely wrong" to suggest a requirement for the attorney general to consent to serious Troubles-related prosecutions was designed to pardon veterans.

The proposal is among a series of government amendments being debated by MPs on Monday after the long-awaited legislation returned to the House of Commons.

Speaking to BBC News NI, Bryant said it was a "sensible measure" to ensure there was "more consistency" in how decisions are made.

The legislation seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict in Northern Ireland, which cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.

It was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government.

News.title: Man accused of mass train stabbing admits wounding
News.content:
A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Cambridgeshire last year has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent.

Passengers and staff were injured on the 18:25 Doncaster-London service on Saturday, 1 November after it left Peterborough, causing it to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station.

Anthony Williams, 33, has denied 14 counts of attempted murder, relating to the train and to incidents in London and Peterborough, and is due to stand trial next week.

Appearing at a pre-trial review at Cambridge Crown Court, Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, pleaded guilty to the lesser wounding charges and several other offences.

He appeared via video link from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire.

At an earlier hearing, Williams pleaded not guilty to attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the train near Huntingdon on 1 November.

In front of Mr Justice Calver this Monday, Williams pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent in relation to incidents on the train, and earlier in Peterborough and London.

News.title: Trial hears Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.

Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.

The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."

Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.

Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case â and said his court fees to date had cost him Â£400,000.

News.title: Masts from explosives-packed ship taken to museum
News.content:
Three masts removed from a bomb-laden shipwreck in the Thames Estuary have been successfully taken to a maritime museum.

The poles, delicately removed from the SS Richard Montgomery in September, will be kept at the Historic Dockyard Chatham.

The masts had been visible from the Essex and Kent coasts since the doomed vessel sank with 1,400 tonnes of explosives onboard in 1944.

Junior transport minister, Kier Mather said removing the masts had reduced the risk of them toppling on to and detonating the bombs.

"As the vessel has aged, the masts continued to place significant load on the structure," he said in a written statement to Parliament.

"Their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site."

News.title: Man held after three Jewish women report assaults
News.content:
A man has been arrested after three Jewish women, one of whom was pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in north-east London.

Police were called to the Clapton Common area of Hackney at about 13:40 BST on Monday after a man had been detained by members of Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group.

Officers arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of racially aggravated common assault. The women are believed to have suffered minor injuries.

The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a suspected antisemitic hate crime and had increased patrols in the area.

The man has since been further arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with a separate incident in Islington on Friday, the force said. He remains in custody.

Ch Insp Erica Crawshaw said it had been "an alarming and distressing incident" and thanked Shomrim volunteers for detaining a suspect before officers arrived.

"We recognise the concern that this incident will have caused the Jewish community here in Hackney," she said.

"We have increased patrols in the area and we are speaking to community leaders to provide further reassurance."

The Met has appealed for anyone with information, or anyone else who believes they may have been assaulted, to come forward.

News.title: Charging battery believed to have caused house fire
News.content:
A house fire in Leicestershire is believed to have been caused by a charging lithium-ion battery, firefighters have said.

Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service (LFRS) said crews were called to reports of the blaze in North Street, Ashby-de-la-Zouch, shortly after 15:00 BST on Saturday.

The fire, which is thought to have started following an electrical fault involving a battery, caused extensive damage to the property, particularly in the kitchen where it had been left charging.

The service said four firefighters wearing breathing apparatus were deployed to extinguish the blaze, but the occupant managed to safely evacuate the house.

News.title: Southport killer faces trial for alleged prison attacks
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana is due to face trial next year over allegations he threw boiling water mixed with sugar at a prison officer.

Rudakubana, who is serving a life sentence for the murders of three young girls in 2024, appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey on Monday where he spoke only to confirm his name.

He has been charged with attempted grievous bodily harm of a prison officer, two other assaults of officers and possession of a knife or other offensive weapon across separate dates last year at HMP Belmarsh, south London.

Rudakubana was not asked to enter any pleas and a preliminary hearing has been set for 5 February, with a provisional trial date of 8 October 2027.

Rudakubana, 20, is serving a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

On 8 May last year, it is alleged he threw hot water through a hatch in his prison cell door.

It is further alleged that two days before, on 6 May, Rudakubana threatened to "soak" a female officer outside his cell if she did not pass him a newspaper and then threw liquid at her.

Rudakubana also allegedly punched a male officer on 28 October.

The offensive weapon charge relates to sharpened stone shards that the prosecution say had seemingly been prised from the floor of the defendant's cell.

In July, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh, where the attacks allegedly took place, to Broadmoor high-security psychiatric hospital.

News.title: Richard Riehle, dependable TV and film character actor who was in 'Glory and 'Office Space,' dies
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor in TV and film who often played authority figures but was equally skilled at comedy, notably playing a sad-sack product manager in “Office Space,” has died. He was 78.

Wright Entertainment Inc. said Monday that Riehle had died Oct. 15 but disclosed no cause or details. “Our industry has lost an exceptional talent, and our community has lost a truly wonderful man,” said a statement.

Riehle's almost five-decade career included playing a quartermaster in the Civil War drama “Glory,” a prison guard in “The Fugitive,” an air marshal in “Executive Decision,” a police officer in a guest spot on “The West Wing” and a principal on the TV adaptation of “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.”

“If a casting director has found themselves in need of a burly, blustery, mustachioed man for their project, Richard Riehle has likely been near the top of their list,” The AV Club said in 2017.

He fell into acting as a senior at the University of Notre Dame. He couldn’t really afford to stay another year but was told he could take all the credits he needed in speech and drama in one semester. He stayed.

“I spent a semester doing anything and everything that you do in the theater — acting, directing, building sets, etc. — and then for some reason they liked what I did enough that they got me a teaching assistantship at the University of Minnesota. So I went on and got my MFA (Masters of Fine Arts). I figured, ‘What the heck? If they’re gonna pay me to do it, I’m gonna do it!’” he told the AV Club.

He had his first lines in the 1977 movie “Joyride” alongside Desi Arnaz Jr., Anne Lockhart, Robert Carradine and Melanie Griffith. He'd go on to appear in the broad comedy “Bridesmaids,” the comedy-mystery “Shadows and Fog” for Woody Allen, “Black Rain” with Michael Douglas and the sitcom “Grounded For Life.”

He had an affinity to the “Star Trek” world, landing parts in three franchises — “Star Trek: The Next Generation” in 1992, “Star Trek: Voyager” in 2000 and “Star Trek: Enterprise” in 2004. He was on Broadway three times, including with Paul Giamatti in a 1999 revival of “The Iceman Cometh.”

One of his most beloved roles was in the 1999 film “Office Space,” as Tom Smykowski, an expendable employee at Initech facing getting laid off despite insisting, “I have people skills!”

“Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity,” Wright Entertainment said.

News.title: Healey rejects calls to raise capital gains tax at the Budget
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

John Healey has rejected calls to hike capital gains tax at the Budget, amid concerns it could hamper economic growth.

Several prominent Labour voices have called in recent months for a rise in the tax, which applies to the profit made from selling off assets like a house or shares.

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both spoke of raising capital gains tax over the summer before Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.

But Mr Healey has ruled out the move after warnings it could end up costing the Government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets, according to the Times.

Lord O’Neill of Gately, who has advised Mr Burnham and worked on the Northern Powerhouse project, told the newspaper that “raising capital gains tax would send very much the wrong message to business”.

The biggest revenue raising measure set to be in the Budget is an increase in the rate banks pay on their profits, widely reported across the media last week.

That is expected to fund cost-of-living support for households and businesses.

The Chancellor has acknowledged that Britain finds itself in a “tough” position ahead of the Budget, and is reported to be downplaying the prospect of major revenue-raising measures in his October 28 statement.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is meanwhile due to warn the Government to slash its spending plans, and reduce its borrowing at the Budget.

In a speech on Tuesday, she will urge Mr Burnham and his Chancellor to “live within our means”, and signpost the Tories’ package worth £70bn of cuts to spending – including to welfare and the civil service headcount – as a place to start.

Pre-Budget polling by Ipsos has meanwhile revealed that the majority of the public have a mixed opinion of the Chancellor, as 67% of them believe he is doing neither a good nor bad job.

The survey of 1,077 Britons carried out between October 9 and 12 also found that 65% of the public is expecting some form of tax rise at the Budget.

News.title: Parents face childcare 'postcode lottery' as more schools extend October half-term break
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

More than one in seven state school teachers in England now have a fortnight off in October, according to a survey shared with the Press Association.

Teacher Tapp polled 8,112 state school teachers in England and found 15% said their school had a two-week October half term this year. The proportion has grown quickly, from 12% last year and 7% in 2023.

The shift is creating increased childcare challenges for parents, it has been suggested.

An education expert has warned that a lack of strategy over the break risks creating a “postcode lottery” for families, especially parents juggling children in schools with different holidays.

Leaders have said state schools are increasingly switching to an extended autumn break to give teachers and pupils more time to “rest and reset” during a long and demanding term.

Some schools have seen reductions in pupil absence and staff illness since making the move, the leaders said. The majority of councils in England still run a one-week half term in their schools.

But the growth in academies, which are state schools independent of councils that set their own term dates, has meant a two-week half term is increasingly being explored by schools and academy trusts.

Council-run schools in England must open for at least 190 days during a year. Teachers can be required to work an additional five days for training, which are usually Inset days.

open image in gallery A new survey has found one in seven state school teachers now have two weeks off in October ( PA )

Some local authorities, like Nottinghamshire and Bromley in London, have a shorter summer holiday to accommodate the two-week break in schools. Many academies have opted to keep the other school holidays the same.

Instead they lengthen the school day slightly or they reallocate staff training into “twilight” sessions. That has left working parents having to juggle an extra week of childcare not long after a six-week, summer break.

Lee Elliot Major, professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, has called on the Government to launch a “nationally co-ordinated programme of trials” to evaluate the extended break.

He warned of a “more fragmented system” without knowing whether children are actually benefiting.

He told PA: “My concern is that we’re seeing a piecemeal revolution in the school calendar, with individual schools and trusts making changes without a wider strategy.

“That risks creating a postcode lottery for families, particularly parents juggling childcare and work when neighbouring schools operate different holiday dates.”

Anthem Schools Trust, which runs 15 schools in the East Midlands, London and Thames Valley, has introduced a two-week, October half term across all of its schools for the first time this year.

David Hatchett, chief executive of the trust, said some “logistical concerns” were raised by parents who had other children in nearby schools with different holidays.

But he said about 60% of families were in favour of the extended half term. Some said they were happy about the prospect of booking more affordable holidays earlier in the month.

The initiative is being rolled out across the trust as leaders believe the extended break has boosted pupil attainment and staff wellbeing in one of its schools in south London.

Mr Hatchett said feedback and analysis of absence data from St Mark’s Academy found that staff attendance was better after introducing the two-week break.

open image in gallery Teachers are now getting more time off in October ( PA )

He said the extended holiday was “critical to keeping concentration and energy levels up” among staff and pupils.

He told PA: “When you have had such a long holiday over the summer and then you return to a long and intensive first half term, it is quite a big adjustment for a teacher and school leader; a one week break at the end of October is arguably too late and short for a proper rest and reset.”

The NAHT school leaders’ union is hearing of more state schools that have recently adopted a two-week October half term, or are considering it.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT, said: “The autumn term can be particularly demanding for both pupils and staff, and an extended break may help support wellbeing, motivation and readiness for the remainder of the term.”

Unity Schools Partnership, which runs 40 schools in the east of England, has seen a fall in the number of days lost to sickness absence for staff since introducing a two-week break in 2023.

Dominic Norrish, chief executive of Unity, said the move to a longer half term appears to be “increasingly popular”. He has heard of more trusts introducing it in Norfolk and Suffolk.

He told PA: “I think as soon as one trust locally moves, it seems to be that other trusts follow because it does make sense for lots of reasons if you can prove the impact.”

But Mr Norrish acknowledged that the change is “not universally popular” with families.

“It creates a longer time when children are not in school, which is particularly challenging for working parents, and we have received that feedback as well,” he added.

Lydia Hodges, head of the Coram Family and Childcare charity, said: “Holiday childcare costs an average of £191 per week in Great Britain, which is a substantial cost for many families.”

Ms Hodges acknowledged that an extended half term can be helpful to families if the long six-week break is shortened.

But she said finding childcare could be “tricky” as a number of holiday clubs may not run during the half term.

She added: “Where schools are instead making up the education hours in a different way – for example by having longer days throughout the term – this can mean an additional week of childcare costs for parents every year.”

A Department for Education (DfE) spokesperson said: “Every child deserves a high-quality education, and that begins with being in school.

“While we stipulate the minimum number of days a school must be open for per year, local leaders and schools themselves are given the flexibility to set school term and holiday dates in the interests of pupils and their parents.”

The survey figures suggest the two-week October break remains a minority arrangement among England’s state schools, but one that has more than doubled in prevalence since 2023.

News.title: Strictly judge Craig Revel Horwood to star in new Sister Act musical tour
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Craig Revel Horwood is swapping the Strictly Come Dancing judging desk for the stage, having signed up to play Mother Superior in a new UK and Ireland tour of Sister Act.

The 61-year-old will take on the role made famous by the late Dame Maggie Smith in the 1992 film. He is no stranger to the musical, having directed and choreographed its UK tour in 2015.

The story follows lounge singer Deloris Van Cartier, who goes into hiding and lives as a nun after witnessing a crime. Her disguise is quickly put in jeopardy as she begins to transform the struggling convent choir.

Zoe Birkett, a Pop Idol singer and West End star, will play Deloris, the character portrayed by Whoopi Goldberg in the film.

Comedian Paul Chuckle, 79, will join them as Monsignor O'Hara.

open image in gallery Revel Horwood has been a Strictly judge for over two decades ( BBC, Strictly Come Dancing )

The tour opens in London in September 2027 and runs until March 2028. It then moves on to Sunderland, Sheffield, Dublin, Manchester and Birmingham. Further dates are scheduled in Cardiff, Nottingham, Brighton, Belfast and Derry.

The part adds to a string of theatre credits for Revel Horwood.

He has played Munkustrap in Cats, Dance Captain in Miss Saigon and Miss Hannigan in Annie, and was one of the original cast members of Crazy For You.

His choreography on the musicals Spend, Spend, Spend and My One And Only earned him Olivier Award nominations. Revel Horwood has sat on the Strictly panel since the show began in 2004, making him its longest-serving judge.

Earlier this month, Revel Horwood defended the show’s new presenting trio, comments made by the press towards broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe as “disgusting”

The Strictly star praised the new trio, who have replaced Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, for the 2026 series.

“We are putting people together and it is like a family and you have to form relationships,” he said during an appearance on BBC Breakfast. The show had its third elimination on Sunday, with Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon being shown the exit door.

Revel Horwood is also an author, and his debut novel, Dances And Dreams On Diamond Street, was published in 2020.

News.title: Experts reconstruct face of man from Roman Scotland after 2,000 years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An international team of experts have digitally reconstructed the face of a man who died on the Roman frontier in Scotland almost 2,000 years ago.

The man’s skull will be displayed alongside the digital facial reconstruction in the exhibition, Roman Scotland: Life On The Edge Of Empire, which opens at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh next month.

Researchers used “cutting-edge” scientific techniques to determine the man’s genetic make-up and discovered he was likely to have been in his early 50s when he died at Inveresk, near Edinburgh, between AD 140–165.

He was originally from southern Britain and had travelled hundreds of miles to the Firth of Forth coast.

An examination of his skeleton found that he had suffered several injuries and was not a soldier at the time of his death, as he could not have swung a sword.

Experts noted the man had limited use of his right arm due to an extensive bone growth near the elbow joint, which was likely caused by septic arthritis, while he had suffered a broken nose which had healed.

open image in gallery The facial reconstruction of the man from Inveresk ( PA )

Dr Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistory and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland (NMS) said: “I have worked with the finds from Roman Inveresk for years, but this facial reconstruction finally gives me a sense of what one of its inhabitants looked like.

“Archaeology tells us about people who had hopes and fears just like us, and it is a privilege to present a vision of this resident of Inveresk using contemporary scientific techniques.

“We cannot know how exactly he looked, but we think his family and friends would have spotted the likeness.”

open image in gallery The man's skull will be displayed alongside the digital facial reconstruction in the exhibition ( PA )

The man was among several people whose burials were found around the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Experts said the burials, which are rarely discovered from Roman Scotland, are particularly unusual because four of the six adult men buried at Inveresk, including the one whose face has been reconstructed, were decapitated after they died.

They are said to be among the earliest known examples of the practice in Britain and the first in Scotland.

The reasons for post-mortem decapitation are not clear, however, it may have been linked to supernatural concerns or beliefs around how the people died, or might have been used as a form of punishment.

open image in gallery Dr Jess Thompson examining the skull of a man from Roman Scotland ( PA )

Dr Jess Thompson, curator of osteoarchaeology at NMS, said: “The burials at Inveresk are exceptional and incredibly rare survivals from Roman Scotland.

“Taking an interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of human remains allows us to understand the physical attributes of these individuals as well as their life stories.

“We can investigate where these men had travelled from to reach the frontier, what they were doing there and what became of them.

“This facial reconstruction by Dr Chris Rynn unites cutting-edge science with artistic vision to create an instant connection with the past, offering a dynamic portrait of what he may have looked like and who he may have been.”

The exhibition will explore life on a frontier, from the soldiers who tried to conquer the land to the communities living around each military base as well as the experiences of local people whose way of life was threatened by the Roman invasion.

NMS said the facial reconstruction was informed by an osteoarchaeological assessment carried out at the museum, previous isotopic analysis led by scholars at Durham University, and ancient DNA research by a team based at the Department of Archaeology at the University of York and Harvard Medical School.

Dr Rynn combined the findings to create the reconstruction.

The exhibition will run from November 14 until April 18 2027.

News.title: Criminals detained in hospital to be stripped of benefits, government says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Serious criminals held in hospital including killers and sex offenders are to be stripped of benefits following demands from victims’ families.

The government has confirmed action to end "double provision", a mechanism allowing offenders to collect hundreds of pounds a month for living expenses while undergoing NHS psychiatric treatment.

Regulations laid in parliament on Tuesday intend to close this loophole, preventing serious criminals from receiving up to £800 monthly in universal credit over several years and saving an estimated tens of millions of pounds annually.

According to the government, the decision follows consultation with experts and victims’ families as part of a strategy to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".

Pending approval by parliament, the revised rules are scheduled to come into force early next year.

Parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023, welcomed the announcement.

Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

open image in gallery Ian Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley Kumar were killed by Valdo Calocane in 2023 ( Nottinghamshire Police )

Emma Webber, Barnaby’s mother, said: “This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do.

“It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers’ money.

“A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused.

“Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve.”

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Miss O’Malley-Kumar’s father, said: “Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.

“On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated.

open image in gallery Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility ( Nottinghamshire Police )

“We are grateful to the Secretary of State Pat McFadden for taking action and listening to our campaign which always been about what is good for the country.”

The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.

The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.

Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape, who was given a hospital order detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.

The victim’s mother Linda Westcarr said: “I believe it is right that the government reviews benefit entitlement for those who have committed the most serious offences, particularly where public money, funded by taxpayers, is involved.

open image in gallery Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche was killed by her boyfriend ( Family handout/PA )

“For many victims’ families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.

“In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised.”

She added: “Kennedi mattered. Her life mattered. The voices of victims’ families must be heard, and their suffering must never be overlooked when decisions are made about the consequences of serious crime.”

The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the Government said.

open image in gallery Gogoa Lois Tape was given a hospital order detaining him indefinitely ( Metropolitan Police/PA )

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: “We said we’d act to tackle this gross unfairness and we’re delivering on that promise.

“For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

“That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it.”

Murder is not included as a hospital order is not applicable because the offence attracts a mandatory life sentence.

The full financial impacts of the approach will be published as part of the 2026 budget on October 28.

The NHS will continue to provide appropriate mental health support to the offenders affected.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.

“Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.

“The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers’ money goes only to those who genuinely need it.”

News.title: Singletons want to meet in real life – we’re embracing that, says Tinder boss
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tinder is not “running away” from the fact that more young singletons would rather meet in person than online, its boss has insisted as the dating app hopes real-life events can drive a resurgence in interest.

Spencer Rascoff, the chief executive of Tinder owner Match Group, said the app had undergone a turnaround after years of declining usership.

It comes as a new study conducted by the group found that 61% of single adults in the UK said they would like more of their social life to happen face to face.

This is despite 43% saying most of their socialising happens through a screen – rising to 51% of Gen Z respondents.

Just 4% of Gen Z met their most recent partner in the pub, bar or club, the survey found.

Mr Rascoff told the Press Association: “We have so much research that shows that people want to meet in person, at events, including from this new study.

“So rather than running away from that observation, we decided to run towards it, and embrace events by integrating them into the core Tinder experience.”

Tinder has launched in-person events in more than 50 cities around the world. The feature is not yet in the UK but is expected to launch in London.

The US-based boss said this has involved partnering with local operators who are already running events, and bringing them onto Tinder for singletons to connect with each other before or after.

“For example, a run club or a karaoke night or a matcha tasting or a singles meet-up in a dog park – these are events that already exist in the world,” he said.

“If they didn’t have the courage or the time to ask that person out at the run club or at the dog park, they can find them on Tinder afterwards, see their profile and message them safely.

“So basically we’re doing it in a scalable way.”

Mr Rascoff said other changes to the app – including improving the algorithm for recommending matches and rolling out new features – were “having the intended effect of turning the company around”.

open image in gallery 2RPK0HK New Delhi, India 4 September 2023:- Hinge dating app on iphone 13

He told the PA: “When I joined about two years ago, Tinder had seen almost around four years of declining usage year-on-year.

“Through the social road-map and a lot of hard work and improved marketing, we have almost entirely turned Tinder’s usage trends around.

“People sometimes say that dating apps are a thing of the past or they’re not popular anymore. I don’t believe that to be true.”

Match Group is expecting its annual revenues to total 885 million-895 million US dollars (£665-£673 million) for 2026, which would nonetheless be 2%-3% lower than the previous year.

But Tinder’s rival dating app Hinge, which is also owned by the group, has been growing with revenues rising by more than a fifth in the second quarter.

The apps make money from subscriptions which offer features like “unlimited likes” and “super likes” for paying members, as well as from advertising.

Mr Rascoff said it had not started putting events on Tinder “for the purpose of making money for Match Group”.

“We’ve done it to rejuvenate interest in the category of online dating,” he said, in a bid to attract more users who may eventually pay for premium features.

News.title: The NHS is not ready for winter, top A&E doctors warn: ‘We can’t tell where one crisis ends and the next begins’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Emergency care doctors have warned the NHS is not ready for the colder months, with overcrowding, corridor care and a looming surge in demand “creating perfect conditions for a terrible winter”.

A new survey of 163 doctors in charge of A&E departments across the UK, conducted by the Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM), found that more than nine in 10 (92 per cent) described current pressure as either high or very high, while 88 per cent said they are under greater strain now than this time a year ago.

Around nine in 10 (91 per cent) told the poll they were very or extremely worried about pressures in the coming months.

And after A&Es in England saw a record 7.3 million people attending hospital for emergency care this summer, leading accident and emergency (A&E) doctors have said the NHS is at the point “where we can’t tell where one crisis ends and the next begins”.

An early rise in flu cases and a smaller number of beds than last year could mean this winter is more challenging than usual for the health service ( PA )

Three in five doctors have warned their A&E departments are currently unsafe for patients, with conditions expected to worsen after the UK experienced higher levels of flu last month compared with the previous four years. The RCEM also warned the NHS is entering this winter with almost a thousand fewer beds in English hospitals compared to last year.

Dr Ian Higginson, president of the RCEM, said: “Overcrowding, corridor care, the impending surge of demand from winter, and lack of meaningful preparations, are creating perfect conditions for a terrible winter.

“Colleagues from across the four nations have been crystal clear: we are not managing now and we simply are not ready for winter.

“We have patients scattered all over our departments, many stuck in trolleys or on chairs for hours upon hours. The sickest and most injured among them can’t get into a hospital bed and end up staying with us, sometimes for days.

“It’s a disgraceful state of affairs and I cannot believe it has been allowed to get this bad. Patients are dying unnecessarily every week whilst politicians continue to focus on the wrong solutions.”

Dr Den Langhor, emergency care lead for the British Medical Association, said in response to the survey findings: “Having only just managed the busiest summer on record in emergency departments, we have not yet had time to take a moment to breathe before we face the onslaught of what we expect to be another horrific winter on the frontline. These pressures are no longer seasonal – they are continuous.”

The most recent figures show the average number of patients who waited more than 12 hours from arrival to being seen, treated or discharged from A&E between June and August hit 149,583, up from 126,511 in 2025 and 129,646 in 2024.

In September, 10 per cent, 157,00, of patients attending A&E waited more than 12 hours, while an average of 2,549 people a day were left waiting in A&E corridors.

In a survey of 163 A&E doctors, the Royal College found just 3 percent believe they are well prepared for the colder months. Around nine in 10 told the poll they were very or extremely worried about pressures in the coming months, while two-thirds said they are under more pressure now than they were a year ago.

Of the 119 responses gathered from A&E clinical leads in England, almost nine in 10 (89 per cent) described pressure at the moment as high or very high.

The latest NHS England data shows there was an average of 3,310 patients who received corridor care each day in September, with 2,549 in A&E departments and 761 in other hospital areas.

This is up from an average of 2,865 per day in August, made up of 2,297 in emergency departments and 568 in other areas.

Meanwhile, the number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments in England from a decision to admit to actually being admitted stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.

Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine, in response to the RCEM survey, said that hospitals are not heading into a winter crisis; they are “carrying an existing healthcare crisis into winter.”

She added: “The reality is that these problems have been building for years. An ageing population with increasingly complex health needs, shortages in community and social care, and hospitals operating at high occupancy mean patients are struggling to move through the system.”

Over the weekend, health secretary Yvette Cooper announced the NHS would receive a £140 million boost for urgent care this winter and vowed to end corridor care for children.

However, Dr Higginson warned the “Existing winter preparations represent the same old same old, and will yield the same disastrous results,” adding “it beggars belief that we are going into winter with nearly a thousand fewer beds than last year, and with recruitment freezes stopping us recruiting doctors and nurses to help reduce risk for our patients or to get hospitals working.”

News.title: French bond sell-off spreads across Europe
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The cost of French government borrowing has risen at the fastest pace among G7 nations after a second night of riots.

The yield on 10-year French bonds, known as OATs, climbed from 4.80pc to 4.85pc on Monday, the steepest increase among major world economies.

Bond yields are effectively the interest rate paid by governments when they borrow money by issuing bonds to financial markets.

Emmanuel Macron is facing a crisis after shops were looted and vandalised across the country.

More than 2,300 people were arrested on Saturday after protests against the cost of living and poor school conditions.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “This won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs, so the modest recovery in French spreads over the last week or so will be tested today.

“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham seeks EU embrace over AI | UK presses for access to a scheme that will prioritise investment in sovereign technology

2) Larry Ellison’s TikTok bans ad account for Musk documentary | Social media company blocks promotion for the film because of its political content

3) Profit warnings rise ahead of Budget | Most companies blame government policy and geopolitical uncertainty for worsening outlook

4) Istanbul airport stockpiles jet fuel over shortage fears | Turkish hub can sustain flights for three weeks without topping up tanks

5) GB News to launch ‘all-British’ radio station | New broadcast venture will attempt to win market share from BBC

What happened overnight

Oil prices fell more than 1pc after Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

On Friday, the President signed an executive order that delayed a wave of fresh sanctions and tariffs as they were set to take effect.

Brent crude edged down by nearly 1pc to just under $109 a barrel, with West Texas Intermediate hovered at around $101 a barrel.

Asian shares were mixed as volatility in technology stocks persisted.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.1pc to 5,729.58 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 18pc over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.8pc to 64,799.03. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron lost 2.1pc, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 3.6pc.

Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.2pc higher to 3,722.20, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5pc for its economy in the third quarter.

CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7pc despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.

China’s official growth data is set to be issued on Monday, giving the markets a glimpse into how the world’s second-biggest economy is faring.

The data is expected to show that China’s economy expanded by 4.4pc in the third quarter, improving on a multi-year low in Q2 but still falling just short of its annual target.

Beijing is aiming for growth of around 4.5pc to 5pc this year, which is its lowest goal in decades.

However, experts think China is on course to miss its annual economic target, weighed down by the Iran war energy shock.

China’s economy has been under pressure from mounting energy costs and faltering domestic demand. Researchers polled by AFP suggested exports were its sole outperformer.

Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1pc. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, were down 0.6pc. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.3pc higher at 8,832.20. India’s Sensex edged down 0.1pc.

Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell another 5pc to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11pc on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.

News.title: Europe records highest ever number of West Nile Virus cases
News.content:
Mainland Europe has seen the largest number of cases of a debilitating mosquito-borne illness, with Italy hardest hit by the disease.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control there have been 1,715 locally acquired cases of West Nile Virus so far this year, compared to 989 cases at the same point last year. Italy has been hardest hit, with 748 cases, followed by Greece with 445 cases, France with 144 and Spain with 139.

There have been 130 deaths, with the greatest number occurring in Italy, which saw 56 deaths.

The number of cases is likely to tail off over the next few weeks as the weather across Europe becomes cooler and less favourable for the Culex mosquito which spreads the disease.

West Nile Virus is in the same family of viruses as dengue, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis. It causes flu-like symptoms and sometimes vomiting and diarrhoea but in around one in 150 cases it can develop into a disease that affects the brain and nervous system and can be fatal. There is no vaccine or treatment.

The disease is widespread in birds, but humans can only acquire it if they are bitten by an infected mosquito. The disease does not spread from human to human. Most cases of severe disease occur in older people and those with weakened immune systems.

News.title: Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City
News.content:
In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough
News.content:
Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

News.title: Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation
News.content:
Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

News.title: Ruthless Daniel Dubois dispatches Fabio Wardley in just two rounds
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley.

When Wardley dragged himself out of the ring at Manchester’s Co-Op LIVE Arena, the physical damage was obvious, but the psychological sting was far deeper. Wardley had Dubois severely hurt early on, flooring the Londoner twice and teetering on the verge of a career-defining stoppage. Instead, he let the knockout slip away, allowed Dubois to find his rhythm, and was ultimately broken down and halted in the 11th round - surrendering his WBO heavyweight belt in a dramatic comeback victory.

Now, just five months after that gruelling night, the two heavyweights meet again at London’s O2 Arena in an immediate rematch that carries potentially massive implications for the entire division.

For Wardley (20-1-1, 19 KOs), the decision to trigger his rematch clause was instant. Dismissing concerns over the severe punishment he absorbed down the stretch, the Ipswich man is motivated entirely by redemption and the belief that his early success proved Dubois is beatable.

Dubois (23-3, 22 KOs), however, views things very differently. Entering as The Ring’s No. 1 heavyweight contender and a proven two-time world champion, Dubois has brushed off Wardley’s power, claiming his rival “punches like a baby” and insists Wardley threw away his one and only chance at glory in Manchester.

With Oleksandr Usyk approaching the final chapter of his career and the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury blockbuster looming just eight weeks away, this London clash is far more than a personal grudge match. The winner won’t just walk away with the WBO strap; they will stake an undeniable claim as the torch-bearer for the heavyweight division’s next era if they can land another title fight in short order.

News.title: Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working
News.content:
Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

News.title: Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card
News.content:
Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

Sports.title: Egypt bosses and player slapped with combined 11-MATCH ban after World Cup chaos against Argentina
Sports.content:
Next

EGYPT bosses and player Mostafa Zico have been hit with a combined 11-MATCH ban.

The punishments come after the Pharaohs’ chaotic exit from the World Cup in the summer.



Egypt were dumped out of the tournament across the Atlantic by eventual finalists Argentina.

Mohamed Salah and co were beaten in heartbreaking fashion after they threw away a two-goal lead in the round of 16 clash



After full-time, there were accusations towards referee François Letexier of bias towards the South Americans.

Sports.title: England and Premier League star Morgan Gibbs-White, 26, convicted of ignoring police after running red light
Sports.content:
RED CARD England and Premier League star Morgan Gibbs-White, 26, convicted of ignoring police after running red light







Next

PREMIER League star Morgan Gibbs-White has been convicted of ignoring police letters after his car was caught running a red light.

The Nottingham Forest midfielder has landed a £1,000 fine after the offence back in January.



The 26-year-old’s Range Rover was caught on traffic cameras going past a light in Nottinghamshire, 1.1 seconds after it turned red.

According to court documents, he failed to respond to two police letters asking to identify the driver at the time of the offence.



In January, Nottinghamshire Police put out an alert on the footballer’s car when investigating the incident.

They found the number plate on the star’s car was one letter different to that of Gibbs-White’s car.



In April Staffordshire Police pulled over the vehicle and confirmed it belongs to the star.

Last week the Nottingham Forest captain was found guilty by the Southern Derbyshire Magistrates’ Court.

He was fined £660, given six penalty points and ordered to pay £120 and £264 in costs and victim surcharge, respectively.

According to a court official, Gibbs-White did not enter a plea.



This is not the first time the footballer has gotten in trouble while driving.

He was banned from driving for six months in May, 2025, after admitting to speeding six times in two months.

He was fined nearly £4,000 and handed three points for each offence.

Gibbs-White confessed after being caught doing a staggering 96mph in one instance.

Initially, the footy star was told he’d have to cough up an eye-watering £6,000 for his offences but the price was slashed after he eventually pleaded guilty.



The penalties were dropped to £666 and he was told to pay an additional £1,598 victim surcharge and £110 in court costs.

He also faced 19 penalty points on his license – a sizeable amount given that most drivers face a ban if they accumulate 12 points on their license within a three year period.

The Nottingham Forest midfielder was recently called into the England squad for the UEFA Nations League.

Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel used Gibbs-White as a substitute in all four games.

Sports.title: Tottenham 3 Coventry 1: Marmoush and Maddison rockets fire Spurs to vital first Premier League win of season
Sports.content:

MAYBE all Tottenham needed was a holiday.

After a week sunning themselves in Marbella, two Spurs showstoppers ended their desperate wait for a first Premier League win.



James Maddison and Omar Marmoush each delivered a blockbuster strike having met up with heavyweight hero Anthony Joshua in Spain, with Ben Davies adding the knockout blow in injury time.

The Brit boxer clearly laid on a lesson in fighting spirit, with Roberto De Zerbi’s side climbing off the canvas and discovering a backbone after Jack Rudoni’s equaliser burst the bubble of Maddison’s opener on his first start in 536 days.



The goals were glamorous, but a lot of the football was hard to watch at times. But it is all about baby steps at Spurs.

Maddison started a game for the first time since May 2025, the Europa League semi-final against Bodo/Glimt.



And Dejan Kulusevski, himself injured that month, was back in a squad for the first time since then and welcomed like a hero as a late sub.

Their club has been through the mill while they have been away.

Three managers have graced the home dugout in that time, there is a new chairman in charge and Spurs have been the butt of almost every joke going.

This win is just their second league victory at home this calendar year, and there have been as many Beyonce concerts in this ground as their six Premier League wins since November 2024. There is a long way to go yet.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But just as a night on the lash, organised by De Zerbi, helped Spurs to safety last season, it appears his dose of sun has done the trick this time around.

The Italian wanted some time away with the squad having complained that their pre-season trip to Australia was not much use, with time difference troubles and too many commercial duties.

Whatever they got up to in Spain, the squad will surely be pushing for a return to the Costa del Sol.

Spurs fans have become accustomed to seeing their side race out of the traps before quickly falling away in games this season.

So they would have been doubly depressed at the sight of De Zerbi’s winless men getting off to a nervy start.



Tosin Adarabioyo had been brought into the backline to make his first start since joining from Chelsea, but was beaten after 13 seconds, allowing Brandon Thomas-Asante to get a shot off.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto caused early trouble, with Antonin Kinsky fumbling a cross before Jan Paul van Hecke diverted the winger’s shot over the bar with his face.

Tottenham needed settling – and something to lift the mood. Maddison enjoys the spotlight and was certainly happy to rise to the challenge of being Spurs’ saviour.



The former Coventry player has watched on largely from the outside as Tottenham have endured so much hardship during his long absence.

But back in the starting XI, having played just 85 league minutes from the bench this season before last night, he was there, ordering and orchestrating.

With others stuck playing overly careful and cautious football, Maddison went for the spectacular and changed the mood.

After Mohammed Kudus twice beat a dizzy Jay Dasilva, he laid off for Maddison to sweep a peach of a strike into the far corner from the edge of the box.

The stadium erupted, Maddison beamed and every single outfield player joined his celebration.



It was emotional for the No10, his first goal since that last game in May 2025, and his first in the Premier League for 611 days, but also blessed relief for an entire club and the fanbase, whose voices grew noticeably louder.

Maddison continued to try and cause trouble, bending a cross just wide of the far post from the left, but his team-mates largely remained stodgy, stuck within themselves despite being up against a Coventry side who were offering little.

If there was a rousing half-time speech to free his players, it did not work.



Rather than open up going forwards, they quickly fell apart at the back after the restart, allowing Rudoni a leveller both sides would have been rather embarrassed by.

Rudoni strode down the left before driving inside, where he exchanged a smart one-two with Caleb Yirenkyi.

The following one-two, with a cross blasted at Thomas-Asante, who sent a header straight into the ground before Rudoni collected the loose ball, was rather more industrial.

But neither Rudoni nor boss Frank Lampard will have cared about how it looked when he fired through Kinsky.

Having sounded carefree after Maddison’s fine opener, the Tottenham supporters were ridden with angst and anger once again. It was a story they had seen unfold too many times before.



But this time, the XI on the pitch wanted to deliver a twist, write a new ending.

Andy Robertson fed Marmoush, who with a show of strength and perhaps a prod to the face of Milan van Ewijk, spun his man and whipped a fine finish into the far corner.

Fans experienced elation again at long last, with Kulusevski’s entrance and Davies’ late, low strike, adding to a party mood. The challenge now is to ensure it lasts.
