World.title: Findings from fatal CFB Wainwright fire investigation will be made public, top commander says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's top military commander committed on Monday to publicly releasing the findings of the investigation into the fire at the training range in Wainwright, Alta., which claimed the lives of four soldiers and left dozens of others injured.

There are three separate parallel investigations underway — two military and one civilian, said Gen. Jennie Carignan, the chief of the defence staff, in her first interview since a sudden brush fire swept through an exercise area at the sprawling military base.

Speaking on CBC's Power & Politics, Carignan said the military's investigative service is on the scene and there will be a board of inquiry (BOI), a technical investigation into the circumstances, as well as a civilian coroner's investigation by the province of Alberta.

The military is under no obligation to proactively release its findings. Normally, the board reports to the defence chief and the minister. In fact, it took public pressure for the board of inquiry investigation into the 2004 fatal fire aboard HMCS Chicoutimi to be made public.

Carignan said she was drafting the terms of reference, which set out the scope of the inquiry, for the board, but she couldn't commit on Monday to saying when the review panel will convene.

"We want to make sure that the board of inquiry starts on firm ground," Carignan told host David Cochrane, referring to the instructions she is preparing.

"I want to make sure that we also make the findings public once the board of inquiry is completed."

WATCH | Carignan speaks about training near brush fires: 'Normal' for Armed Forces to conduct training near fires: top military commander | Duration closed caption 0:59 Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan says that Canadian Forces personnel on the ground determine whether or not to continue training. She spoke with Power & Politics following the deadly fire on Saturday at CFB Wainwright.

Separately, Carignan said the Canadian Forces fire marshal is reviewing what happened. The RCMP have been asked to assist Alberta's medical examiner.

There were tributes in the House of Commons on Monday to the soldiers killed in what military officials describe as a swift-moving brush fire that overwhelmed members of C Company 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry who were using the Wainwright training range to prepare for deployment to Latvia.

The military said the brush fire was already burning when a sudden change in the wind drove it toward roughly 84 troops who were practising hand grenade throwing and small group attacks at one portion of the exercise field.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark all died in the fire. Another 39 troops were injured, 19 of them critically.

Carignan said it's normal for troops to continue training even if there's a brush fire nearby because it adds to the realistic conditions they'd face in combat. There are however, she said, limits and safety is paramount.

"The folks on the ground make a determination on how this could affect training, and mitigation measures are put in place," Carignan said. "To address this, we also have firefighting equipment or support on site to respond to potential fires, of course, depending on the magnitude."

Military regulations dictate the range safety officer makes the call on whether an exercise can continue and under what circumstances.

Retired colonel Rory Fowler, a former military lawyer now in private practice, suggested the public should temper its expectations about what it will see in the board of inquiry report, particularly if there is blame to be had.

"BOIs are not supposed to investigate wrongdoing," Fowler said. "In fact, a little over 10 years ago, [the regulation] was amended to remove an article that directed that a BOI was to identify if anyone was at fault."

Fowler said if there is blame, it might be handled through the military justice system — or disciplinary system.

PHOTOS | The aftermath of the fire:

"Unlike a coroner's inquest, the underlying purpose of a BOI is not to serve a public purpose other than the governance of the Canadian Armed Forces," Fowler said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, after paying tribute to the fallen soldiers, said he has confidence in the system.

"The military wants to get to the bottom of what exactly happened," Carney said. "There's a few processes that we'll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary."

In his House of Commons remarks, Carney committed to giving the military "all the resources that they need" to investigate.

WATCH | Carney on the military investigation: Carney says military 'aided by' feds and RCMP to investigate CFB Wainwright fire | Duration closed caption 0:39 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Canadian military has 'started a comprehensive investigation' into what caused the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright to get answers 'as expeditiously and transparently as possible.'

Military law expert and retired colonel Michel Drapeau said Carignan's commitment to releasing the findings is important, but only "a first step."

Drapeau, who has represented families at a number of boards of inquiry over the past 20 years, said there needs to be more transparency as the process unfolds.

He'd like to see a commitment to proceedings being held in public where the families can attend.

"National security is not at stake here," Drapeau said. "The family has a right to know, and the Canadian public has a right to know."

Drapeau has long advocated for an independent body — such as an inspector general — that would conduct arm's-length investigations.

"There is merit to the argument that the Canadian Forces should have in place a mechanism for true public inquiry," Fowler said.

World.title: Alberta referendum results expected late after 106 polling stations slow to open
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Polls are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. across the province for the final day to vote in Alberta's historic 2026 referendum.

Referendum day: What you need to know

More than 100 polling stations failed to open on time for referendum voting Monday, which means those stations will stay open late and results will be delayed.

Elections Alberta released a list of stations and their new closing hours late Monday afternoon. The latest polling station to close will be Edmonton’s Westminster School, which will remain open until 10 p.m. MT. Polls were scheduled to close at 8 p.m.

Elections staff said anyone in line when the station closes will be allowed to vote, and results will not be released until after all polls are closed.

The delays frustrated some voters.

Steve Koristka said he arrived 10 minutes early to vote in Calgary's Rocky Ridge neighbourhood on Monday, only to wait more than an hour before the station opened. By the time it did, he said 20 people were in line and several voters had already left.

“You could see people getting frustrated, and coming up and banging on the door and shaking the handles,” said Koristka.

“I chose to stick around because this election is important for everyone to get out there and have their say.”

At another polling station, at Westminster School in Edmonton, voters in line told CBC News the polling station closed down shortly after 9 a.m. It still wasn't open at 11:30 a.m.

Myrna Doiron said she came at 9:30 a.m. to vote, but wasn't able to finish until around noon. Those in line were told the station had to be set up again and rechecked.

She said she waited because she believes it's important.

"I've been taught: you vote and state your opinion. If you really want a say, you should vote."

Edmonton voter Myrna Doiron arrived at the Westminster School polling station around 9:30 a.m. and found it temporarily closed. (Mrinali Anchan/CBC)

There were also reports of polling stations running out of ballots in Maskwacis, comprised of four First Nations south of Edmonton. In an email to CBC News, Elections Alberta said it was seeing strong turnout at that location and has couriers delivering ballots.

Albertans are voting in Monday's referendum on whether the province should pursue a second binding referendum to separate from Canada, and on nine other questions about immigration and the Constitution.

Elections Alberta workers will begin counting advanced voting and special ballots at 5 p.m. The provincial election agency has said 1.3 million people voted prior to referendum day via mail-in and advanced ballots.

Elections Alberta say enough staff hired

On Monday, Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan said the organization hired 47,000 elections officers, which she called a “fantastic response” after launching a recruitment campaign ahead of the referendum.

The agency had hoped to hire 60,000.

“We’re really happy with the response and with the number of people we have,” Hanrahan told CBC Radio’s Calgary Eyeopener on Monday.

“This is enough people for us to run the voting places and the count.”

LISTEN | Elections Alberta on what to expect for referendum day: Calgary Eyeopener 7:07 Referendum 2026: Elections Alberta It's finally referendum day across the province. Hear from Elections Alberta for what your need to know about casting your ballots if you haven't voted yet.

Elections Alberta will first count Question 10, on separation, before it counts questions one through nine.

Its online results page will go live once all the voting stations are confirmed to be closed, Hanrahan said.

Short wait to vote early at some stations

Voters at Hinton’s lone polling station, located at the Hinton Centre, reported short wait times and no lines Monday morning. The parking lot outside is full of cars, but voters were moving in and out of the centre quickly.

Simon Chislett said that voting took under five minutes, and that the process was straightforward.

“No matter which way everybody votes, I think everybody has to be heard, no matter what," he said.

Brent Bertsch didn't have issues either. He voted in a historic church on the edge of downtown Medicine Hat.

"It was perfect, professional, polite, courteous and all good," he said. "I'm glad it's finally the day to do it. I'll be happier when we get results."

Lisa Quakenbush, left, and Kendall Alcorn visited a polling station at the Southern Alberta Ethnic Association in Lethbridge. They faced no lineups while voting over the lunch hour. (Stephen Tipper/CBC)

Outside a polling station in Lethbridge at noon, Kendall Alcorn said he found the voting process easy. He’s concerned about Alberta's future and growing polarization.

“Even amongst my own family, with my adult relatives, this is a topic we can’t discuss because it will sometimes turn into throwing fists," he said. "I don’t understand that strict division, because in the end we all want what's best for Alberta. We just have different ways of approaching that.”

In Calgary, Shannon Shirt cast a ballot in the southwest Windsor Park neighbourhood around 9:20 a.m., and even without a voter card, faced little trouble as a registered voter.

"I'm feeling relieved now,” said Shirt. "It was really quick."

Tearra Johnston visited the polling station at the First Assembly Church on Elbow Drive Monday morning. She was relieved there were no lineups. She moved houses recently and staff helped her fill out a declaration form so she can vote in her new neighbourhood. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Tearra Johnston voted at First Assembly Church in Calgary on Monday morning. She said her professor at Mount Royal University gave students the day off to vote.

“I think he just wants to make sure that we go out and vote, and just do it. But it was really easy,” said Johnston.

She added that earlier this year, some of her classmates thought of the referendum as a joke. But quite a few have now changed their minds to take the potential consequences of the referendum questions more seriously, she said, and planned to vote on Monday.

Over in Calgary's Riverbend neighbourhood, Chané Neveling brought her mug of coffee along when she went to vote. She said she read all 10 questions carefully as she voted, even though she had researched them before.

“From start to finish, 10 minutes. We didn’t wait at all. But come noon or after work, I think people are going to come.”

A steady flow of people stopped by the polling station at St. Damien School in Calgary's Dover neighbourhood Monday morning, including from left to right, Andrew Pawelko, Yohannes Yohannes and Danara Robson. Both Yohannes and Robson had the wrong polling station location and were directed to a new location a short distance away. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

In Calgary’s Dover neighbourhood, 19-year-old Danara Robson took the day off her retail job to make sure she had time to vote. She checked online where to vote and entered her home address, but was sent to the wrong polling station.

“It’s not a huge deal, just a short walk. But a little inconvenient,” she said.

She said she was nervous about the results, hoping people would come out and make their position known. It was her first time voting.

As for the results, some voters say they’ll be checking for results tomorrow morning; others will be refreshing the news sites and Elections Alberta results page tonight.

“Generally, I’ll just wait until the next day unless my mom starts sending me updates,” said Andrew Pawelko, who added he got to the voting station just before the lines started to build.

How to follow the results

For live results and analysis on referendum night, watch Alberta Votes: Referendum Night starting at 7 p.m. MT on CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton, CBC Gem, CBC News YouTube, CBC News App, CBC News Network, and listen live on CBC Radio One.

Referendum results will also be covered live on the CBC Edmonton and CBC Calgary websites.

Then, tune into Alberta Morning on Oct. 20 starting at 5:30 a.m. MT on CBC Radio One and CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton.

World.title: Cop killer Curtis Dagenais returns to Saskatoon courtroom to argue about fate of his truck
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been more than 17 years since a jury sat in courtroom No. 1 at Saskatoon Court of King's Bench for Curtis Dagenais's murder trial.

Since then, the courthouse has been expanded and renovated. Its name changed too, after the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

The third-floor courtroom itself looks a little different — the jury's seats were relocated to the other side of the room and the windows no longer have an exterior view — but it was there, in March 2009, that a jury convicted Dagenais of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder, for killing RCMP constables Robin Cameron and Marc Bourdages and wounding Const. Michelle Knopp.

He shot the officers on July 6, 2006, after Cameron and Bourdages chased him down rural roads before ramming his truck and dying in the shootout that followed. Knopp arrived moments later.

Dagenais appealed his convictions to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, which dismissed his appeal in a ruling issued in 2012.

For the last 20 years, the 1986 blue GMC 1500 truck that Dagenais was driving has been sitting in storage. Through an oversight, the Crown didn't apply to have it forfeited until years later.

For prior hearings on the application, Dagenais appeared via video link from the Saskatchewan Penitentiary, where he is serving his three life sentences. He opposes the Crown's application, saying the truck holds evidence that proves his innocence, which he still maintains, and that its parts have some monetary value.

A photo from Curtis Dagenais's trial shows the RCMP vehicle that hit the side of his blue truck. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

On Monday, Dagenais was transported to the courthouse to appear in person, representing himself after he did not get a lawyer.

At first, the deputy sheriff seated the 61-year-old in the prisoner's box, but when Justice Daryl Labach arrived and opened court, he asked Dagenais to come forward to the long tables where the lawyers sit, and for his leg shackles to be removed.

He then patiently explained the law to Dagenais and repeatedly asked him if there are any reasons why his truck shouldn't be forfeited.

Dagenais gave a variety of answers, ranging from comments about ballistics and evidence, to comments about the rarity of parts for that make of truck.

He characterized the actions of the Crown as "kicking me in the shins" and taking away "another few dollars" that he can't use to defend himself.

Crown prosecutor Scott Bartlett, one of the two Crown lawyers who prosecuted Dagenais at the 2009 murder trial, repeated the arguments he has made previously , that the truck is offence-related property and should be forfeited.

Labach is scheduled to give his decision on Dec. 4.

World.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.

That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.

"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.

However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.

Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.

"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.

"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

Industry concentrated in Quebec

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.

More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

World.title: Calgary Opera replaces performer who unfurled Palestinian flag during Tosca bow
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Calgary Opera has replaced a performer who unfurled a Palestinian flag during the curtain call of the political opera Tosca.

On Friday, the bass singer Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega held up the flag at the end of Giacomo Puccini's drama about love and betrayal during political upheaval in Napoleonic Rome.

In a statement issued Sunday, the Calgary Opera called the action "unexpected and unauthorized," adding that individual political protest violated company policy.

The institution apologized for the "discomfort and distress" some may have felt and said Sanchez-Ortega's role will be performed by another artist for the remainder of the shows.

Sanchez-Ortega played a character named Cesare Angelotti, an escaped political prisoner.

In a post to Instagram, Sanchez-Ortega wrote that he had "no regrets" and that "this is the state of cultural institutions in Canada."

The Calgary Opera and Sanchez-Ortega did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In its statement about the Oct. 16 performance, the Opera said individual political protest contravenes its "responsibility to create a more connected, caring and civil society through shared artistic experiences."

Sanchez-Ortega said he holds no resentment.

"After the theatre, [political or otherwise] we all have to go home, and look at ourselves in the mirror," Sanchez-Ortega continued in his statement.

"It was my honour to play the role of Angelotti, an escaped political prisoner."

World.title: 'You Can See Everything' sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You Can See Everything is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled.

Maybe that's why so many people rushed to theatres on opening weekend to see the nearly three-hour documentary about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Whatever the reason, the film made more than $15 million US in ticket sales during its debut weekend — the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.

It's a considerable achievement, considering You Can See Everything had a limited release at just 855 theatres in Canada and the U.S.

The reviews following its debut were overwhelmingly positive: rated 99 per cent fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, and scoring a 4.8 on Letterboxd, making it the highest-rated movie in the site's history. (Both those ratings have come down since then, but only slightly.)

As the five-star reviews started pouring in online, so too did the comments: "My mouth was agape for basically the entire last two hours," from Letterboxd user James (Schaffrillas).

"Just an absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream of a documentary," said user vgoodatkissing.

You can read everything — no spoilers here

The documentary's premise is straightforward. A film crew, including dual director-producers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, briefly move in with Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their children, and document their lives, 34 days before she is due to start serving an extended prison sentence for fraud.

Toronto film critic Teri Hart says watching You Can See Everything in theatres was a visceral experience.

"People were actually physically leaning into the screen," she told CBC News. "There were gasps at times; people applauded at the end of the movie, lots of laughter."

"You leave this movie and you don't know if you want to talk about Nathan Fielder, if you want to talk about Elizabeth Holmes, if you want to talk about Billy or if you want to talk 'where did they put the camera.'"

The trailer gives audiences a glimpse into Fielder and Holmes's unusual dynamic.

"Nathan Fielder is not afraid of awkward. Nathan Fielder is not afraid of asking questions in a way that is unlike anybody else," said Hart. "He has a level of provocateur, I think, that is so fascinating to watch.

Boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documented Elizabeth Holmes's life during the 34 days before she was sent to prison for defrauding investors. (A24)

"Place him with Elizabeth Holmes, who also has a unique way of communicating, and you have magic."

Indeed, the documentary delivers on the intense and deliberately uncomfortable interviews that Fielder, a Canadian who was born in Vancouver, became known for on shows like Nathan for You, as well as his paradigm-shifting approach to the truth.

Hart calls the documentary a theatrical experience few people will have ever had — one that may lead audiences to question what we think of as the truth.

Another win for A24

You Can See Everything was distributed and partly produced by A24, the same company behind some of this year's most talked-about films, including Olivia Wilde's The Invite, the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and the record-breaking horror Backrooms.

"A24 is a distributor that has a brand. And that brand is — to my mind — working with auteurs, working with writer-directors or even just directors that really have a specific vision and have a strong, strong artistry associated with them," said Hart.

WATCH | CBC's Jackson Weaver has more on the documentary: Nathan Fielder searches for truth in You Can See Everything | Duration 2:45 Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes. The documentary about the jailed Theranos founder examines the absurd nature of truth.

She said that's helped A24 make a splash, as the company pushes back against the general consensus that Hollywood has no new ideas.

As a movie lover, Hart said she is grateful for anything that gets people back in the theatres and talking about what they've seen. She says You Can See Everything is a great example of that.

"They're, like, shocked and surprised or walking out of the theater with all kinds of thoughts and ideas and questions. Because let's be clear, this movie does not tie anything up with a nice pretty bow. It does not. So people have questions.

"And I think that that is a really thrilling experience for people to share with strangers. "

World.title: DFO searching for injured whale struck by B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Marine conservation officers are searching for an injured humpback whale that was struck by a B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound on Sunday.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said the collision involving the Queen of Surrey vessel happened between Grace Point and Keats Island.

It said two humpbacks were observed in close proximity to the ferry at the time and one was struck.

Passengers aboard the ferry, which was sailing from Langdale on the Sunshine Coast to Horseshoe Bay, said they felt the whale being struck and watched it in distress behind the vessel.

B.C. Ferries said it takes incidents like the whale strike on Sunday very seriously. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

Aspen Wing was travelling with her son when she said they felt the collision at 1:33 p.m. PT.

She said a group of girls shouted that a whale had been nearby, and her son spotted the injured humpback off the stern of the vessel.

"A lot of people on the ferry were really distraught and upset by what they were witnessing," Wing said.

She recorded a video of the whale splashing in the water and said she watched the whale blow blood into the air.

Aspen Wing says she saw the whale blowing blood into the air after it was struck. (Aspen Wing)

"To watch that animal in obvious distress was really disheartening and upsetting for a lot of us, I'm still kind of sick to my stomach about seeing it," Wing said.

Crews searching for humpback whale

B.C. Ferries said in a statement that it is deeply concerned about the incident and potential impact on the whale.

"Based on initial reports, the whale surfaced directly in front of the vessel, leaving the crew with very little time to react," said spokesperson Kit Billings.

Billings said the immediate focus has been on "responding to the incident, notifying the appropriate authorities and gathering accurate information about what happened, including the potential impact on the whale."

DFO said in a statement that B.C. Ferries is cooperating.

WATCH | What is B.C. Ferries doing to prevent whale strikes?: What is B.C. Ferries doing to prevent whale strikes? | Duration closed caption 3:41



Canada's Marine Mammal Regulations state that any vessel operator that’s involved in contact with a whale must immediately notify DFO.

"DFO is reviewing the situation and will work to identify the whale and assess its condition," DFO said.

A crew from DFO is in Howe Sound on Monday trying to locate the whale.

Fatal whale strikes

Almost one year ago, on Oct. 23, 2025, a humpback whale was struck by a whale-watching company off Keats Island in Howe Sound, near Sunday's incident.

A few days later, a four-year-old humpback whale washed up dead in the same area.

A humpback whale was found dead and floating in the water off Keats Island on Oct. 26, 2025. (Alex Cole)

DFO identified the dead humpback whale found at Keats Island as BCY1464, also known as Wisp, and said there was an active investigation.

Whales have been hit in other coastal areas recently, too.

A humpback whale was struck by a Hullo Ferries vessel off Vancouver, a person driving a Sea-Doo struck a grey whale near English Bay, and a humpback whale was found dead after being reported hit by a B.C. Ferries vessel in Wright Sound.

"It's a busy wildlife corridor, and especially at this time of year, there have been times I've been on that ferry, and I've seen 11 humpbacks like on that one sailing," Wing said.

She feels the communication on Sunday could have been handled better.

"There was no announcement made on the ferry. There was no attempt to like … it didn't feel like there was a slowdown," Wing said. "It was disturbing."

Push for slower vessel speeds

Jackie Hildering with the Marine Education and Research Society said Howe Sound, where the strike happened Sunday, is well-known to be frequented by humpbacks from October to December.

"This has to be about prevention," Hindering said. "We want very much, [for] these tragedies to lead to positive change."

The society is pushing for vessels to be limited to slower speeds in whale habitats.

In June, the Northern Expedition route, where a humpback whale was fatally struck in Wright Sound, adopted a travel speed of 10 knots, down from the previous 18 knots.

Hildering said that speed could still cause a fatality, but is far less likely to.

The Queen of Surrey was travelling at 16 knots at the time of the strike Sunday, B.C. Ferries spokesperson Lilian Kim said in an email, and typically travels at between 19 to 19.5 knots in that area, depending on conditions.

Hildering said she's working to determine which whale was struck.

"It is extraordinarily unlikely that a humpback would have survived that," she said.

World.title: What health-care promises have B.C. parties made ahead of the provincial election?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C.'s provincial parties are sharing their priorities for health care ahead of the Oct. 24 election, with promises ranging from more recruitment and accelerated training to new health centres.

Several changes have been introduced to tackle B.C.’s health-care challenges in recent years, including a new family doctor payment model as an alternative to the older fee-for-service system, and a streamlined process for internationally trained physicians to work in the province.

The B.C. NDP also launched the Health Connect Registry , an online portal linking patients to care providers, and expanded pharmacists’ ability to treat minor ailments and prescribe contraceptives.

The party says it’s attached 700,000 more people to a family doctor or nurse practitioner in the last three years.

But challenges remain as staffing shortages force regular ER closures in some communities and more than 1.2 million British Columbians remain without a family doctor.

So what are some changes parties are proposing for health care this provincial election?

B.C. Conservatives

The B.C. Conservatives say they are standing firm on keeping B.C.'s system universal and publicly funded, despite the NDP warning the Conservatives will move towards health-care privatization.

"I want a fully public system that everyone in this province can access, said leader Lorne Doerkson at the leaders’ debate on Wednesday.

The party says within its first 100 days, it will launch an expert commission to bring proven solutions from other public systems to B.C.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says he supports a public health-care system and is focused on hiring and retaining more doctors. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

On Thursday, the party pledged a new women and children’s hospital in Surrey, so families no longer have to travel to Vancouver for care.

It's also vowing to keep emergency rooms open, hire and retain more doctors and nurses, and speed up international credential recognition for Canadians who studied abroad.

The party says it will support rural medical practices at risk of closing, and invest $50 million into what it is calling an emergency fund.

" We will protect health care funding, recruit and retain more doctors and nurses, and cut wait times. Your health card will always be all you need," the party said in a statement.

B.C. NDP

B.C. NDP Leader David Eby said he is committed to public health care and has echoed the shortage of health-care workers as a major challenge.

"We’ve got to recruit more doctors. That’s why we are tripling our recruitment of American health-care workers," Eby said at the leaders' debate, noting 800 U.S. workers have been hired so far.

The party said it will launch an accelerated training program for international medical graduates already living in B.C. and add 1,000 more training seats for nurses, nurse practitioners, allied health workers and care aides, including a 20 per cent increase in nursing seats.

B.C. NDP Leader David Eby's priorities include tripling the recruitment of U.S. health-care workers and creating regional surgical waitlists. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

The party is proposing new regional waitlists that offer patients the earliest surgery date possible in their region or, if they prefer, to still choose a specific surgeon or hospital.

Currently, surgery wait times can depend on the surgeon patients are referred to, the NDP said.

Promises also include eight new MRI machines and 10 CT scanners, 20 additional team-based primary care clinics, and the opening of Canada’s first perinatal mental health unit at B.C. Women’s Hospital.

"We will pay for these actions by asking the top four per cent of earners in B.C. to pitch in a little bit more. Ninety-six per cent of people will see no change in their taxes," the party said.

B.C. Greens

The B.C. Green Party is pledging funding that establishes community health centres in every riding in the province.

"That would mean you could walk into your neighbourhood and you would have access to a physician, a nurse practitioner and imaging all under the same roof," said leader Emily Lowan at the leaders' debate.

B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan has pledged funding for community health centres in every riding. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

The party’s platform online also includes increased funding for nurses in the public system to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios and end reliance on private agency nurses.

It also wants to centralize referrals for surgeries, and non-surgical and pre-surgical care rather than using distributed lists.

CentreBC

CentreBC has set a goal of providing a family doctor or nurse practitioner to anyone wanting one by the end of 2031.

Leader Elenore Sturko’s promises include 600 more nurse practitioner positions by 2030 and 100 more medical residency spots by the same year.

"A family doctor or nurse practitioner team for everyone who wants one, shorter waits that people can see for themselves, treatment for mental health and addiction when people ask for it. We are committed to public health care, not private pay," the party said in a statement to CBC News.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko's promises include adding more nurse practitioners and doubling B.C.’s assessment program for internationally trained family doctors, (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The party wants to increase the assessment program for internationally trained family doctors, from 96 to 200 positions a year by 2028.

To help keep emergency rooms open, CentreBC is pitching an ER Accountability Act to cut unplanned closures in half by 2029/30 while allocating $25 million a year to stabilize rural ERs.

Pledges also include the creation of a single public health dashboard showing surgeries, scans, specialists and ER statuses by hospital and region, five more MRI machines, and a new children’s hospital for Surrey and Langley with construction starting in 2031.

OneBC

OneBC is currently the only party platform listing support for private health care alongside fully-funded public health care.

The party wants to shift administration and HR spending to front-line employees.

It wants to repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act (HPOA) , which regulates health professions in B.C.

OneBC says it would support private health care alongside fully-funded public health care. Leader Dallas Brodie is pictured. (Mike Zimmer/CBC)

OneBC says it also wants to adopt the findings of the Allison Inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries to help shape B.C.’s vaccine protocols.

The inquiry, held in September by Conservative MP Dean Allison, did not hear from Health Canada and was unsanctioned by the federal government.

The inquiry's website says, "it will not make findings of fact or reach conclusions. The focus is to listen to Canadians."

Voters can have their say on health care in B.C. on Oct. 24.

World.content: Writes Ivison: “Earlier this month, I wrote that universities across the country are finally getting together to address the epidemic of antisemitism that has broken out on campuses across the country. I referred to a review of antisemitic incidents at Toronto Metropolitan University undertaken by retired justice Mary Lou Benotto and delivered to TMU last August. World.title: Alberta votes on leaving Canada: 1.3 million ballots cast in advance; record turnout expected today
World.content:
Article content

The referendum, which includes one question on proposed separation and another nine on various other constitutional matters, is expected to draw record numbers to the ballot box. Elections Alberta estimates record turnout as high as 85 per cent, compared with an average of just over 50 per cent in recent general elections. According to the agency, 1,356,873 voters, or 43.1 per cent of eligible voters, have already cast advanced ballots or special ballots before Monday. That compares with 809,988 advanced and special ballots cast in the 2023 election, or 27.5 per cent of eligible voters.

Estonia is followed at the top of the rankings by Latvia and New Zealand in the rankings.

World.title: Scott Stinson: Ontario’s electricity-import deal with U.S. undercuts Doug Ford’s energy tough talk
World.content:
Article content

The new deal to import electricity to Ontario would seem to undermine any future sabre-rattling that Ford might do on the energy file, although there are several caveats to be noted here. The Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) is, as the name suggests, not making decisions at Ford’s behest. And its contract with Alpha Generation is a short-term arrangement to provide electricity in case Ontario needs it during the cold winter months and while the Pickering nuclear plant is undergoing a refurbishment. In the days since the Alpha contract was announced, the IESO said that Ontario will still be a net exporter of electricity to the United States and that it exported seven times as much as it imported last year. The new contract is about increasing the flexibility of the provincial power grid during the high-peak demand of the winter months.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.
