World.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warns Germany is falling behind in AI race
World.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warned that Germany is falling behind in the artificial intelligence race as he spoke to members of the media in London last week.

 

Despite its strong potential and wealth of talent, Huang believes progress in Europe is being blocked by too much hesitation and analysis and has called on policymakers to be quicker to put AI into practice.

In response to concerns about the country's technological competitiveness, the German government has been planning closer cooperation with the US company.

At the Invest in Germany investment summit in Berlin this week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Huang are set to unveil a joint AI pact intended to speed up the integration of AI products across German industry.

The German government is preparing to commit hundreds of millions of Euros to the initiative.

Alongside start-up Black Forest Labs, around 10 established German companies including Siemens and Audi are expected to take part.

The partnership builds on the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models initiative, an alliance dedicated to developing powerful open-source AI systems.

The funding is to be used primarily to buy computing capacity in Deutsche Telekom's Industrial AI Cloud, which is equipped with Nvidia's latest Blackwell hardware.

The government hopes the investment will make Germany a more attractive destination for innovation and technological development.

On Tuesday, senior international executives, investors and government officials at the Invest in Germany summit will discuss new investment in Germany, focusing on artificial intelligence, energy and infrastructure, as well as the competitiveness of the German economy.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV holds call with Zelenskyy, Vatican says
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV held a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy late on Monday afternoon, just days after he spoke with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, the Vatican said.

 

During his conversation with Putin, the pontiff had called for a humanitarian truce in Oleshky, a city under Russian siege, to allow food and medical aid to arrive and for civilians to be evacuated safely.

According to a statement from the Vatican's Press Office, Oleshky was also the focus of his talks with Zelenskyy.

"During the conversation, the Holy Father drew attention to the serious situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, referring to the request for a humanitarian truce already submitted to the President of the Russian Federation," the statement reads. "The Holy Father expressed the hope that the cooperation of both sides will allow food and medical aid to reach the city and ensure the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population."

Ukraine and Russia are in the process of finalising the details of a civilian evacuation in the city and six nearby settlements, the Ukrainian Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has announced.

Chicago-born Leo has kept in regular contact with Zelenskyy.

In May 2025, Leo held an initial telephone call with the Ukrainian leader, in which Zelenskyy invited him to Kyiv and reiterated his country's readiness for further negotiations.

The two met later that month, immediately after the mass marking the beginning of the pope's pontificate in St Peter's Square.

They met again on 9 July 2025 for a private audience at Villa Barberini, the papal residence in Castel Gandolfo, where they discussed the possibility of hosting future peace talks at the Vatican.

And once again on 9 December, again in Castel Gandolfo, to discuss the need to keep dialogue open, questions surrounding prisoners of war and the return of Ukrainian children deported to Russia.

On 3 April this year, the pope again spoke to Zelenskyy as Russian drone and missile attacks ramped up across Ukraine.

He expressed his solidarity with the Ukrainian people, underlining the urgency of humanitarian aid, the release of prisoners and a negotiated peace.

World.title: Video: Priest dies after cross falls on him during Mass in Ecuador
World.content:
Ecuadorian priest Patricio Sánchez died after a large cross fell on him while he was celebrating Mass at a church in Guayaquil on Saturday evening.

 

Footage captured the moment the cross came loose from the wall behind the altar and struck Sánchez as he addressed the congregation.

The service was being streamed live on social media. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil later confirmed his death and expressed its condolences to the religious congregation he belonged to.

A memorial Mass was held at the church on Sunday, attended by clergy and parishioners.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo suspended for 30 days after quitting Portugal camp
World.content:
Portugal legend Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) after leaving an international camp last month.

 

In addition to the ban, Ronaldo will have to pay a fine of €255.

According to a ruling by the association's disciplinary committee, part of the player’s suspension has already been served, as he had already been suspended.

Ronaldo, who now plays his club football for Saudi side Al-Nassr, began his punishment on 1 October, leaving 11 days left to serve. That means he could be available for the national team’s upcoming matches against Denmark on 14 November and Wales on 17 November.

'Mitigating circumstances'

The ruling said Ronaldo had asked that "mitigating circumstances be taken into account," in particular his "lack of any disciplinary record in the current season and the previous three seasons, provision of services of relevance to football, commendations for sporting merit and contribution to establishing the material truth."

"With regard to the mitigating circumstances of providing services of relevance to football and commendations for sporting merit, the defendant Cristiano Ronaldo submitted his sporting CV, including the awards and recognitions he has received over the course of his career," the document reads.

It adds that, in terms of "contribution to establishing the material truth," the player referred to the statement published on his Instagram page on 6 October.

Related Cristiano Ronaldo suspended by Portuguese FA for leaving training camp

The ruling sets out in detail the sequence of events after Ronaldo left the training camp.

On 30 September, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United star walked out of a camp before a training session at Parken Stadium in Copenhagen.

The player is said to have left without notifying anyone from the FPF or the squad in advance.

The document states that the player informed FPF President Pedro Proença of his decision by phone, saying that he did not feel in the right frame of mind to play.

"During the aforementioned telephone conversation, the defendant player informed the president of the FPF that he was not in an emotional condition to remain with the National Team at the training camp," the disciplinary committee noted.

Media coverage

In assessing the case, the committee acknowledged Ronaldo's services to football and his multiple awards. The body also took into account "his conduct after the events, in particular the remorse shown in the statement of 06.10.2026."

Even though certain mitigating factors were recognised, there were also aggravating elements in the FPF's view, notably the media coverage of the case and his role as team captain.

World.title: Rubio puts Trans-Caspian trade and critical minerals at centre of Central Asia talks
World.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.

 

The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.

A trade route to Europe

The Trans-Caspian route, also known as the Middle Corridor, connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey, bypassing Russia.

"We're going to enhance the infrastructure of the Trans Caspian trade route and give our partners more ways to reach American and Central Asian markets," Rubio said.

Washington also wants to diversify supplies of critical minerals used in energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The six governments identified mineral processing, energy cooperation and cybersecurity among their priorities, but the joint statement gave no figures for new infrastructure funding.

C5+1 ministerial meeting in Samarkand Uzbekistan Kylie Cooper/Pool Photo via AP

Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov proposed cooperation extending from mineral exploration to processing and local industrial clusters. He also called for closer links between the C5+1 diplomatic forum and the B5+1 business platform to involve companies in identifying projects.

The US push comes as the five Central Asian states maintain extensive economic ties with Russia and China. Speaking separately to Euronews in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington was seeking competition, not exclusivity.

"This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he told Euronews.

Bilateral talks with the five ministers

Rubio also held separate meetings with each of his Central Asian counterparts.

Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed trade, energy, critical minerals and technology with Rubio. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry said the US Secretary of State expressed interest in visiting the country after the G20 summit in Miami in December, although no date was announced.

The US State Department said they also discussed Kazakhstan's commitment to join the Abraham Accords, a US-backed framework for normalising relations with Israel.

Rubio also met Kyrgyzstan's Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev to discuss bilateral cooperation. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin raised trade, investment and regional security, according to his ministry.

Rubio held talks with Turkmenistan's Rashid Meredov, with the two countries preparing another round of political consultations in Ashgabat in November.

Uzbekistan and the US held the first session of their Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, covering trade, energy, technology and security. Following the talks, Foreign Minister Saidov signed the Artemis Accords in Rubio's presence, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to join the international framework for peaceful space exploration.

World.title: Lavrov backs Iran, hours after Trump says Russia doing 'very little' to help Tehran
World.content:
"I am confident that Iran's cause, like Russia's, is a just cause," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday at a joint press conference in Tehran with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi.

 

Lavrov accused Washington and Israel of launching what he described as an unprovoked military campaign against the country whilst reaffirming Moscow's commitment to continue supporting Tehran.

His remarks came hours after US President Donald Trump defended easing economic pressure on Moscow, arguing that further sanctions could jeopardise negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. He said he also wanted to ensure that Russia did not provide further support for Iran.

"Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

The US president said he did not want to risk driving Russia away from the negotiating table by imposing further economic pressure, despite criticism of his recent decision to waive some sanctions targeting Moscow.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote.

Moscow pledges continued support for Tehran

Lavrov said Russia remained willing to help find a diplomatic solution to the conflict between Iran and the US and Israel, which he characterised as a crisis caused by US and Israeli military action.

"We once again expressed our country's readiness to assist in finding mutually acceptable solutions to overcome this man-made crisis," he said, according to remarks reported by Kremlin-controlled media.

He welcomed Tehran's stated willingness to pursue diplomacy and called for a return to conditions that prevailed before the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, including restoring freedom of navigation and securing guarantees against renewed military action.

Lavrov also claimed Moscow had worked at the United Nations to prevent attempts to justify US and Israeli strikes against Iran, whilst providing humanitarian assistance, including medicines and regular food shipments.

Beyond diplomatic support, he made clear that Russia had no intention of abandoning its economic relationship with Tehran.

"Despite the difficult circumstances, Russia does not intend to abandon the implementation of agreements with Iran in the economic and investment spheres," Lavrov said.

Trump defends easing pressure on Moscow

In the same Truth Social post, Trump also directed fresh criticism at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusing him of damaging global diesel markets by continuing Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.

Trump claimed it was Kyiv's attacks and not Moscow's invasion or Washington's war on Iran that was hurting American farmers, businesses and consumers, as he praised Russia for agreeing to supply diesel to international markets at relatively low prices.

He also accused Zelenskyy of having little interest in ending the war, suggesting that Ukraine had missed earlier opportunities to negotiate a more favourable settlement.

His comments followed Washington's decision to waive a new sanctions package targeting Russia and to ease restrictions on Russian diesel, measures that have drawn criticism over their potential to provide Moscow with additional revenue whilst its war against Ukraine continues.

The White House has defended its approach as part of efforts to preserve peace negotiations and relieve pressure on global fuel markets.

World.title: Albanian PM Rama accuses anti-government protesters of crossing 'red line' amid violent demonstrations
World.content:
Edi Rama has accused some of those taking part in anti-government protests in Albania as having crossed a "red line" as demonstrations continued across the country on Monday.

 

Anti-government "Flamingo" protests have been ongoing in Albania for months amid calls for Rama to resign as prime minister, but clashes ramped up early last week as a student movement calling for action over high tuition fees launched fresh demonstrations.

"Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime, and this red line will be drawn firmly at this critical stage of our democratic development," Rama wrote in a post on social media on Monday.

"The rioters must and will bear the legal and financial consequences of their blindness," he continued, whilst also urging protesters to "distance themselves" from rioters.

"I and the governing majority are ready for dialogue with anyone except the rioters and political parties that do not distance themselves from violence," Rama added.

Violent clashes with police in recent days have seen protesters set buildings alight, hurl molotov cocktails, and shoot fireworks at officers, who have responded with rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas.

Hundreds of people, including police officers, have reportedly been injured in the violence.

Protesters throw fireworks at riot police during an anti-government protest in Tirana, Albania, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

"We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country," Leka Sina, a 22-year-old student, told the AFP news agency.

"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," Sina added.

Rama has sought to pin the blame for the unrest on foreign influence.

The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."

"Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values, to be respected and exercised peacefully," the Commission said in its statement. "In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process and making important progress on its EU path, grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner."

World.title: Trump signs order aimed at boosting women’s health research
World.content:
President Donald J. Trump, alongside First Lady Melania Trump, signed an executive order on Monday creating a Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House Women’s Health Task Force to close research gaps and modernise women's care.

 

“My Administration is committed to advancing women’s health and ensuring that medical research, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment reflect the highest quality scientific evidence, with the goal of improving health outcomes in all phases of life,” Trump said.

Speaking before the signing, Melania Trump called this “a transformative moment for women in America”.

“Previous generations fought for women's rights,” she continued. “Our generation will fight to discover the cure that will ensure that women can live their lives in health and to the fullest.”

The task force, which is meeting on the day the order was signed, is led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

They are tasked with coordinating women’s health policy across federal agencies. The task force's role is to translate research into evidence-based healthcare, improve prevention and access to care throughout women's lives, and identify policy and regulatory reforms to improve health outcomes.

In the meantime, the Women's Health Division will be established within the NIH over the next 90 days.

It will coordinate and expand research into understudied women’s health conditions, improve the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials, and accelerate the development of better diagnostics and treatments. It will also strengthen accountability for researchers to account for sex-based biological differences in their studies.

The goal, according to Melania Trump, is to improve women's health outcomes “in all phases of life,” using the advantages of new scientific discoveries, including super intelligence and advanced biotechnology and other therapies.

She outlined five priorities: directing research towards diseases that affect women “in a unique way”; using super intelligence to better understand women’s health and develop new treatments; speeding up access to new discoveries from labs to patients; ensuring access to all despite financial situation and addressing previously neglected conditions.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: France: Partial curfews issued in Paris, Nice after unrest
World.content:
Skip next section Are there more protests planned in France?

Rioting on the weekend overshadowed demonstrations against rising costs of living Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/picture alliance

The answer is yes. French unions have called for a new round of rallies on November 5.

Earlier on Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron blamed organized ultraleft groups for the rioting and looting on Saturday.

Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday that he was "fully resolved to restore public order."

He called for imposing localized curfews, as is in place overnight into Tuesday (see below), but said there was "no question" of imposing a full curfew on entire cities.

But Lecornu refused to rule out declaring a state of emergency, which would give authorities sweeping powers to restrict public gatherings.

World.title: Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
World.content:
A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

What do we know about the incident in Bulgaria?

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

What is the potential tie-in to a Polish sabotage case?

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver
World.content:
A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

Nividia's Jensen Huang, seen here in Davos in 2026, is to be a key guest Image: Mattias Nutt/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

Don't expect too much: Economic institute

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

World.title: Kenya: Cult leader guilty of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
World.content:
Preacher Paul Mackenzie was accused of encouraging his followers to starve themselves to death. He ran a Christian doomsday cult called the Good News International Church that claimed the end of the world was imminent.

A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday found self-proclaimed preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult as part of a notorious Christian starvation cult.

Mackenzie established his so-called Good News International Church in 2003 and was alleged to have incited his followers to starve themselves to death in order to "meet Jesus."

He was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group informed authorities.

Some of his acolytes were rescued but the subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of mass graves at a forest site near the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi.

Local media dubbed the case the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."

Shakahola Forest Massacre: What did the judge say?

"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," said Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache after a hearing which lasted over eight hours.

Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache delivered the verdict Image: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

The prosecution had said Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325 hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.

Post-mortems and police reports revealed that the children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said.

The court in Mombasa also heard that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

"This is a very, very important day," said Francis Wanje, 62, who lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, at Shakahola.

"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he told the AFP news agency, expressing anger over the government's initial inaction.

Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted of murder To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mackenzie facing even more Shakahola charges

Since the initial discovery of the graves, even more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400. The soaring death toll has even required sporadic pauses in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.

In January 2026, Mackenzie was charged over a further 52 bodies found at a nearby village.

There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.

He was arrested in 2017 on charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.

His sentencing will take place on November 6.

World.title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
World.content:
Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's government.

Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.

The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.

Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.

What will happen during the vote?

Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.

They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).

Results will then be published as they come in.

At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.

The 'no to the nine' campaign urges voters to refuse all nine proposal up for debate, not just the most significant one on setting the wheels in motion for a potential independence referendum Image: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

What has led to the vote?

Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.

The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.

Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.

Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.

"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.

PM Carney has been campaigning in Edmonton and elsewhere, trying to maximize turnout among those who favor staying part of Canada Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.

The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.

"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.

Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this.

Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner.

US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months.

When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario.

World.title: Can diplomacy stop another Ethiopia-Eritrea war?
World.content:
Ethiopia has installed a new administration in conflict-hit Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters. But tensions with Eritrea continue to raise fears of a wider regional war.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced an interim government in the country's northern Tigray region, giving it six months to prepare for regional elections and restore stability.

Abiy's announcement on Friday followed a military offensive launched in September by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups. They were ultimately forced to retreat and lost control of the region.

"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ​and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle ⁠of conflict," ​Abiy said in a statement posted on X.

Shishay Amare, the new mayor of the regional capital Mekelle, said they would "create the right conditions for elections by ensuring peace and stability across Tigray," as reported by French news agency Agence France-Presse.

"I am confident that this will be done within six months, according to our plan," Amare said, adding that their priorities included restoring peace, helping displaced residents return home, reopening markets and ensuring humanitarian assistance reached those in need.

Why relations with Eritrea matter

The fighting has revived concerns about a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Around 1 million people remain displaced from that conflict. The African Union has estimated that the war resulted in around 600,000 deaths from combat, famine and the collapse of healthcare.

The new administration faces unresolved disputes over political authority and territory, including western Tigray, which is claimed by both Tigray and neighboring Amhara state.

Egypt and Ethiopia have repeatedly clashed over the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which is located in northwestern Ethiopia and opened in 2025 Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ethiopia and Eritrea were once bitter enemies but signed a peace agreement in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the Tigray war. But the countries' relationship has since deteriorated.

Addis Ababa has accused Asmara of supporting Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory. Eritrea has denied the accusations.

Reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border have heightened concern, although the extent of any current deployment remains disputed.

Tsedale Lemma, journalist and publisher of the prominent Addis Standard magazine, told DW earlier this month that the danger reflects years of unresolved tensions and failures to implement the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the Tigray war.

Lemma said the international community was "absolutely underestimating" the threat of conflict. She argued that international actors had failed to ensure effective monitoring of the agreement and respond adequately as the peace process weakened.

A wider regional risk

The confrontation comes amid instability across the Horn of Africa, including Sudan's war and tensions between Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile mega-dam project.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in September 2025, a move that was not well received by neighboring Egypt and Sudan, both downstream countries.

Competition over access to the Red Sea has added another strategic dimension: Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.

Journalist Martin Plaut, who specializes in the Horn of Africa, has warned that the region is at a crossroads. He has raised the possibility of Ethiopian forces entering Eritrea, but an invasion remains a scenario, not a confirmed decision by the Ethiopian government.

Any wider conflict could threaten regional trade and maritime security. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connect shipping routes between Europe and Asia, making the region strategically important well beyond Africa.

Can diplomacy avert war between Ethiopia and Eritrea?

The United States and the United Kingdom have called on Ethiopia and Eritrea to exercise restraint and return to dialogue under their 2018 peace framework.

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the military buildup on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border could escalate into a wider conflict.

Rubio said Washington hoped lifting some sanctions would improve communication with both sides and stressed the need for a "wise and measured" response to avoid a broader regional war.

The United Kingdom has also called for renewed talks between both sides. "We urgently call for de-escalation and a return to dialogue. We reiterate our support for the African Union's role in facilitating this," said a UK government spokesperson in a statement on October 15.

For now, the recapture of towns in Tigray has changed the military balance but has not resolved tensions in the region.

Whether international pressure can prevent a wider war will depend on whether the governments involved choose dialogue over further escalation.

Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Geleta and Christine Mhundwa contributed to this report.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Houthi strike on Yemen government military camp kills at least 50
World.content:
The Iran-backed group has claimed responsibility for the attack which killed new recruits at a military camp. The strikes follow deadly attacks over the weekend blamed on Saudi-led forces.

At least 50 Yemeni government forces were killed in a strike by Houthi rebels on a military camp in the south of the country on Monday, military officials said.

The group fired three ballistic missiles at the al-Alam camp in the province of Shabwa. Some 200 recruits were also wounded, according to the provincial government.

The Houthis confirmed that they had targeted the camp.

Deadliest attack in recent surge of violence in Yemen

Military sources had originally put the death toll at 30, but this rose to at least 50 later in the day, with the Associated Press giving a toll of 53 and citing provincial authorities.

"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa said, according to AFP.

Al-Khalifi added that local hospitals had been overwhelmed and some of the more seriously wounded had been transferred to facilities in other provinces.

The increased death toll makes Monday's attack one of the deadliest in the recent uptick of violence in Yemen.

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yemeni government vows response to Houthi attack

Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has been going on for years, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and other factors have sparked renewed fighting in the peninsula, with the Houthis also carrying out major attacks on Saudi Arabian soil.

Officials said that the soldiers who were killed and wounded in the attack had been recruits for a new Rapid Intervention force which is supposed to defend the local area.

The missiles reportedly struck while they were lining up in formation ahead of training.

Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, vowed a "firm response" for the killing of the recruits and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."

Monday's strikes follow several attacks over the weekend that killed more than 30 people in Houthi-held areas. The Houthis have blamed Saudi-led forces for the attacks.

World.title: Myanmar refugees find hope in Thailand's work program
World.content:
A year ago, Thailand granted long-staying refugees from Myanmar the right to work legally. Refugees and rights groups welcome the move but say the program's first year has exposed significant shortcomings.

At a glance, Ray Boe doesn't stand out from the tens of thousands of other foreign workers toiling at countless construction sites that push Bangkok's soaring skyline ever higher.

Unlike most of them, though, the 31-year-old came to Thailand's capital from one of the country's nine camps for refugees who have fled decades of civil strife inMyanmar.

The camps, which hug the Thai-Myanmar border, are home to more than 100,000 people — in some cases since the 1980s, when the refugees first started arriving.

Until a year ago this month, the Thai government had refused to let them leave the camps to find work, forcing most to live hand-to-mouth on foreign donor aid.

That changed in October 2025, after foreign aid cutbacks — mostly by the United States — forced the camps to slash the food support and healthcare they could provide.

New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Around the same time, fighting between Thailand and Cambodia over territorial claims had sent hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from Cambodia back home, leaving behind a yawning labor gap.

Myanmar refugees allowed to work outside of camps

To cope with the aid cuts and labor deficit, the Thai government reversed decades of policy and began issuing the refugees permits to work outside the camps, to help them meet their own needs.

Ray Boe is one of the 6,800 camp refugees the government said have entered the Thai labor force in the first year of the program.

"After the cuts by USAID and other organizations, there is no more regular support for our daily needs, like rice and other rations. And there is not enough healthcare in the camps anymore," he said.

The cuts forced him and his parents to borrow from neighbors and to pare down their already modest meals.

Underpaid and overworked: Myanmar migrants in Thailand To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since last month, he has earned 400 baht (about $12) a day pouring concrete and erecting scaffolding around what's to be a 12-story apartment building in central Bangkok. He hopes to start sending money home soon.

"It will help us pay for food and other basic needs, and for health are for my parents," Ray Boe said.

"Compared to how we were living in the camp before, it will be a big difference, having my own income and supporting my family on my own, not having to wait for other people to support us day to day," he told DW.

Refugee work program offers hope, but faces a rocky start

The program allows the refugees to work in 43 of Thailand's 76 provinces and in any sector not reserved by law for Thai citizens only.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the government has improved the vocational training on offer inside the camps to better prepare refugees for work outside.

"We are hopeful that this policy would enhance opportunities and empower the [refugees] to realize their potential, as well as contribute to Thai socioeconomic development," said Praporn Waenluang, a spokesman for the ministry's information department.

Labor and refugee rights groups have welcomed the program.

"I have met a lot of camp [refugees] who have come outside and worked. They are so happy to work and earn money, a lot of money compared to what they [can] get in the camp," said Siwawong Sooktawee, Thailand project coordinator for the International Detention Coalition.

"This is good because they feel they can help themselves, they can support themselves, not depend on aid anymore," he added.

Myanmar workers in Thailand struggle to work legally To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet he and others have said the program has gotten off to a slow start, with many flaws to work out.

They said many of the refugees who have taken part have not been given contracts by their employers, only to find the conditions rougher, the work harder, or the pay lower than what they were promised before leaving the camps. The program also lacks a clear system for lodging and settling complaints, according to observers.

"Many refugees go, come back, go, come back so many times. Some refugees, their families have to raise funds or borrow money in the refugee camps so that their father or their family member will be able to return," said K'nyaw Paw, general secretary of the Karen Women's Organization, an NGO serving the camp's ethnic Karen group.

Financial burdens placed on Myanmar refugees

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees are sometimes made to repay employers through wage deductions for hiring them, including medical exams, government permits and transportation to job sites. As a result, they often start work already in debt, sometimes without prior warning.

Akwah, a father of two who goes by one name, left his camp with 20 other refugees in November 2025 for what was supposed to be a job harvesting sugarcane on a farm on the other side of the country for 250 baht per day.

When he arrived, however, he was told to cut eucalyptus trees — a much more difficult and dangerous job, he said — for only 200 baht per day. Workers had to sleep outdoors, with no electricity and only a nearby pond for water.

"We spoke to the boss, but the boss did not care. He said, 'Just do the work because you are already here.' But we said we could not do it," said Akwah. They left after three months.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply to DW's request for comment on the program's alleged problems. The Labor and Interior ministries, which mainly oversee the program, did not reply to requests for an interview either.

Rights groups say program still needs to improve

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees who take part should be guaranteed clear and detailed contracts — translated if needed into Burmese, Karen or Karenni, the main languages spoken in the camps — and an easy-to-access system for filing and settling complaints.

They also suggest that the government open more provinces up to the program and screen the job brokers coming to the camps as middlemen, to weed out the unscrupulous ones.

They said their NGOs and others are working with the government on making some of the upgrades, and that they're hopeful the program will improve with time, so that more of the refugees are able and willing to take part.

Thailand-Myanmar border clinic helps people fleeing war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For all the program's flaws, though, they said most of the refugees are still eager to apply, even those who have run into problems.

"I had a bad experience, but I still want to go again, because food in the camp is a problem," said Mu Dah Hsit, who fell ill at her job and had to quit after her boss refused to cover the health insurance the program is supposed to guarantee.

"I have no mother, and a father who is sick, and siblings I have to take care of," she said. "So, I have to go; otherwise, we cannot live."

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

World.title: La Generalitat levanta el confinamiento en los municipios de Valencia y Alicante afectados por las lluvias torrenciales y las inundaciones
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

Una mujer de 79 años y un hombre de 64 han fallecido en Oliva. Ha habido personas atrapadas con difícil acceso para rescatarlas

La dana Adam está castigando con extrema violencia e insistencia diversas poblaciones del norte de la provincia de Alicante, como Dénia y Pego, y del sur de Valencia, como Gandia. En Oliva (Valencia) los cuerpos de una mujer de 79 años y un hombre de 64 han sido rescatados sin vida, según fuentes gubernamentales. Una sobrina de la fallecida advirtió a los servicios de emergencia de que su tía tenía movilidad reducida y vivía sola, pero cuando los equipos acudieron al domicilio, la encontraron ya muerta. El varón de 64 años murió al sufrir un infarto en un camping de la localidad. Estas dos víctimas mortales se suman a la mujer que falleció en Sagunt al internarse en el mar, este domingo, y otra encontrada en Cabrera de Mar (Barcelona).

La Generalitat ha levantado además en torno a las ocho de la tarde el confinamiento en ocho municipios de las provincias de Valencia y Alicante, que todavía estaban en vigor. “Tras estudiar la evolución del fenómeno, la mejoría que se ha producido tanto a nivel meteorológico como del temporal marítimo, se ha procedido a desconfinar los municipios que hasta la fecha” tenían restricciones. En torno a las 11.00 de la mañana de este lunes, la comunidad autónoma ha publicado una orden con la lista de 145 municipios cuyos vecinos, unos 850.000, debían quedarse en sus casas, pero a las dos de la tarde ha reducido el confinamiento a solo ocho municipios: Bellreguart, Daimús, Miramar, Oliva y Piles, en la provincia de Valencia; y Xàbia, Pego y Els Poblets, en la de Alicante. Pasadas las ocho de la tarde, todo el territorio valenciano ha quedado libre del confinamiento.

Los acumulados en algunos puntos de la geografía valenciana superan los 700 litros por metro cuadrado, lo que ha provodado que mañana martes sigan suspendidas las clases en los municipios de El Verger y Els Poblets, en Alicante; y en las localidades de Miramar, Oliva, Bellreguard y Piles, en la provincia de Valencia.

Las tareas de rescate se han centrado a lo largo del día en socorrer a las personas que están atrapadas en sus casas por la crecida del agua en las calles. El consejero de Emergencias ha reconocido las dificultades para acceder a los lugares desde los que se pide auxilio. Algunos ciudadanos pedían ayuda desde los tejados de sus viviendas, como en Pego (10.800 habitantes) o en Oliva (26.813). Ambas poblaciones se encontraban en una situación crítica. Los rescates se multiplican desde primera hora de la mañana, varios en helicóptero. La Unidad Militar de Emergencias (UME) ya ha sido activada. Hay unas 2.000 personas evacuadas y se han llevado a cabo un millar de rescates a lo largo del día, según el balance a las ocho de la tarde.

Valderrama ha recordado que pesa todavía a partir de las nueve de la nueve de esta noche y hasta las 3 de la madrugada aproximadamente un aviso naranja en el litoral sur de la provincia de Alicante. “Vuelvo a repetir que esto significa 40 litros por metro cuadrado en una hora y 80 litros por metro cuadrado aproximadamente en 12 horas. Tenemos que estar atentos a la evolución”, ha indicado el consejero de Emergencias.

El río Girona se ha desbordado en la madrugada de este lunes a su paso por varios municipios. Hasta 700 litros por metro cuadrado se han acumulado en menos de 36 horas en L’Atzúbia. Este temporal se ha saldado hasta el momento con cuatro muertes, según ha confirmado la delegada del Gobierno en la Comunidad Valenciana, Pilar Bernabé.
