World.title: Kazakhstan Wins Two Gold Medals at Asian Para Games in Japan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan won two gold medals at the fifth Asian Para Games in Japan, with Yerkin Gabbasov and David Degtyarev taking gold in para shooting and para powerlifting.

Gabbasov secured Kazakhstan’s first gold in the men’s 10-meter air rifle standing event (R1), scoring 249.1 points in the final, reported the National Olympic Committee’s press service on Oct. 19.

Degtyarev claimed the second gold in para powerlifting in the up to 54-kilogram category, lifting 191 kilograms to set a new Asian Para Games record.

Kazakhstan also earned silver in para powerlifting, with Tursynai Kabyl finishing second in the up to 41-kilogram category after completing all three attempts and lifting 104 kilograms in her final attempt.

The games opened in Nagoya on Oct. 18 and will run through Oct. 24 across venues in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, bringing together around 4,000 athletes from 45 Asian countries. Kazakhstan has sent 150 athletes to compete in 12 sports, including wheelchair tennis, where the country is making its debut.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Representative Elected OIC Assistant Secretary-General
World.content:
ASTANA – Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issagaliyev called for resolving conflicts through political and diplomatic means during the 52nd Session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on Oct. 18. Baghdad Amreyev was elected OIC assistant secretary-general for administration and finance.

Kazakhstan reaffirmed its commitment to resolving international conflicts through diplomacy and strengthening multilateral cooperation at the meeting, which brought together representatives of OIC member states to discuss regional and global challenges, the ministry’s press service reported on Oct. 18.

Delegations addressed the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, humanitarian crises and other security challenges affecting the Islamic world. Participants emphasized the need to intensify diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East and promote regional peace and stability.

In his statement, Issagaliyev stressed that conflicts should be resolved exclusively through political and diplomatic means, in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter. He called for stronger multilateral dialogue and coordinated efforts among OIC member states to advance peace, security and sustainable development.

Kazakhstan also highlighted priorities including nuclear non-proliferation, food security, transport and logistics connectivity, artificial intelligence, digitalization and advanced technologies. The Kazakh delegation also raised environmental cooperation, notably the rehabilitation of the former Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site.

Kazakhstan’s representative elected OIC assistant secretary-general

A key outcome for Kazakhstan was the election of Baghdad Amreyev as assistant secretary-general of the OIC for administration and finance. The appointment reflects member states’ support for Kazakhstan’s active participation in the organization.

Following the session, OIC member states adopted a package of resolutions covering political, economic, legal, cultural and humanitarian topics. All initiatives proposed by Kazakhstan have been incorporated into the relevant outcome documents.

World.title: EFSD Raises Kazakhstan’s 2027 Growth Forecast to 5%, Expects Inflation to Ease
World.content:
ASTANA – The Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD) has raised its forecast for Kazakhstan’s economic growth in 2027 to 5%, up from 4.6% in its previous outlook, while projecting a gradual decline in inflation through 2029.

The fund expects Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by 5% in 2026, following 6.5% growth in 2025. Growth is projected to remain at 5% in 2027 before slowing to 4.2% in 2028 and 4.1% in 2029, according to the EFSD’s autumn regional economic outlook.

The revised forecast reflects expectations of sustained oil production, major investment and infrastructure projects, and a more expansionary fiscal policy. However, the fund warns that strong domestic demand and continued budget stimulus could complicate efforts to bring inflation under control.

“The main challenge for economic policy will be to strike a balance between supporting economic growth and maintaining price, fiscal and external stability,” said Sergei Ulatov, the EFSD’s chief economist.

Oil production and investment to support growth

The EFSD expects Kazakhstan’s economy to maintain relatively strong growth despite less favorable global conditions, including geopolitical tensions, higher transportation costs and volatility in commodity markets.

The fund forecasts 5% GDP growth in 2026, unchanged from its summer outlook. The estimate reflects the recovery of oil production at the Tengiz field to full capacity in the second quarter, steady performance in non-oil sectors and high investment activity by the quasi-public sector.

Additional support is expected from fiscal policy in the second half of the year, including a planned targeted transfer of 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3 billion) through the Infrastructure Development Fund.

Elevated commodity prices amid global uncertainty are also expected to support export revenues and activity in resource-producing companies. The outlook for 2027 has improved, with the EFSD raising its growth forecast from 4.6% to 5%. The revision is based on expectations that oil production will remain stable, large-scale investment and infrastructure projects will proceed, and fiscal policy will provide stronger support.

However, the fund expects consumer demand to remain relatively subdued because of moderately tight monetary conditions, slower retail lending and weak growth in real household incomes. In 2028-2029, growth is expected to moderate as the effects of increased oil production fade and domestic demand returns to more sustainable levels.

Inflation to decline gradually through 2029

The EFSD expects inflation to reach 9.5% by the end of 2026, down from its previous forecast of 9.8%. The revision reflects slower price growth amid weaker increases in regulated services and fuel and lubricants prices, as well as a stronger tenge.

Inflation is projected to decline further to 8.8% in 2027, 7.8% in 2028 and 6.8% in 2029. However, the fund expects inflation to remain above the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s 5% target throughout the forecast period. Persistent domestic demand, elevated inflation expectations and potential increases in utility tariffs and fuel prices remain key risks.

The National Bank is expected to continue cautiously easing monetary policy. The average base rate is projected to decline from 16.9% in 2026 to 14.8% in 2027, 12.8% in 2028 and 10.8% in 2029.

The outlook suggests that monetary policy will remain relatively tight even as inflation gradually slows, reflecting the challenge of containing price pressures without undermining economic activity.

Current account deficit expected to narrow

The EFSD expects Kazakhstan’s external position to improve in 2026, supported by favorable terms of trade and commodity export revenues.

The current account deficit is projected to narrow to 1% of GDP in 2026, compared with 4.1% in 2025. The fund attributes the improvement to stronger external trade conditions, although the effects of higher commodity prices vary across countries depending on their export and import structures.

The fund noted that trade remains the main channel through which external shocks affect economies across the Eurasian region. Higher energy and transportation costs, alongside slower global demand, continue to pose risks.

In Kazakhstan, oil production disruptions at Tengiz and interruptions to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure have constrained output and exports. Nevertheless, non-oil industries and investment activity are expected to sustain growth.

The labor market remains stable. Employment reached 9.4 million people in the second quarter, up 0.9% year on year, while unemployment under the International Labour Organization methodology fell to 4.5%, from 4.6% in 2025.

Fiscal policy presents a balancing challenge

The EFSD has revised its assessment of Kazakhstan’s fiscal policy toward a more expansionary stance throughout the forecast period, following the publication of the draft 2027-2029 national budget and the resumption of targeted transfers from the National Fund.

The fund estimates the budget deficit at 2.7% of GDP in 2026, with a further widening expected in 2027 as the government implements a large infrastructure program. The deficit is projected to narrow to 2.5% of GDP in 2028-2029.

The fund expects the global economic environment to remain uncertain at least through the end of 2026, with the Middle East conflict continuing to affect energy markets, transportation costs and inflation in major economies.

Despite these risks, most economies in the Eurasian region are expected to maintain solid growth in 2026, supported by domestic demand, rising incomes, credit expansion and investment. The EFSD noted that the region’s resilience will depend on policymakers’ ability to sustain economic momentum while preserving price stability and fiscal discipline.

World.title: Slovenian Port Seeks Stronger Transport Links with Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Slovenia’s Port of Koper sees opportunities to strengthen transport links with Kazakhstan through the Middle Corridor and share its digital port-management expertise to improve cargo handling and logistics efficiency, said Nevenka Kržan, president of the port’s management board, in an interview with The Astana Times.

The potential cooperation comes as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

Kržan said Luka Koper had developed its own information technology systems in cooperation with an IT company, supporting billing, predictive analytics, storage planning and warehouse management. These systems could offer useful experience for Kazakhstan’s ports as they work to improve operational efficiency and handle growing cargo volumes.

“We are always ready and willing to assist. We developed our own IT systems, which have grown with us over the years, and they could be useful for your ports as well,” she said.

The port’s digital systems allow operators to track cargo in real time and manage storage more efficiently. Kržan said the port can locate individual vehicles among tens of thousands stored on its premises.

“We can have almost 45,000 cars in the port at one time, and we know where each car is. Our systems are efficient, predictive and operate in real time,” she said.

Building stronger links with Kazakhstan

Kržan described her visit to Kazakhstan as an initial step toward identifying opportunities for closer cooperation. She noted that Luka Koper would like to establish direct connections with Kazakh railway operators, freight forwarders, logistics companies and agents.

“We have a very active port community. We know that without freight forwarders, agents and logistics companies, we cannot do anything on our own,” she said, emphasizing the importance of coordination across the logistics chain.

She added that cooperation could extend beyond commercial arrangements to exchanging best practices and improving coordination among ports, railways and customs authorities.

The port has also introduced a single point of contact to coordinate customs officers and other inspection services, including food inspections, with the aim of reducing paperwork and streamlining procedures.

These practices could be relevant to Kazakhstan as it works to address logistical bottlenecks and improve the movement of cargo across different transport systems.

In 2025, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar discussed expanding transport and logistics cooperation, including the potential involvement of Luka Koper in the Middle Corridor.

Slovenian Minister of Infrastructure and Energy Jernej Vrtovec also highlighted the importance of strengthening transport connections between Europe and Asia. Kazakhstan’s strategic geographical position made it a key partner in developing these connections.

“Slovenia attaches great importance to the further development of safe, efficient and resilient transport connections between Europe and Asia, as well as to the diversification of transport routes and supply chains. In this context, we recognize the increasingly important role of the Middle Corridor, which provides an important link and offers opportunities for further strengthening multimodal connectivity,” he said in a recent statement.

A gateway to Central Europe

Located on the northern Adriatic coast, the Port of Koper connects maritime shipping routes with rail and road networks serving Central and Eastern Europe. Its proximity to major European markets and its position at the intersection of the Baltic-Adriatic and Mediterranean transport corridors are among its main competitive advantages.

Kržan highlighted that the port’s location and established rail and road connections make it a convenient entry point for cargo arriving from the Middle East and Far East.

“We are a multipurpose port. We were established almost 70 years ago, and we are focused primarily on two major cargo groups: containers and cars,” she said.

In 2025, Luka Koper handled around 23 million tons of cargo, including 1.27 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), a standard measure of container capacity. The port also handled nearly 915,000 vehicles, maintaining its position as a major automotive hub in the Mediterranean.

“We are not competing with northern European ports because they are much bigger. But we are the main gateway to Central Europe and offer one of the shortest routes from the Middle and Far East to this part of the world,” Kržan said.

The port is continuing an investment program launched under its 2024-2028 strategy. The planned investment cycle totals 785 million euros (US$883 million) and includes expanding container facilities and increasing vehicle storage capacity.

“The container terminal’s annual capacity is expected to reach up to 1.8 million TEUs once the planned expansion is complete. The port is also building a multi-story garage with space for around 11,600 vehicles. Together with existing facilities, the garage will provide covered parking for around 25,000 vehicles,” Kržan said.

Connecting the Middle Corridor with European markets

The Middle Corridor has gained importance as countries seek to diversify trade routes and strengthen transport links between Asia and Europe. For Kazakhstan, the route provides an alternative connection to European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

Kržan noted that the corridor could create opportunities not only for transport and logistics but also for regional production, manufacturing and closer economic cooperation.

She identified the possibility of establishing more direct shipping connections between Istanbul and Koper as one area worth exploring.

“I think it would be very important if cargo currently going through Istanbul could be transported directly by ship to our port. That would mean shorter transit times, greater efficiency and lower carbon emissions for customers in Central Europe,” she said.

Kržan said the port serves markets across Central Europe, including Hungary, Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, southern Germany and southern Poland. Around 85% of the cargo passing through Koper is destined for markets outside Slovenia.

She added that maritime transport can sometimes be more efficient than rail, depending on the cargo and route. Closer coordination between shipping lines and logistics operators could help identify the most effective transport options.

“As trade routes continue to evolve, developing new connections and strengthening existing partnerships will become increasingly important. We can cooperate not only commercially but also by exchanging good practices,” Kržan said.

World.title: Armenia considers restricting regional cars from entering Yerevan
World.content:
Cars from regions banned from Yerevan

A statement by Yerevan Deputy Mayor Suren Grigoryan has sparked widespread debate in Armenia. He said that one of the city administration’s strategic goals was to create car parks at the entrances to Yerevan, where drivers arriving from other regions could leave their vehicles and continue their journeys by public transport.

The proposal has prompted heated discussions among both experts and residents.

Traffic experts suggest increasing parking fees in the capital rather than restricting vehicle access. Meanwhile, residents have raised concerns that the initiative could limit freedom of movement and lead to discriminatory measures.

People are also questioning how they would navigate Yerevan using public transport if travelling with young children or elderly relatives, or bringing a family member to the capital for medical treatment.

What else did deputy mayor say?

Deputy Mayor Suren Grigoryan said the city administration had no plans to introduce restrictions immediately. He explained that creating car parks and expanding the public transport fleet would take time. Grigoryan did not specify when a possible ban on cars from other regions entering Yerevan might come into force.

According to him, the number of cars in Armenia has doubled from 500,000 in 2014 to one million. Meanwhile, the number of vehicles in Yerevan is increasing by around 15,000 or more each year.

The deputy mayor also addressed plans to purchase new vehicles for public transport. He said the city planned to acquire 171 new buses in the near future.

However, Grigoryan acknowledged that he could not say with certainty whether all residents of Armenia’s regions would be able to switch from private cars to public transport.

Clarifications following statement

Following a wave of outrage on social media, the deputy mayor issued further clarifications. He stressed that he had been referring not to a measure that would be introduced immediately, but to a strategic goal that would be implemented gradually.

“There has been a misunderstanding. Some citizens assumed that vehicles from the regions would be banned from entering Yerevan. I said nothing of the sort,” Suren Grigoryan emphasised.

He attributed the confusion to the headline of his interview:

“It had nothing to do with the actual content of the interview. This is a clear example of what happens when people judge a news story solely by its headline.”

Expert opinion

Traffic expert Artak Gaboyan believes that banning private cars from Armenia’s regions from entering the capital would make little sense:

“Nowhere in the world do authorities simply tell people they are banned from entering a city. Instead, they create conditions that make leaving a car outside the city a more convenient and financially attractive option.”

To ease congestion in central Yerevan, Gaboyan suggests increasing parking fees to 1,000 drams ($2.60) per hour, roughly three times the current rate.

“In addition, free shuttle buses should operate near the car parks [at the entrances to the city], taking drivers to the nearest transport hub, metro station or interchange where they can transfer to regular public transport services heading in different directions,” he explained.

Gaboyan also believes that implementing his proposal would require ensuring the “uninterrupted movement of public transport”.

As an example, he cited Isakov Avenue, one of the capital’s busiest roads, where one lane is reserved exclusively for public transport.

Social media reactions

“Are you now dividing society into Yerevan residents and people from the regions? How long will you continue dividing society? Instead, ease congestion in the capital and sort out the traffic problems.”

“This violates people’s right to freedom of movement. The current city administration has already made life unbearable for us.”

“And what about the fact that many people are simply too lazy to travel one or two stops by public transport and prefer to use their own cars?”

“We come to Yerevan with small children and loads of bags. How does he expect us to get around on public transport?”

“Why not simply ban people from the regions from entering Yerevan unless they carry an ID card, an income declaration, a CV and at least three letters of recommendation? And then, why not require people from the regions to obtain police permission before leaving their villages?”

“The deputy mayor could start setting an example today: take public transport home, use it to get to work tomorrow, take his children to school and then go to the doctor. All by public transport. In short, let him try living like that for at least a week, and then we’ll see.”

“According to the deputy mayor, implementing this idea would require building car parks at the entrances to the capital and introducing dedicated public transport lanes. Given that over the past eight years the city administration has made no progress beyond a single dedicated lane on one avenue — failing to establish a proper network of such lanes or make progress in expanding the metro system — expecting them to resolve the issue of restricting cars from the regions from entering Yerevan is simply wishful thinking.”

World.title: South Ossetia’s new authorities seek to crack down on illegal trade in ‘award’ weapons
World.content:
The new president of South Ossetia, Marat Kambolov, has ordered an investigation into the legality of the circulation of civilian, service and military firearms, as well as bladed weapons.

The Prosecutor General’s Office is carrying out the president’s order. Kambolov’s fellow villager, Soslanbek Kozhiyev, was recently appointed first deputy prosecutor general.

A smuggled ‘award’

The authorities will pay particular attention to a practice that took hold under previous presidents: handing out Glock and Beretta pistols left, right and centre under the pretext of awarding them as honours. Smugglers brought the pistols into South Ossetia from Georgia.

Officials often used these supposed “awards” as a cover to sell the weapons to members of the criminal underworld or simply to anyone who wanted one. And plenty of people in South Ossetia want a gun “just in case”. However, Kambolov believes this “tradition”, which dates back to the 1990s, has run its course. He says that civilian gun ownership no longer serves a relevant purpose and that real security risks no longer justify it.

“Today, South Ossetia leads a peaceful life and is building a state governed by the rule of law. In a peaceful state, the law — not tradition, personal merit, official position or private arrangements — must determine the right to own a gun.

The republic has suspended all awards of weapons until the investigation ends. The state must know exactly where each weapon is, to whom and on what grounds it was issued, how it was registered and who is responsible for it,” the president said.

At the same time, he proposes extending permits to possess and carry most types of civilian firearms to ten years, while retaining mandatory checks and periodic permit renewals:

“This approach will allow us to bring order to the firearms register without imposing excessive bureaucracy on law-abiding owners. The republic’s Security Council will make the final decision on this matter, following a proposal from the prosecutor general.”

A rifle as a gift

These measures come amid criminal proceedings against former Interior Minister Erislav Mamiyev and his first deputy, Atsamaz Sagkayev.

Investigators suspect that Sagkayev “gifted” his boss, Mamiyev, a sniper rifle and an assault rifle in 2025 and 2026.

Authorities have opened two criminal cases against Sagkayev on suspicion of “abuse of official powers for personal gain or other personal motives”, an offence under the Criminal Code.

Some Telegram channels claim that over those two years, Sagkayev used the pretext of awarding weapons to sell 400 firearms to unknown buyers.

Both Sagkayev and Mamiyev lost their jobs at the Interior Ministry in August 2026, when Marat Kambolov, then prime minister, launched the first stage of a purge of South Ossetia’s security agencies.

The roots of the problem

Many consider Erislav Mamiyev a close friend of local crime boss Alexander (Alik) Gagloyev, the brother of former president Alan Gagloyev.

Social media has also circulated claims that Alan Gagloyev and his team planned to use his gangster brother and their friends, armed with weapons presented as “awards”, to hold on to power by force if he lost the 2027 presidential election.

But that scenario never materialised. In mid-2026, the Kremlin itself ousted Gagloyev from the presidency and effectively installed its own envoy, Marat Kambolov, in his place.

The new president is now trying to clean up his predecessor’s “legacy” and deliver on his promise to restore order, a pledge he repeatedly made to the people of South Ossetia over the past several months.

However, Alan Gagloyev was not the only former president involved in illegal arms trafficking. His predecessor, Leonid Tibilov, also had a record of such activity. One case came to light relatively recently, in autumn 2025. The major scandal that erupted at the time also implicated former Interior Minister Akhsar Lavoyev and Russian debt collector Eduard Budantsev, alongside Tibilov.

It emerged that back in December 2015, Budantsev and several former colleagues had exchanged gunfire in central Moscow using award weapons from South Ossetia. He had acquired the weapons through Tibilov and his inner circle.

“The trade in Glocks and Berettas in South Ossetia became a well-oiled operation under Tibilov and his associates. Gagloyev and his people simply continued the lucrative business,” a local expert said on condition of anonymity.
