World.title: Iran's electricity imports from Azerbaijan reach over 33M kWh
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Iran imported 33.16 million kilowatt-hours of electricity from Azerbaijan in January–August 2026, generating $942,000 in revenue for Azerbaijan, according to the State Statistical Committee of Azerbaijan.

According to Trend’s calculations, electricity exports to Iran increased by 12.237 million kilowatt-hours, or 1.6 times, compared with the same period in 2025. In value terms, exports rose by $348,000, also increasing 1.6 times.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan imported 23.806 million kilowatt-hours of electricity from Iran worth $676,000 in the first eight months of 2026. Compared with the same period in 2025, the value of imports increased by $57,000, or 9.2%, while their volume rose by 2.011 million kilowatt-hours, or 9.2%.

In January–August 2026, Azerbaijan exported a total of 319.040 million kilowatt-hours of electricity worth $16.629 million to three countries: Russia, Georgia and Iran.

Compared with the same period in 2025, Azerbaijan’s electricity exports fell by $36.105 million, or 3.2 times, in value terms and by 600.885 million kilowatt-hours, or 2.9 times, in volume terms.

During the same period, Azerbaijan imported 143.724 million kilowatt-hours of electricity worth $7.0945 million from these countries. Compared with the first eight months of 2025, the value of imports increased by $2.146 million, or 43.4%, while their volume rose by 28.1 million kilowatt-hours, or 24.3%.

Economic cooperation between Azerbaijan and Iran continues to develop across trade, transportation, energy, transit and logistics. The two countries are deepening cooperation under the International North–South Transport Corridor and implementing joint initiatives involving electricity and natural gas exchanges.

The two sides are also working to increase bilateral trade, expand cross-border economic ties, strengthen industrial cooperation and promote investment projects, with energy remaining a key area of bilateral cooperation.

World.title: Azerbaijan reduces greenhouse gas emissions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Azerbaijan reduced its greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 compared with the previous year.

According to the 2026 report prepared by the European Commission’s Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR), the country’s total emissions fell from 58.52 million tons in 2024 to 57.72 million tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2025. This represents a decrease of 0.8 million tons, or approximately 1.4%.

The report puts Azerbaijan’s share of global greenhouse gas emissions at 0.11%, down from the 2024 level. This was recorded against the backdrop of a 0.7% increase in global emissions in 2025, bringing the total to 54.15 billion tons.

According to the 2026 EDGAR report, total greenhouse gas emissions in regional countries in 2025 were distributed as follows:

- Russia: 2.57 billion tons — 4.75% of global emissions;

- Iran: 1.12 billion tons — 2.07%;

- Türkiye: 610.78 million tons — 1.13%;

- Azerbaijan: 57.72 million tons — 0.11%.

According to the report, China was the world’s largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, accounting for 15.98 billion tons of CO₂ equivalent, or 29.51% of the global total.

U.S. emissions amounted to 6.02 billion tons, representing 11.11% of the global total, while India accounted for 4.51 billion tons, or 8.33%.

Thus, Azerbaijan’s reduction in emissions in 2025, despite the rise in global figures, serves as further evidence of the country’s commitment to its voluntarily undertaken environmental obligations.

World.title: Uzbekistan, U.S. sign agreements worth $12 billion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Business representatives from Uzbekistan and the United States have signed agreements worth a total of $12 billion following a meeting of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council held in Samarkand. This was reported by the press service of Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.

“A package of 54 agreements in trade, investment and technological cooperation was signed as part of business events held during the visit of the U.S. delegation to Uzbekistan. Their implementation provides for investments totaling $12 billion,” the statement said.

The agreements are aimed at modernizing Uzbekistan’s industrial sector, transport and energy infrastructure, developing critical mineral resources, and advancing the financial sector, digital technologies, agriculture, healthcare and education.

In the transport sector, cooperation with GE Aerospace предусматривает the supply of engines for new Uzbekistan Airways aircraft. Meanwhile, initiatives with Wabtec focus on localizing the production of railway equipment and components, helping modernize the industry technologically and expand domestic manufacturing capabilities.

Agreements with companies including Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer & Co., Citigroup and BlackRock are expected to help Uzbek companies access international capital markets, attract institutional investors and secure financing for infrastructure projects.

Agreements and cooperation with ReElement Technologies, Traxys and Trafigura in the mining sector are aimed at developing new deposits, promoting technological cooperation and supplying mineral resources. Particular emphasis was placed on strengthening Uzbekistan’s domestic capabilities in the critical minerals sector.

Meanwhile, projects in the digital and social sectors involving Amazon Leo, GE HealthCare and Valmont Industries предусматривают the development of satellite communications, the introduction of advanced medical technologies and improvements in agricultural efficiency.

“The signed package lays the foundation for a new stage in Uzbek-American economic cooperation, combining international capital and advanced technologies with Uzbekistan’s industrial potential. The next priority will be to consistently translate the agreements reached into tangible results,” the ministry’s press service added.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 20, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 24-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev addressed the people of Azerbaijan.

- In his address to the people, President Ilham Aliyev said that the city of Zangilan and 24 villages had been liberated from occupation.

- President Ilham Aliyev renamed the liberated Vang village of Khojavand district to Chinarli.

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a publication on her Instagram account about the liberation of the city of Zangilan and a number of villages of Fuzuli, Jabrayil, Khojavand and Zangilan districts.

- The Azerbaijani flag was raised in Zangilan.

- Video footage of the destruction of Armenian armored vehicles had been released. The list of destroyed Armenian military equipment had been announced. A group of mercenaries from the Armenian side refused to fight.

- Armenian Armed Forces shelled the territories of Tartar and Aghdam districts, killing two civilians.

- Video footage of the destruction of a large number of Armenian servicemen and military equipment had been released.

- Armenian anti-aircraft guns were destroyed in the direction of Ganja.

- Video footage of the destruction of units of the Armenian Armed Forces in the direction of Gubadli had been released.

World.title: Azerbaijan, UN discuss issue of declining water level of Caspian Sea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Azerbaijan and the UN discussed the issue of the declining water level of the Caspian Sea.

This was announced by Mukhtar Babayev, Representative of the President of Azerbaijan on Climate Issues, in a post on his X social media account.

"Pleased to meet with Dmytro Shlapachenko, UN Resident Coordinator in Azerbaijan, to discuss advancing cooperation on climate and environmental priorities.

Building on Azerbaijan’s partnership with the UN, including our successful collaboration at COP29, exchanged views on advancing climate action and enhancing resilience.

Discussed the need for greater international attention to the Caspian Sea’s declining water levels, one of the most pressing environmental challenges facing our region. Also discussed deepening regional cooperation on transboundary water management, drought preparedness, early warning systems and data sharing.

Explored opportunities to further strengthen cooperation on these priorities towards COP31 and beyond," the statement said.

World.title: Con man who fleeced millions of dollars dies in self-declared 'kingdom'
World.content:
One of the South Pacific's most infamous con men, Noah Musingku, has died in his self-declared kingdom in the south of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea.

Musingku fleeced millions of dollars from people in PNG, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Australia and elsewhere from the late 1990s through his Ponzi scheme U-Vistract, before fleeing authorities to his hometown of Tonu where he declared himself King Peii II of Papaala.

A death notice posted on the Bougainville Independence Movement Facebook page said Musingku died last week from "an illness he has fought over for more than three weeks".

Noah Musingku was buried by people in military uniform. (Facebook: Bougainville Independence Movement)

A later post showed pictures of what was said to be his burial, with men dressed in military fatigues burying a coffin as a small crowd watched on.

"It's confirmed," said Timothy Masiu, the member for South Bougainville in PNG's national parliament.

"He died … and they kept his body for three days and then they decided to lay him to rest on Saturday.

A death notice said Noah Musingku died last week. (Facebook: Bougainville Independence Movement)

"I am sad to hear of his passing because he is from my electorate and he was my schoolmate.

"His passing brings mixed feelings throughout Bougainville. Everybody has their own dreams and Noah had his dream and I think if he did it the right way, that dream would have come true for him."

'There goes my money'

Musingku's death brings to a close one of the region's most extraordinary, high-profile financial scams.

He started U-Vistract in PNG's capital Port Moresby in the late 1990s, promising investors 100 per cent interest per month.

As with all successful Ponzi schemes the first investors did receive those returns and word spread prompting thousands more to hand over millions of dollars.

Bougainville's con man 'king' Bougainville could become the world's newest nation, but it's been unable to deal with a fugitive con man who has spent decades on the run.

Musingku even managed to open a branch of his Royal Reserve Bank of Papaala near the headquarters of the Bank of PNG, the country's central bank.

When authorities eventually moved to shut down his operation, he shifted to Solomon Islands before returning to his home village of Tonu, where he declared himself King Peii II and formed an armed militia to keep the law and disgruntled investors at bay.

Noah Musingku printed his own money, the Bougainville kina, and included his face on some notes. (Supplied: David Hempenstall)

Bougainvillean journalist Gorethy Kenneth invested in U-Vistract back in 1998 with money her parents had given her to pay university fees.

"I learned that he passed away and I said, 'There goes my money,'" she said.

But she also felt sadness on hearing of Musingku's death after speaking to him recently about organising an interview.

"He sounded more like he needed to change his life, like he wanted to, but he didn't know how to do it," she said.

"He needed help."

'There is no big pot of money'

The notice that announced Musingku's death also said, "All clients will be paid for all the investments they have invested in all our investment programs."

Anthony Regan, a constitutional lawyer at the Australian National University and a long-time adviser to the Autonomous Bougainville Government, said any investors hoping for a payout would be disappointed.

"The money's all been eaten up and he never had large amounts of money," Dr Regan said.

"Like any Ponzi scheme, you only have the revenue that you're pulling in from investors and if you're not paying out, the money doesn't come in and he hasn't been able to pay out really since the late 90s."

Dr Regan has watched Musingku's journey closely and said it was hard to predict what his followers in Tonu would do next and what would happen to the guns held by his militia.

"Nobody really knows outside what the leadership structures are, if any, and what continuity there will be," Dr Regan said.

World.title: Barber who intervened in Haines attack denies he is a hero
World.content:
A barber who confiscated a knife and detained the driver who allegedly struck independent MP Helen Haines says he is no hero and is just one of many who rushed to the scene.

Ricky Jefferies, whose business neighbours Ms Haines's Wangaratta electorate office, heard a loud bang shortly after 3:30pm on Monday when Ms Haines was critically injured.

The federal member for Indi was rushed to a local hospital and then airlifted to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne where she remains in a critical condition.

A 43-year-old man, now named as Brendan Nugent, was arrested and spent the night in custody at Wangaratta Police Station.

Police said he would be interviewed this morning and officers had not yet identified any motive.

Ricky Jefferies says he was back at work early this morning to provide for his family of five. (ABC News)

Mr Jefferies dismissed his own heroism and instead highlighted the actions of others.

"It was crazy, I just ran out the front to see what was happening and I saw amazing members of the Wangaratta community who I know, or know most of them, and they were helping," he said.

" I didn't realise the seriousness of the situation initially and once it became relevant I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do. "

The young father said he did not exactly pin the driver down but "asked him to jump out of the car and got him out of the car".

"I just lent over him. Once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him and told him that he can't leave, he's not free to leave and that he'll be alright," he said.

Mr Jefferies said he told the man "everything is alright mate, you'll be alright".

"It was the right thing to do and to show him kindness and grace at a time that could have escalated from there," he said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has labelled him a hero, but Mr Jefferies put his actions down to simply being there at the time.

"I don't think I'm a hero, I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way," he told a large pack of reporters.

Mr Jefferies said the driver had a knife but did not pull it out.

"I just wasn't comfortable with his movements and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.

Ricky Jefferies says he's been praying for Helen Haines. (ABC News)

His first thought at that point, the barber said, was that his wife would be disappointed if he got injured.

"I was just trying to not get injured and trying to not let anyone else be injured after the initial incident," he said.

"I'm humbled and I feel grateful and blessed to have been here to help."

He emphasised there were others who had done much more than he had.

"They did so much more than me ... the other people here, like they deserve the credit," he said.

"A lot of people got involved immediately and they didn't even check for danger, they just ran to help."

He highlighted the actions of one person who had sat in front of the vehicle while the driver was still inside it.

"They sat in front of a rolling car — that's not an exaggeration — there is a man that sat in front of a moving car to help someone," he said.

"That really happened, that's not just a sound bite. A man sat down and refused to leave. I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do."

Locals have been leaving flowers outside Helen Haines' electorate office since yesterday's attack. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

Barber says he's praying for Helen Haines

"She's a mother, she's a member of the community and no one's job should put them at risk but I can tell you from my own personal dealings that she is a genuine kind person," Mr Jefferies said.

"Her and her family, I've prayed for them and I hope that her recovery begins immediately, spiritually and physically.

"I pray that she's in good hands and that she recovers."

Mr Jefferies said the reactions from everyone in the town of dismay and concern for Ms Haines showed how respected she was.

"No one's saying anything bad about Helen at all. We're all genuinely surprised that this would happen."

World.title: Toxic sea hares wash up on NSW beach, posing threat to pets
World.content:
Thousands of toxic jellies have been washed up at a popular beach on the NSW far south coast, triggering curiosity and a warning to pet owners.

Sea hares, which are a type of sea slug, began washing up at Aslings Beach at Eden a week ago.

Macquarie University marine biologist Culum Brown said it was no coincidence they arrived alongside a naturally occurring algal bloom.

"They graze on algae," he said.

"The danger here is that some of the algae they eat contain various toxins which the slug can maintain and use as a predator defence."

Thousands of sea hares were first spotted at Aslings Beach on Tuesday, October 13. (Supplied: Bega Valley Shire Council)

High tides caused many of the toxic sea hares to disperse back into the water.

The Bega Valley Shire Council also organised local contractors to remove them from the beach.

However, some still remain in patches along the shore, causing intrigue among beach goers.

"When they're underwater, they have protrusions that look a bit like the ears of a rabbit or a hare," Professor Brown said.

" They produce an ink-like excretion when they're alarmed, a bit like squid. "

The tides and council clean-up efforts have reduced the number of sea hares at Aslings Beach. (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

Toxic and slimy

The algae itself was identified by the Bega Valley Shire Council (BVSC) as a mix of red macroalgae native to south-eastern Australia and non-toxic.

But sea hares feeding on the algae can pose a serious risk to dogs if they lick, mouth or ingest them.

Pet owners visiting the beach are advised to keep a distance.

“Council crews removed thousands of sea hares from Aslings Beach last week," BVSC sustainability manager Derek Van Bracht said.

"The volume of sea hares on the beach has since reduced, however a visible algal bloom remains offshore.

"So dog owners are advised to stay vigilant when walking their pets in the area."

The algal bloom at Eden, photographed on October 9. (Supplied: Joanne Korner)

Professor Brown said although sea hares were a bit "odd looking", it was not unusual to see them wash ashore in large numbers on the southern-Australian coastline.

He said their arrival usually coincided with rough seas and strong on-shore winds.

Professor Brown said while sea hares were not dangerous to humans, precautions should still be taken.

"If you do handle them, you should definitely wash your hands," he said.

"Don't touch your eyes, because they can cause irritation."

World.title: Ten songs named after famous people from Nicole Kidman to Elon Musk
World.content:
Celebrities have long inspired name-dropping musicians, with famous people often referenced in music.

But it's a special honour indeed to have a whole song named after you.

Sometimes, however, the song in question doesn't have anything to do with the muse.

Here are 10 songs named after prominent people.

Adéla

Nicole Kidman

Academy Award winner Nicole Kidman. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Slovak artist Adéla's track about Oscar winner Nicole Kidman has caught the attention of the Australian Hollywood star herself, with Kidman using the song to soundtrack an Instagram reel.

She's not the only star to do this, with everyone from Madonna to Lizzo sharing the song on TikTok, where it has gone viral.

The track is featured on Adéla's debut album Prima, and has risen to number nine on the Billboard Hot 100 charts.

In case you're wondering who Adéla is, the now solo star and ex-ballerina was cut in the first round of a YouTube reality show aimed at forming the next big girl group.

Those who made it became Katseye.

The singer told W Magazine that she was inspired to write Nicole Kidman after scoring an invitation to the Golden Globes.

"I've never been in a movie," Adéla said.

" But I got all glammed up, and my corset was so tight that I thought, 'I feel like Nicole Kidman right now.' "

Elton John

Roy Rogers

Bernie Taupin (The One Who Writes The Words For Elton John) is famous for his fascination for America's Wild West — and for old movies and TV.

Those obsessions came together on this minor classic that turned up on side four of the classic double album Goodbye Yellow Brick Road(1973).

The song is not really about the great sequined cowboy singer and actor — it's really about the comfort that someone gets from watching a familiar and much-loved character on late night TV — yet another warm, cozy, nostalgic song from one of the great albums of the 1970s.

Eagles

James Dean

Just like Bernie Taupin, the Eagles also had an obsession with the Wild West — but also with the dark side of the California Dream.

Mostly written by Jackson Browne, the song mentions Dean's most famous film role, Rebel Without A Cause, then cryptically alludes to his tragic death: "along came a Spyder and picked up a rider, and took him down the road to eternity".

On September 30, 1955, Dean was driving to a race in California when he was hit by a car that turned onto the highway in front of his Porsche 550 Spyder.

He was killed instantly … but his name, his look, his legend lives on more than 70 years later.

Taylor Swift

Elizabeth Taylor

British and American actress Dame Elizabeth Taylor. (Supplied: Binge)

Elizabeth Taylor is from Taylor Swift's 12th studio album, The Life of a Showgirl.

Swift describes Taylor in the official notes for the album as "one of the most ultimate, quintessential showgirls" she could ever imagine.

"This is a love song kind of through the lens of the motif of what she had to go through in her life and sort of the parallels that I feel in my own life," Swift said.

"You know, role models are pretty hard to come by, but I would absolutely say that she's one of mine."

Weezer

Buddy Holly

Sometimes songs that name check celebrities in the title tell the story of that star's life — but sometimes they don't.

A classic example is Buddy Holly by the 90s US rock group Weezer.

The song has nothing to do with the doomed early rocker who died in music's most famous plane crash (Weezer also mentions the TV star Mary Tyler Moore in the song).

Buddy Holly is best known for its clever music video — seamlessly blending their modern performance with old episodes of the 70s TV comedy Happy Days.

The film clip is more memorable than the song itself.

Charlie Puth feat Meghan Trainor

Marvin Gaye

American musician Marvin Gaye. (Supplied: Universal Music Group)

Marvin Gaye was the lead single from American singer-songwriter Charlie Puth's debut studio album Nine Track Mind.

The single was released in 2015 and features singer Meghan Trainor.

Gaye's name is used as a verb in the song, which draws inspiration from Motown.

The song reached number four in Australia and went two times Platinum, but it was savaged by critics around the world.

Time Magazine even wondered why Gaye's estate didn't sue for tarnishing the star's legacy.

Puth said the song was a musical icebreaker for "any guy who wants to go up to a girl at a bar", saying it would be hard to not have a conversation about the track if it was playing.

Duck Sauce

Barbra Streisand

American singer songwriter and actress Barbra Streisand. (Reuters: Tobias Schwarz)

Canadian American DJ duo Duck Sauce's catchy 2010 hit has nothing to do with the most successful female singer in history — but naming the song after her got people's attention and helped it to the top of the charts all over the world — including the top 10 in Australia and number 15 on triple j's Hottest 100 for 2010.

The lyrics of the song mention all sorts of random things with regular interruptions from people saying Barbra Streisand.

So far Babs hasn't returned the favour by recording a song named Duck Sauce … but never say never …

David Bowie

Andy Warhol

David Bowie became a huge fan of Andy Warhol after seeing the pop artist's play Pork in London in 1971 — but apparently had already written this song before seeing it.

It first appeared on his classic LP Hunky Dory.

Bowie flew to New York to meet Warhol and play him the song — which the notoriously self-conscious artist apparently didn't like because of the line "Andy Warhol looks a scream".

Many years later — after Warhol's death in 1987 — Bowie played him in the 1996 film Basquiat — wearing one of Warhol's infamous wigs. Apparently, the likeness was so convincing that even Warhol's brother thought that it was Andy.

High praise indeed.

Ice Spice

Princess Diana

Princess Diana in 1996. (Reuters)

Princess Diana was released in 2023 by drill rapper Ice Spice, who hails from the birthplace of rap music — The Bronx.

There's a remix version featuring rapper Nicki Minaj. That version peaked at number four on the Billboard Hot 100.

The song is a nod to memes comparing portraits of Ice Spice to the late princess.

The rapper has also been given the nickname "The People's Princess", a title synonymous with Princess Diana.

DDG featuring Gunna

Elon Musk

Owner of X and CEO of Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk. (Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes)

Named after the richest person in the world, Elon Musk is a melodic track with a galactic-themed music video.

American rapper and online streamer DDG says the song came to him while he was freestyling on a day that Musk was going viral on X.

DDG was asked in an interview uploaded by pop culture site and content studio Uproxx what he would do with a billion dollars.

"I feel like I'd be giving away a lot of money," DDG said.

"I like buying stuff for other people.

"I get more satisfaction out of giving people stuff than giving myself something."

World.title: Man in custody over attack against Helen Haines named
World.content:
The man arrested after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines can be revealed as Brendan Nugent.

The 43-year-old has been in custody since he was arrested yesterday afternoon and has spent this morning being questioned by detectives.

Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason said: "They are ascertaining exactly what occurred, how and why".

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

A source with close knowledge of the investigation told the ABC that Mr Nugent was known to police.

It is understood he has undergone a mental health assessment.

Ms Haines, 65, who has represented the people of Indi since 2019, suffered critical injuries and remains in hospital in Melbourne.

She was retrieving items from the boot of her vehicle at the time of the alleged attack.

Victoria Police are working to establish the motivation for the attack, including whether it was politically motivated.

World.title: NAB to slash up to 2,500 jobs in massive restructure
World.content:
National Australia Bank says it will cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, by mid-2027.

That would include up to 1,500 roles before the end of this year, NAB said in a statement to the stock exchange.

In addition to the internal cuts, NAB also plans to "materially reduce its use of consultants and external contractors".

The announcement, lodged with the ASX on Tuesday morning, said it was part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers".

The bank has flagged a restructuring charge of approximately $300 million, pre-tax, with more details to come in its full-year results announcement on November 5.

Australian banks, large and small, have been cutting their workforces, with a major restructure at ANZ leading to thousands of job losses in the past year.

Last month, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank proposed cutting 137 jobs as part of an ongoing restructure.

'Rapid technological change' contributes to cuts

While there was no direct reference to artificial intelligence in the NAB release, it did refer to "rapid technological change".

"NAB is implementing these changes as part of a broader review to identify the nature of the workforce required to support NAB's strategic ambition in an evolving operating environment," the bank said.

"These actions will help make NAB a stronger bank, better placed to navigate risks and opportunities arising from more challenging economic conditions, increasing customer expectations, competitive intensity and rapid technological change."

NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said there would be no material effect on customer-facing banking roles.

"These changes are expected to improve outcomes for customers by reducing duplication and speeding up decision-making," he said.

"We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions … We have also deliberately made deeper changes to senior management positions, which will broaden leadership responsibilities across the bank."

Mr Irvine acknowledged it would be a "difficult period" for the employees affected and pledged to treat everyone "with dignity and respect".

World.title: NFL QB in hospital at 4am before London game due to blood clots
World.content:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in both lungs, according to his team and his agent, with media reports saying the former Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season.

Hurts was clinically stable but his treatment would involve blood thinners, which would rule him out of contact activities, the Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said in a statement.

The 28-year-old was initially diagnosed with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis after an ultrasound in London before Philadelphia's 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which Hurts played in.

The current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bilateral pulmonary embolism is where a blood clot travels from a deep vein in the body, often the leg, and blocks an artery in both lungs.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," the statement said.

"We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners."

It said no long-term effects were expected.

According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of the game and did not sleep the night before the contest as a health precaution.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, local time, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said the team cared about its players and he trusted the medical staff.

"I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them," Sirianni said.

"We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players' health first and foremost in every situation. And, you know, that's where we were there."

The Eagles said in a statement on Thursday that their medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the ultrasound results and concluded that "activity and mobility were important" and that Hurts could safely play in the game against the Jaguars, adding that he "played without limitation".

Hurts guided the Eagles to the Super Bowl title in February 2025, throwing for two touchdowns and running in another against the Kansas City Chiefs to earn the game's Most Valuable Player trophy.

Reuters

World.title: Lawyer says video from Town Hall protest shows 'degrading' police treatment
World.content:
New footage has emerged in court of what protesters allege was unlawful force by police at a Sydney rally against the visit of Israeli President Isaac Herzog.

Adam Adelpour and 15 other protesters are set to face trial next year on charges including assaulting police at the Town Hall demonstration on February 9.

The defence played dozens of videos in the local court on Friday to explain the relevance of certain documents police were avoiding giving the protesters.

Hours of footage were cut into a 32-minute compilation for the court by the defence and not all the clips showed the moments leading up to the clashes.

Solicitor Nick Hanna, representing some of the protesters, told the court the footage showed unlawful arrests and excessive force.

In multiple videos, police could be seen grabbing protesters by the head or neck as they brought them to the ground.

Vision from Sydney protest against Israeli President Isaac Herzog at Town Hall. (Supplied)

'They've had all day to pray'

The montage included different angles of police forcibly moving on a group of men performing the Muslim sunset prayer, a moment that went viral online.

Loading...

Mr Hanna said the CCTV showed a police officer had made a false statement by claiming the worshippers started praying after being told to disperse.

"At some point before police start moving, you see that people are already praying," he said.

In police body-worn camera footage, protesters could be seen pleading with officers to allow the men to finish praying.

Some of the footage comes from police body-worn cameras. (Supplied)

A female officer was heard saying, "They've had all day to pray", before officers began to break up the group.

In another clip, a male officer could be heard saying, "Try and walk him in the s**t", as his colleagues led away a man in handcuffs.

Mr Hanna said it was presumably a reference to the horse faeces left on the ground that night by mounted police.

He said it constituted improper conduct because it was degrading and humiliating.

Request for ministerial messages

The defence team is trying to gain access to communications between senior officers and Premier Chris Minns, Police Minister Yasmin Catley, Sports Minister Steve Kamper and their staff.

Other documents it has sought to subpoena include standard operating procedures for things like the use of capsicum spray.

Sydney anti-Herzog protest hearings begin The Town Hall protest against the Israeli president's visit to Sydney generated hundreds of complaints about police misconduct.

A NSW Police spokesperson said they were unable comment as the matter remained before the court.

Barrister Bradley Dean, acting for Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon, argued against the release of the material.

"The subpoena is not an occasion for a fishing expedition," Mr Dean said.

On Monday, local court Judge Scott Nash ruled in favour of the protesters, agreeing the material had a "legitimate forensic purpose".

But whether all the documents will be released to the defence remains to be seen, with police also claiming public interest immunity over some categories.

Probe into 'directions police were given'

Outside court on Monday, Mr Hanna told the ABC the police were going to great lengths to stop the defence from getting the documents.

"We suspect [the police's arguments] will involve a suggestion that to release these documents would be to jeopardise police operations and to reveal secrets that the public shouldn't know," he said.

Mr Hanna said the alleged unlawful policing at the protest were not isolated acts carried out by individual officers.

Nick Hanna is representing some of the protesters. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

He said the defence would argue it reflected a coordinated police response that was "likely from the top down".

"We have sought the communications between Minns and other ministers and the police to really find out what directions were the police given," Mr Hanna said.

He said the defence hoped more charges would be dropped after police withdrew almost half of about 30 prosecutions.

The matter is back in court on October 30, with trials expected to take place in July 2027.

World.title: TV’s best (and worst) celebrity travel hosts
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Stanley Tucci is sifting rice in an antique Italian mill near Verona. Tony Shalhoub is weeding wheat fields in Japan. Conan O’Brien is cosplaying a Viking in Norway. And Eugene Levy is kind of regretting he left home. All aboard for the celebrity travel experience, although it’s a good idea to be careful which tour you choose, because some are more rewarding than others. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Chaotic kills with Linda Cardellini, plus five more picks There’s a sizeable catalogue of performers – frequently actors and comedians, many of them Brits – who’ve parked their day jobs and taken the role of TV travel guides. Michael Palin and Billy Connolly were engaging early adopters, followed by Joanna Lumley and Martin Clunes. Chef Anthony Bourdain brought his maverick style to food-focused excursions; Ewan McGregor and Charley Boorman rode motorcycles across continents; Miriam Margolyes explored Australia in a campervan. For producers, celebrity hosts provide potentially marketable names above the title. For viewers, these tours can offer experiences flavoured by the personality of the presenter. The best hosts have an infectious energy and a genuine curiosity about (and appreciation for) the places they visit and the people they meet. Because who wants a blasé travel companion? In recent years, a new crop of hosts has been roaming the globe. Here’s a guide to some of them, listed from best to, well, maybe look elsewhere. Stanley Tucci tries lampredotto, Florentine street food made from the fourth stomach of a cow and served in a bread roll.



Tucci in Italy It started with a drink. During the pandemic, Stanley Tucci’s negroni-mixing video went viral, the award-winning actor charming people with his unfussy assurance and urbanity. Since then, his passion for food and drink has blossomed from a happy side-hustle into a mini-industry incorporating books, cookware and TV series combining travel in Italy with a culinary focus. Related Article Australian TV ‘Let’s get back to real food’: Adam Liaw’s new show is a long way from MasterChef First came Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy (2021-22), which eventually ran here on SBS and Foxtel. Now there’s Tucci in Italy, which is more interested in the technical side of food production but equally scenic. There’s a palpable love of process, a pleasure in charting how Veneto became a region renowned for radicchio and why the once-impoverished Puglia has grown into the country’s celebrated breadbasket. With a mellow voice and a twinkle in his eye, Tucci is an ideal travel companion: erudite, amiable and knowledgeable. Helpfully, he also speaks the language, making interactions with farmers, manufacturers and chefs flow easily. As he often remarks after a tasting a dish whose ingredients and preparation he’s admiringly documented, “It’s very buono.” SBS, Thursday, 7.35pm, SBS On Demand and Disney+ The Marvellous Mrs Maisel star investigates all kinds of carbs in Breaking Bread with Tony Shalhoub. Breaking Bread With Tony Shalhoub While sampling rye and pumpernickel loaves from a famed Manhattan bakery, Lin-Manuel Miranda chuckles with incredulity to his actor friend, “I don’t know how you convinced people to make this a show, that we just get to eat delicious bread.” It’s a reasonable observation and his host modestly responds, “Like I’ve been saying for 40-odd years, ‘Fooled them again.’”



Well, yes and no. That’s unduly humble because Emmy winner Tony Shalhoub clearly has the goods. He’s probably best known on TV for playing Midge Maisel’s loving, fussy dad on The Marvellous Mrs Maisel and the obsessive-compulsive detective in Monk. In this six-part series, he’s relishing various combinations of flour and water. But as his guest succinctly notes of the production’s underlying philosophy, “We’re talking about bread and bagels, but what we’re really talking about is culture and what we pass on.” Shalhoub’s approach is akin to Tucci’s, relating food to history, customs and the capacity to bring people together. And like Tucci, he’s interested in the fusion of tradition and innovation. He has a fine time sampling pizza in New Jersey, learning about kaizen in Japan and eating “dirty bread” in Sao Paolo. A joyful exploration of his love of baked goods, this is not a show recommended for those keen to cut carbs. SBS On Demand The Fren family take it easy in Travel Guides. Travel Guides While the other series listed here bank on presenters as drawcards, this is the anti-celebrity alternative. Here regular folk, the Average Joe and Joanne, visit places likely to pique viewers’ interest. It’s like a Gogglebox variation that sees the participants getting off the couch and hitting the road. Typically, the mix of guides includes a trio of mates up for a good time; Insta-ready BFFs; a gay couple; a family; and a mature-aged couple. They’re all primed for the challenge of heading to mystery locations and mostly enthusiastic about what they encounter because this is an enterprise that values its sponsors and aims to showcase places in the best possible light. Narrated by Denise Scott with a strong Aussie inflection, the show has true-blue tone and a lively spirit. 9Now*



Eugene Levy catches up with Prince William in The Reluctant Traveller. Eugene Levy: The Reluctant Traveller As an actor with a gift for comedy, Eugene Levy has been a delight for decades, particularly in Christopher Guest’s mockumentaries (Waiting For Guffman, Best in Show, A Mighty Wind) and as a key contributor to the acclaimed Schitt’s Creek. But in this role, he’s not so wonderful. As the title announces, he’s not an enthusiastic traveller. Not really keen to explore, he doesn’t like heat, cold or being in water and he’s happy at home. So why he’d be tapped to front a travel show, except from some notion of novelty or plain perversity, remains a mystery. Related Article Australian TV Sam Pang is the most popular man on TV. Now what? But the offer propelled him out of the house and for three seasons he’s tentatively explored the big wide world and done it in high style, experiencing the ride in a fashion most mere mortals could only dream about: luxuriating in a hotel-palace in Venice; touring Windsor Castle with Prince William; visiting a Maldives resort where he’s the recipient of “Olympic-style pampering” in a 3000-square-foot villa with an expansive ocean view and a private infinity pool. Watching him apprehensively enduring this VIP treatment feels like taking a long-awaited trip saddled with a dyspeptic uncle and feeling only relief when he grudgingly concedes that it’s better than he expected. The whole production just makes me feel crabby that one of the biggest companies in the world isn’t bankrolling my bucket list. Apple TV In Conan O’Brien Must Go, the US talkshow host drops in on foreign fans, but it’s really just an excuse to get dressed up as a viking or tango in Argentina. Binge



Conan O’Brien Must Go The gangly comedy writer, former Tonight show host and current podcaster with the conspicuous ginger pompadour presents a not-especially-likeable impression of an American abroad. The premise of the show is that O’Brien drops in on people who’ve called into his podcast and, over three seasons, he’s covered a lot of ground, from Argentina, New Zealand and Ireland to the Netherlands and Morocco. He’s always ready to play the clown, dressing up in funny hats and period costumes as he pretends to learn about a place. His humour is fast and sharp and some of it, thankfully, is directed at himself. The introduction to episodes, read by German filmmaker Werner Herzog, describes the host, among other putdowns, as a being “fuelled by a bottomless hunger for recognition and the occasional selfie”. It’s all deliberately off-beat and provocative. But while the contrived wackiness minimally assists in elevating the undertaking from being an entirely hollow vanity project, O’Brien’s basically using the world as a backdrop for his antics. It gets old, fast. Binge, Foxtel *9Now is owned by the publisher of this masthead. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: ‘Spelling mistakes everywhere’: How an email from the heart got this AFL prospect a scholarship
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Spelling mistakes everywhere’: How an email from the heart got this AFL prospect a scholarship Marc McGowan October 20, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wil Malady will be drafted into the AFL next month. Most prognosticators expect the jack-in-the-box forward, who boasts some of the best aerial highlights of any prospect in this year’s class, to be gone inside the first 15 picks. Wil Malady is tipped to be a first-round selection at next month’s AFL draft. via Getty Images The AFL academy member has long arms, a big leap, and ran the 20-metre sprint at the draft combine in a blink-of-the-eye 2.9 seconds. Malady’s aunty also happens to be Nicki Malady, Richmond’s media boss. Yet not that long ago, the country boy from Bairnsdale had to resort to begging to land a scholarship at Caulfield Grammar.



Malady previously aborted his plans to relocate to Melbourne for school – privately conceding he was not ready to move 280 kilometres away from family – but a standout performance at the AFL under-16 championships on the Gold Coast two years ago stoked the fire again. He returned home as an All-Australian after being the hero in Victoria Country’s under-16 title win, and told his parents he wanted to apply. AFL draft hopeful Wil Malady takes a strong mark playing in the APS grand final for Caulfield Grammar. TikTok Football was a key driver in Malady’s decision, but he also wanted to prioritise his schooling, given he was weighing up dropping out to be an apprentice electrician if he stayed home. The problem was the scholarship deadlines had long since passed.



“All the applications were closed for scholarships, so I sat down and wrote these rogue emails, with spelling mistakes everywhere. It was horrible,” Malady told this masthead, laughing. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft “I sent one to Dad, and he’s like, ‘You’ve got to fix all this’. I was like, ‘It’s too late. It’s already sent’. “I wrote heaps of emails to all the boarding schools in the APS. I was lucky enough that a few got back to me, which were Melbourne Grammar, Scotch [College], and then Caulfield.” Fortunately for Malady, those schools found his mistakes charming.



Staff at each of the three institutions rang his dad and cheerily told him it was abundantly obvious that his son’s email was authentic and sincere. “I just wrote that I was a country boy from Bairnsdale, and I wanted to play footy and better my schooling,” Malady said. “They rang Dad and were like, ‘We can tell this kid’s written it. There’s no AI – it’s truly from the heart’, which was pretty cool.” Malady’s athleticism is one of his key appeals to recruiters. Getty Images After all that, he never met with Melbourne Grammar, and Scotch College pulled out, but Caulfield Grammar came to the party. Fellow Gippsland Power rising star Marlon Neocleous went to Caulfield, too, which helped Malady’s transition as a boarder, and he never looked back.



It meant more travel at times, but that is nothing new for Malady or many of his Power teammates. Related Article AFL 2026 Who the players rate as the cream of the crop in this year’s AFL draft “It’s crazy. To get to ‘Gippy’ training when I was back home [in Bairnsdale], it was almost two hours,” he said. “I’d leave school at 3.15, bus it down [to Morwell], get back at 10, sleep, get up the next morning, and go to school. It was a struggle, but Mum and Dad helped a lot and would sometimes pick me up instead of me going on the bus that goes through all the towns. “Making the AFL is my dream, so it was all worth it.”



Malady played only seven matches for Gippsland this past season, but kicked 18 goals, including five in the Power’s drought-busting grand final triumph over the Dandenong Stingrays, the same opponent they beat for their inaugural premiership 21 years earlier. The Power were coached by Kris Pendlebury, brother of AFL games record-holder Scott. Malady, left, kicked five goals in Gippsland Power’s Talent League grand final win. Getty Images “It was a massive day,” Malady said. “The build-up was crazy, and then game day came around and nerves were high, but after a bit of a slow start, everything clicked and came together. I was lucky enough to kick five in the second half.”



Malady’s athleticism, rangy frame and marking ability often see him likened to Carlton forward Will Hayward or Geelong’s All-Australian winger Ollie Dempsey, who Malady has studied closely this year. Hawk Jack Gunston is another star he looks up to. Related Article AFL 2026 Why this nephew of a premiership Pie is getting attention ahead of the draft Recruiters mostly view 193-centimetre Malady as a forward, but believe he could also be effective on a wing or even at half-back. The 18-year-old’s marking ability will be an asset in any of those roles. It was on display for Victoria Country at the national championships, including one acrobatic leap against Western Australia on the wing. Malady followed up with an even better one in the APS grand final.



“The ball was put up high, and I had a free path in front of me, jumped, and he sat underneath it, so I got a good ride,” he said. “It’s pretty good when you bring them down. It’s a bit annoying when you’re up there and hold it all away, then you get to the ground and drop it – but I love taking a big hanger.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

The heritage-listed Fellworth Flats, one of the few sandstone structures remaining in Bondi, now houses this cosy little pub devoted to Britpop, mushy peas and Guinness on tap. Cushy booths, sandstone walls and Cheers-style stained-glass lightshades give it a beautifully nostalgic feel, while a hand pub pours Beekeeper’s own beer, the Newtown-made Keepers Cask ale.

Cocktail highlights include two-sip thinking negronis, martinis and a Clover Club – gin, dry vermouth, a little raspberry syrup and a squeeze of fresh lemon, shaken over ice until frosty. If you’re feeling suboptimal, there’s an excellent Bloody Mary with plenty of Worcestershire sauce, which they’ll allow you to turn into a Bloody Maria (tequila instead of vodka) or a Red Snapper (gin instead of vodka or tequila).

The food menu is full of hearty food like the comforting steak pie with flaky pastry, creamy mash, peas and a pool of gravy. See also the Cumberland sausage, mash, caramelised onions and gravy. It’s the kind of place that’s hospitable, family-friendly and dog-friendly, with a casual vibe that’s tightly run at the back end.

World.title: Melbourne Assembly live: Ex-New York mayor, PM share visions to improve liveability
World.content:
As the Melbourne Assembly civic forum takes a short break, we continue to look back on stories we’ve published about shaping the city.

As Royce Millar wrote recently, Sunshine, Dandenong, Broadmeadows and Footscray would see the most significant change in housing density as Melbourne faces “crunch time” finding places to live for its burgeoning population.

Projections of what Melbourne could look like in 2101 if urban sprawl is contained show the number of dwellings increasing by almost 2 million, and the city’s west, as far out as Melton, copping the brunt of that change.

The suburban centre with the largest increase in dwelling numbers would be Box Hill, rising from 6826 today to 24,427. It is followed by Footscray with 20,117 and Sunshine with 11,689 dwellings, demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (.id) estimates.

World.title: Helen Haines attack live updates: Brendan Nugent identified as alleged attacker; Indi MP remains in critical condition after being struck multiple times by car outside Wangaratta office
World.content:
Director-General of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Mike Burgess has warned about “violent rhetoric in public discourse”, as he said the “temperature and trajectory of the security environment” was concerning.

“I acknowledge the horrific attack on Helen Haines and our thoughts are with Helen, her family and loved ones, and also those who responded yesterday,” Burgess said in a statement.

The National Terrorism Threat Level remains at PROBABLE, but the temperature and trajectory of the security environment are concerning.

Elevated levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation continue to create a permissive environment of violence.

I have repeatedly put on the record my concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse.

Words matter.

While political differences, debates and peaceful protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy, ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence.

Disagreement is okay but acts of violence and intimidation are not – especially against those democratically chosen to represent us.

By all means disagree but consider how you disagree. By all means protest but consider how you protest. By all means criticise elected officials but consider how you criticise elected officials.

This incident occurred in an environment where politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years.

I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint.

We must take these threats seriously, protect those being targeted and defend Australians’ right to share their points of view in a peaceful way.

ASIO and our partners in law enforcement will continue to work around the clock to protect Australia and Australians.

World.content:

The Australian sharemarket opened sharply lower on Tuesday, with miners leading the losses and only tech stocks advancing after a rebound in artificial-intelligence stocks on Wall Street. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 89.9 points, or 1 per cent, at 8755.80 as of 10.20am AEDT, with all of its 11 sectors in the red bar technology. The losses come after the bourse added 0.4 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US69.81¢. Miners led declines, with copper heavyweight BHP - the biggest stock on the ASX - down 1.9 per cent after saying its copper output slumped by almost 20 per cent in the September quarter. National Australia Bank dropped 0.8 per cent after announcing it will axe up to 2500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, over the next financial year. Wall Street advanced as AI stocks rebounded following a sharp selloff on Friday. AP On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 rose 0.4 per cent, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1 per cent because it’s full of technology stocks. The majority of US stocks outside of AI and tech fell, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average swung between losses and gains before finishing with a drop of 36 points, or 0.1 per cent.



In Europe, the losses were sharper, and indexes slid more than 1 per cent following violent protests that could ultimately force the French government to increase its spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put even more pressure on bond markets, and yields cranked higher worldwide. Related Article Aviation Vietjet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze Even with all the cross currents flowing through financial markets, AI stocks stood out, as they have for most of the past few years. A frenzy in spending for AI technology has forced them to the forefront of the market, sending them to record prices and driving indexes higher. Last week, AI stocks grabbed the spotlight after tumbling on worries about how expensive it has become to borrow money, which could threaten the boom. Much of the spending on AI chips and data centres has come from borrowed money, and Treasury yields in the bond market have recently hit their highest levels in years or even decades. That has raised the cost of borrowing money for everyone. Nvidia added 1.4 per cent overnight and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total market value, a 1 per cent move for its stock has more effect on the index than any other’s.



SpaceX, which controls the xAI business, rose 1.3 per cent to $US147.96. Its founder, Elon Musk, pledged on Monday to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year. The offer came after Anthropic said over the weekend that it will commit 5 per cent of the shares in its highly anticipated initial public offering of stock to a new “public benefit” fund. The moves for AI stocks were still choppy, though. Consider CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud and has been at the centre of the market’s swings. After initially jumping more than 7 per cent in the morning, it flipped to a loss of 3.5 per cent before finishing with a dip of 0.4 per cent. That followed its loss last week of 25.2 per cent. The swings came ahead of profit reports coming later in the week that could offer more details about the strength of AI-related spending. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Lam Research, which supplies equipment and services for the making of semiconductors, will also talk about how its business is doing on Wednesday. Expectations are high across the board for US companies’ profits from the summer. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of 29 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 from the prior summer, according to FactSet. Those high expectations are what has allowed the US stock market to run to records despite worries about war, high inflation and pressure from the bond market.



Cleveland-Cliffs rallied 16.3 per cent after reporting a bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said it was the strongest quarter for the company in three years and that the outlook for profit in 2027 “has improved materially” from three months ago. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In other international markets, rebounds for AI stocks helped South Korea’s Kospi jump 1.8 per cent to recover some of its 14.5 per cent drop from last week. It is dominated by two huge players in the AI industry, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which has made it much jumpier than other markets. In Europe, bond yields climbed following the French protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The protests could put pressure on governments to boost their spending to offer help, but that would likely only add to their already big piles of debt. Yields rose for French bonds on worries about the government’s already strained budget and climbed much more than yields for German government bonds, which investors have historically seen as a safer bet.



In the US bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.14 per cent from 5.09 per cent late on Friday. It topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002. Oil prices remained shaky. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, swung between $US107 and $US110 through the day before settling at $US109.55, down 0.3 per cent. It has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US110 this month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the energy industry to return to normal. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: TV’s best (and worst) celebrity travel hosts
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Stanley Tucci is sifting rice in an antique Italian mill near Verona. Tony Shalhoub is weeding wheat fields in Japan. Conan O’Brien is cosplaying a Viking in Norway. And Eugene Levy is kind of regretting he left home. All aboard for the celebrity travel experience, although it’s a good idea to be careful which tour you choose, because some are more rewarding than others. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Chaotic kills with Linda Cardellini, plus five more picks There’s a sizeable catalogue of performers – frequently actors and comedians, many of them Brits – who’ve parked their day jobs and taken the role of TV travel guides. Michael Palin and Billy Connolly were engaging early adopters, followed by Joanna Lumley and Martin Clunes. Chef Anthony Bourdain brought his maverick style to food-focused excursions; Ewan McGregor and Charley Boorman rode motorcycles across continents; Miriam Margolyes explored Australia in a campervan. For producers, celebrity hosts provide potentially marketable names above the title. For viewers, these tours can offer experiences flavoured by the personality of the presenter. The best hosts have an infectious energy and a genuine curiosity about (and appreciation for) the places they visit and the people they meet. Because who wants a blasé travel companion? In recent years, a new crop of hosts has been roaming the globe. Here’s a guide to some of them, listed from best to, well, maybe look elsewhere. Stanley Tucci tries lampredotto, Florentine street food made from the fourth stomach of a cow and served in a bread roll.



Tucci in Italy It started with a drink. During the pandemic, Stanley Tucci’s negroni-mixing video went viral, the award-winning actor charming people with his unfussy assurance and urbanity. Since then, his passion for food and drink has blossomed from a happy side-hustle into a mini-industry incorporating books, cookware and TV series combining travel in Italy with a culinary focus. Related Article Australian TV ‘Let’s get back to real food’: Adam Liaw’s new show is a long way from MasterChef First came Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy (2021-22), which eventually ran here on SBS and Foxtel. Now there’s Tucci in Italy, which is more interested in the technical side of food production but equally scenic. There’s a palpable love of process, a pleasure in charting how Veneto became a region renowned for radicchio and why the once-impoverished Puglia has grown into the country’s celebrated breadbasket. With a mellow voice and a twinkle in his eye, Tucci is an ideal travel companion: erudite, amiable and knowledgeable. Helpfully, he also speaks the language, making interactions with farmers, manufacturers and chefs flow easily. As he often remarks after a tasting a dish whose ingredients and preparation he’s admiringly documented, “It’s very buono.” SBS, Thursday, 7.35pm, SBS On Demand and Disney+ The Marvellous Mrs Maisel star investigates all kinds of carbs in Breaking Bread with Tony Shalhoub. Breaking Bread With Tony Shalhoub While sampling rye and pumpernickel loaves from a famed Manhattan bakery, Lin-Manuel Miranda chuckles with incredulity to his actor friend, “I don’t know how you convinced people to make this a show, that we just get to eat delicious bread.” It’s a reasonable observation and his host modestly responds, “Like I’ve been saying for 40-odd years, ‘Fooled them again.’”



Well, yes and no. That’s unduly humble because Emmy winner Tony Shalhoub clearly has the goods. He’s probably best known on TV for playing Midge Maisel’s loving, fussy dad on The Marvellous Mrs Maisel and the obsessive-compulsive detective in Monk. In this six-part series, he’s relishing various combinations of flour and water. But as his guest succinctly notes of the production’s underlying philosophy, “We’re talking about bread and bagels, but what we’re really talking about is culture and what we pass on.” Shalhoub’s approach is akin to Tucci’s, relating food to history, customs and the capacity to bring people together. And like Tucci, he’s interested in the fusion of tradition and innovation. He has a fine time sampling pizza in New Jersey, learning about kaizen in Japan and eating “dirty bread” in Sao Paolo. A joyful exploration of his love of baked goods, this is not a show recommended for those keen to cut carbs. SBS On Demand The Fren family take it easy in Travel Guides. Travel Guides While the other series listed here bank on presenters as drawcards, this is the anti-celebrity alternative. Here regular folk, the Average Joe and Joanne, visit places likely to pique viewers’ interest. It’s like a Gogglebox variation that sees the participants getting off the couch and hitting the road. Typically, the mix of guides includes a trio of mates up for a good time; Insta-ready BFFs; a gay couple; a family; and a mature-aged couple. They’re all primed for the challenge of heading to mystery locations and mostly enthusiastic about what they encounter because this is an enterprise that values its sponsors and aims to showcase places in the best possible light. Narrated by Denise Scott with a strong Aussie inflection, the show has true-blue tone and a lively spirit. 9Now*



Eugene Levy catches up with Prince William in The Reluctant Traveller. Eugene Levy: The Reluctant Traveller As an actor with a gift for comedy, Eugene Levy has been a delight for decades, particularly in Christopher Guest’s mockumentaries (Waiting For Guffman, Best in Show, A Mighty Wind) and as a key contributor to the acclaimed Schitt’s Creek. But in this role, he’s not so wonderful. As the title announces, he’s not an enthusiastic traveller. Not really keen to explore, he doesn’t like heat, cold or being in water and he’s happy at home. So why he’d be tapped to front a travel show, except from some notion of novelty or plain perversity, remains a mystery. Related Article Australian TV Sam Pang is the most popular man on TV. Now what? But the offer propelled him out of the house and for three seasons he’s tentatively explored the big wide world and done it in high style, experiencing the ride in a fashion most mere mortals could only dream about: luxuriating in a hotel-palace in Venice; touring Windsor Castle with Prince William; visiting a Maldives resort where he’s the recipient of “Olympic-style pampering” in a 3000-square-foot villa with an expansive ocean view and a private infinity pool. Watching him apprehensively enduring this VIP treatment feels like taking a long-awaited trip saddled with a dyspeptic uncle and feeling only relief when he grudgingly concedes that it’s better than he expected. The whole production just makes me feel crabby that one of the biggest companies in the world isn’t bankrolling my bucket list. Apple TV In Conan O’Brien Must Go, the US talkshow host drops in on foreign fans, but it’s really just an excuse to get dressed up as a viking or tango in Argentina. Binge



Conan O’Brien Must Go The gangly comedy writer, former Tonight show host and current podcaster with the conspicuous ginger pompadour presents a not-especially-likeable impression of an American abroad. The premise of the show is that O’Brien drops in on people who’ve called into his podcast and, over three seasons, he’s covered a lot of ground, from Argentina, New Zealand and Ireland to the Netherlands and Morocco. He’s always ready to play the clown, dressing up in funny hats and period costumes as he pretends to learn about a place. His humour is fast and sharp and some of it, thankfully, is directed at himself. The introduction to episodes, read by German filmmaker Werner Herzog, describes the host, among other putdowns, as a being “fuelled by a bottomless hunger for recognition and the occasional selfie”. It’s all deliberately off-beat and provocative. But while the contrived wackiness minimally assists in elevating the undertaking from being an entirely hollow vanity project, O’Brien’s basically using the world as a backdrop for his antics. It gets old, fast. Binge, Foxtel *9Now is owned by the publisher of this masthead. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: ‘Spelling mistakes everywhere’: How an email from the heart got this AFL prospect a scholarship
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Spelling mistakes everywhere’: How an email from the heart got this AFL prospect a scholarship Marc McGowan October 20, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wil Malady will be drafted into the AFL next month. Most prognosticators expect the jack-in-the-box forward, who boasts some of the best aerial highlights of any prospect in this year’s class, to be gone inside the first 15 picks. Wil Malady is tipped to be a first-round selection at next month’s AFL draft. via Getty Images The AFL academy member has long arms, a big leap, and ran the 20-metre sprint at the draft combine in a blink-of-the-eye 2.9 seconds. Malady’s aunty also happens to be Nicki Malady, Richmond’s media boss. Yet not that long ago, the country boy from Bairnsdale had to resort to begging to land a scholarship at Caulfield Grammar.



Malady previously aborted his plans to relocate to Melbourne for school – privately conceding he was not ready to move 280 kilometres away from family – but a standout performance at the AFL under-16 championships on the Gold Coast two years ago stoked the fire again. He returned home as an All-Australian after being the hero in Victoria Country’s under-16 title win, and told his parents he wanted to apply. AFL draft hopeful Wil Malady takes a strong mark playing in the APS grand final for Caulfield Grammar. TikTok Football was a key driver in Malady’s decision, but he also wanted to prioritise his schooling, given he was weighing up dropping out to be an apprentice electrician if he stayed home. The problem was the scholarship deadlines had long since passed.



“All the applications were closed for scholarships, so I sat down and wrote these rogue emails, with spelling mistakes everywhere. It was horrible,” Malady told this masthead, laughing. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft “I sent one to Dad, and he’s like, ‘You’ve got to fix all this’. I was like, ‘It’s too late. It’s already sent’. “I wrote heaps of emails to all the boarding schools in the APS. I was lucky enough that a few got back to me, which were Melbourne Grammar, Scotch [College], and then Caulfield.” Fortunately for Malady, those schools found his mistakes charming.



Staff at each of the three institutions rang his dad and cheerily told him it was abundantly obvious that his son’s email was authentic and sincere. “I just wrote that I was a country boy from Bairnsdale, and I wanted to play footy and better my schooling,” Malady said. “They rang Dad and were like, ‘We can tell this kid’s written it. There’s no AI – it’s truly from the heart’, which was pretty cool.” Malady’s athleticism is one of his key appeals to recruiters. Getty Images After all that, he never met with Melbourne Grammar, and Scotch College pulled out, but Caulfield Grammar came to the party. Fellow Gippsland Power rising star Marlon Neocleous went to Caulfield, too, which helped Malady’s transition as a boarder, and he never looked back.



It meant more travel at times, but that is nothing new for Malady or many of his Power teammates. Related Article AFL 2026 Who the players rate as the cream of the crop in this year’s AFL draft “It’s crazy. To get to ‘Gippy’ training when I was back home [in Bairnsdale], it was almost two hours,” he said. “I’d leave school at 3.15, bus it down [to Morwell], get back at 10, sleep, get up the next morning, and go to school. It was a struggle, but Mum and Dad helped a lot and would sometimes pick me up instead of me going on the bus that goes through all the towns. “Making the AFL is my dream, so it was all worth it.”



Malady played only seven matches for Gippsland this past season, but kicked 18 goals, including five in the Power’s drought-busting grand final triumph over the Dandenong Stingrays, the same opponent they beat for their inaugural premiership 21 years earlier. The Power were coached by Kris Pendlebury, brother of AFL games record-holder Scott. Malady, left, kicked five goals in Gippsland Power’s Talent League grand final win. Getty Images “It was a massive day,” Malady said. “The build-up was crazy, and then game day came around and nerves were high, but after a bit of a slow start, everything clicked and came together. I was lucky enough to kick five in the second half.”



Malady’s athleticism, rangy frame and marking ability often see him likened to Carlton forward Will Hayward or Geelong’s All-Australian winger Ollie Dempsey, who Malady has studied closely this year. Hawk Jack Gunston is another star he looks up to. Related Article AFL 2026 Why this nephew of a premiership Pie is getting attention ahead of the draft Recruiters mostly view 193-centimetre Malady as a forward, but believe he could also be effective on a wing or even at half-back. The 18-year-old’s marking ability will be an asset in any of those roles. It was on display for Victoria Country at the national championships, including one acrobatic leap against Western Australia on the wing. Malady followed up with an even better one in the APS grand final.



“The ball was put up high, and I had a free path in front of me, jumped, and he sat underneath it, so I got a good ride,” he said. “It’s pretty good when you bring them down. It’s a bit annoying when you’re up there and hold it all away, then you get to the ground and drop it – but I love taking a big hanger.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

After initially jumping more than 7 per cent in the morning, it flipped to a loss of 3.5 per cent before finishing with a dip of 0.4 per cent. That followed its loss last week of 25.2 per cent. The swings came ahead of profit reports coming later in the week that could offer more details about the strength of AI-related spending. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Lam Research, which supplies equipment and services for the making of semiconductors, will also talk about how its business is doing on Wednesday. Expectations are high across the board for US companies’ profits from the summer. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of 29 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 from the prior summer, according to FactSet. Those high expectations are what has allowed the US stock market to run to records despite worries about war, high inflation and pressure from the bond market.



Cleveland-Cliffs rallied 16.3 per cent after reporting a bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said it was the strongest quarter for the company in three years and that the outlook for profit in 2027 “has improved materially” from three months ago. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In other international markets, rebounds for AI stocks helped South Korea’s Kospi jump 1.8 per cent to recover some of its 14.5 per cent drop from last week. It is dominated by two huge players in the AI industry, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which has made it much jumpier than other markets. In Europe, bond yields climbed following the French protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The protests could put pressure on governments to boost their spending to offer help, but that would likely only add to their already big piles of debt. Yields rose for French bonds on worries about the government’s already strained budget and climbed much more than yields for German government bonds, which investors have historically seen as a safer bet.



In the US bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.14 per cent from 5.09 per cent late on Friday. It topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002. Oil prices remained shaky. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, swung between $US107 and $US110 through the day before settling at $US109.55, down 0.3 per cent. It has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US110 this month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the energy industry to return to normal. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
