World.title: ‘Slowly losing myself’: Elina Svitolina announces end of marriage to Gael Monfils amid Ukraine war
World.content:
SportAustralian Open ‘Slowly losing myself’: Elina Svitolina announces end of marriage to Gael Monfils amid Ukraine war October 20, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

World No.6 Elina Svitolina said she and the recently retired Gael Monfils were ending their marriage, with the Ukrainian adding that the emotional toll of Russia’s war in her homeland left her needing to rediscover herself. The couple married in July 2021 and welcomed a daughter, Skai, in October 2022. Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils teamed up for mixed doubles in this year’s US Open. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II Announcing the separation in an Instagram post, Svitolina described the personal struggles she has faced since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the impact they had on her life away from the tennis court. “This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share,” Svitolina wrote. “Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside.



“Last year, I told you I needed to step away from the court because I wasn’t in the right emotional space. Today, I want to open up a little more. What you didn’t see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself. “Gael saw all of it. He never let go of my hand. We fought through this together for a long time, with everything we had. But some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you.” Elina Svitolina during the 2026 US Open. Getty Images Svitolina asked for kindness and privacy as the family navigates the separation, stressing there was no one to blame. “With time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage,” the 32-year-old Australian Open semi-finalist added.



“It is the hardest truth I have ever had to face and the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love. “Gael listened. He has respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget. Gael has loved me through my greatest joys and my darkest moments, and I have loved him with all my heart ... Skai will always come first. Our marriage is ending, but our family is not. We will always be her parents, side by side, at every step of her life.” ‘I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage.’ Elena Svitolina On the court, four-time grand slam semi-finalist Svitolina recently secured her place at the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California. Frenchman Monfils, 40, a former world No.6 and one of the most charismatic players of his generation, has retired from professional tennis, according to the International Tennis Integrity Agency.



He planned to retire at the end of 2026 and bid farewell at November’s Paris Masters, but the ITIA now lists him as retired. Reuters

World.title: Police officer who stole police-issued firearm starred in police recruitment series
World.content:
A police officer who stole a police-issued firearm starred in a police recruitment series, and was awarded the Commissioner's Award for leadership in his recruit wing, it can now be revealed.

RNZ earlier revealed a police officer had been charged with stealing a police-issued firearm and being in unlawful possession of a police-issued firearm.

On Tuesday, the officer Steven John Karehana pleaded guilty to the charges. Following his guilty plea an interim suppression order was lifted. Karehana will be sentenced in December.

The 42-year-old starred in the police recruitment video series, Ride Along.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

His parts in the series appear to have since been removed from YouTube, and his name has been removed from a press release about the series.

In one episode seen by RNZ, Karehana spoke of his journey to joining the Police.

"I guess for me it was a long journey. Took me around about 20 years from my first application to being accepted into police college, and I've been out for about four months now.

"So I first applied in 2003, and I was denied because of what had happened in my youth, and I applied probably every five years after that until I got a job as a painter, and I stayed in that job for 16 years.

"It wasn't until I went and worked for my iwi, and through that journey, it reignited the love and passion for my community and my people."

A screen grab from Ride Along. NZ Police/Youtube

He said being an older recruit he brought "different life skills, life experiences to the police".

"My why for joining is to be a role model for our people.

"By showing them rather than just talking about it, it can go a long way into helping build those relationships once again."

Karehana's name has also been removed by Police from a press release put out in October 2024 celebrating Wing 378.

The original version, seen by RNZ, said he was awarded the Commissioner's Leadership Award.

"This is the beginning of our journey in the New Zealand Police, but for all of us graduating, there are many people who have sacrificed and worked hard to allow us to be here, and we are very grateful. We could not have done it without you.

World.title: Police failed to objectively examine scene after Rachel Molloy's death in Mt Eden - IPCA
World.content:
Police officers investigating the death of a Mt Eden woman failed to objectively examine the scene and reached conclusions without robust evidence, an Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) has found.

Rachel Molloy was found at the bottom of the 10 concrete stairs that led up to her central Auckland flat, late at night on May 4, 2022.

Despite knowing the 30-year-old was both the alleged victim and central witness in an upcoming sexual assault trial, the fall - and her death - were treated as an accident.

The IPCA found while officers first on the scene did a good job, detectives who arrived soon after failed to take fingerprints or secure the scene.

They also failed to communicate adequately with Molloy's family.

Auckland City District Commander, Superintendent Sunny Patel, said police met with Molloy's family and apologised to them last month.

"At the outset, we extend our deepest sympathies to Ms Molloy and her family for their loss of Rachel," Patel said.

"We acknowledge that it has been an incredibly challenging period for the Molloy family over recent years."

World.title: New Zealand signs $1.6 billion deal to buy five navy helicopters and weapons
World.content:
New Zealand has signed a $1.6 billion deal with the US government to buy five navy helicopters and weapons.

It is one of the biggest single purchases so far under the Defence Capability Plan.

The Seahawks have anti-submarine torpedoes and air-surface missiles.

The Defence Force has been looking into this for months and the US government agreed to it in June under its Foreign Military Sale system.

The NZDF says the Seahawks can fly faster and further than its old choppers, increasing the frigates' offensive, defensive and surveillance capabilities.

The choppers made by a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin are due to arrive from 2030 at Whenuapai air base.

They will cost an additional $110 million a year to operate, plus funding would be needed to upgrade the air base.

One reason Defence went with this deal is that Australia operates Seahawks.

World.title: 'We'll be talking health, my friend': Christopher Luxon, Chris Hipkins prepare for final debate
World.content:
National leader Christopher Luxon says health will be a fixture of tonight's final leaders' debate, as Labour challenges him for a debate on the issue.

Luxon and Labour leader Chris Hipkins will face off for the third time on Stuff this evening.

But ahead of the debate, Hipkins challenged Luxon to a debate squarely focused on health, saying the health system is in crisis.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407107622112

"I'm up for it. I challenge Christopher Luxon to join me," Hipkins said in a social media video released on Monday.

Health is a key issue for many New Zealanders this election.

It is second place on the Ipsos Issues Monitor, with only the cost of living ahead of it as the issue on most people's minds.

Ahead of the debate, Labour released a plan for improvements at emergency departments.

Luxon, who has maintained he has "certainly strengthened healthcare", again spoke of the government's work on Tuesday morning.

TVNZ/Harley Peters

Luxon said the healthcare system was "incredibly challenged," and a "difficult area," but said that was the case all around the world.

"It's challenging. It's definitely not perfect, by any stretch of the imagination. But we have made significant improvements. You know, we've got record investment going into healthcare. We've got record investment going to GPs. We've got record hiring of new workforce and development of homegrown workforce as well."

Asked about Hipkins' challenge, Luxon pointed to Tuesday night's debate.

"We'll be talking health, my friend, tonight, and I look forward to seeing Mr Hipkins tonight. It'll be great fun."

Hipkins said he was disappointed, and he wanted a dedicated debate on health because it was one of the biggest issues facing the country.

"This isn't about tactics. This is about one of the most important issues facing all New Zealanders: whether the health system is going to deliver you the care you deserve."

ACT leader David Seymour has said he is willing to debate Hipkins on health if Luxon would not.

"Chris Hipkins is measurably the worst health minister in modern New Zealand history, capable of vaporising billions of taxpayer dollars while healthcare performance got worse," Seymour said.

"Every one of the government's health targets - emergency department stays, cancer treatment times, elective surgery wait times, child immunisation, and first specialist appointments - has improved under the Coalition."

Luxon, meanwhile, has zeroed in on law and order as a topic for debate.

"Look at the other side. I mean, they want to meet with gangs and they want to pay gangs, and we know they're soft on crime. I haven't seen a single law and order policy from Labour, for example, over the course of this election campaign."

Hipkins, who has confirmed Labour would not give any money to the Mongrel Mob, has said while there is a case to put money into drug and alcohol rehabilitation programmes, the money should not be going to gangs.

Speaking on Morning Report on Tuesday morning, he criticised the previous Labour government's support of the Mob-led programme.

"I think that was a mistake. I think supporting meth addiction is absolutely something governments should do, but giving the money to the gangs is wrong."

The $2.75 million funding, taken from the Proceeds of Crime Fund, was originally signed off by Jacinda Ardern, Grant Robertson, Poto Williams, and Kris Faafoi.

Later on Tuesday morning, Hipkins distanced himself from the decision further.

World.title: Political leaders called on to commit to ending youth homelessness
World.content:
The youth development organisation Kick Back is calling on political leaders to commit to ending homelessness among young people, ahead of the election.

Its general manager Aaron Hendry said in the last five months they have helped 74 children and young people to access shelter in Auckland.

"In some cases these young people have been sleeping rough, sleeping outside on our streets. In other cases they're couch surfing in dangerous situations or living in their cars," he said.

"We're seeing a lot of young people really high in complex trauma, addiction, mental health, disabilities, often in really dangerous and vulnerable situations."

He said they were seeing an "alarming" number of children aged under 14 coming to Kick Back's youth homelessness crisis response and early intervention centre, The Front Door.

"It is getting younger and younger and there's real concerns around the safety of children who are extremely vulnerable and are going through some really tough stuff."

Hendry said Kick Back was asking political parties to agree to a dozen steps, including introducing duty to assist laws, developing a strategy to end youth homelessness and providing access to emergency housing.

"These are things like increasing investment in youth housing services and public housing services, rolling back the emergency housing policy and investing in immediate housing so that when people need housing they can get it," he said.

"Youth homelessness shouldn't be a partisan issue, our children's safety is far too important."

Hendry said so far, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity have accepted all 12 calls to action, Labour has committed to seven and they are yet to get a response from National, ACT and NZ First.

The 12 steps are:

1. Roll back the emergency housing reforms to ensure that everyone who needs immediate access to shelter can get it

2. Stop benefit sanctions against people experiencing - or at-risk of - homelessness

3. Increase investment in Immediate Housing services

4. Introduce Duty to Assist Legislation so that no young person is turned away when they seek help

5. Prevent transitions from state care into homelessness

6. Strengthen youth services for young people experiencing homelessness by resourcing them adequately

7. Increase public housing and youth-focused housing options

8. Develop a national strategy to end youth homelessness

9. Increase investment in outreach and integrated service centres

10. Form a regional and national crisis response rōpū to actively respond to the escalating homelessness crisis

11. Return access to the benefit to 18-19 year olds

World.title: New poll puts election on knife-edge with Opportunity close to 5% threshold
World.content:
Audio player for " Deputy political editor Craig McCulloch on new poll " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2035492%2Fnew-poll-puts-election-on-knife-edge-with-opportunity-close-to-5-percent-threshold

Deputy political editor Craig McCulloch on new poll Morning Report

The latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll is pointing to a neck and neck result with the two major parties just over a single percentage point apart.

Labour has edged slightly ahead on 29.7 percent with National close behind on 27.6 percent while Opportunity stands poised as a potential kingmaker at 5.4 percent despite sitting close to the threshold to enter Parliament.

The results are holding steady from September's poll as the election enters its final stretch ahead of the beginning of early voting next week.

The Green Party remains stable at 14.3 percent, NZ First has dipped to 11.8 percent, ACT is holding its position on 9 percent while Te Pāti Māori remains on the fringes at 2 percent.

The result raises the stakes for both of the major parties and will see leaders Chris Hipkins and Christopher Luxon eager to take points of the other as they meet for their final major debate, hosted by Stuff and The Post, on Tuesday night.

RNZ deputy political editor Craig McCulloch told Morning Report this election was shaping up to be New Zealand's most unpredictable during the MMP era given Opportunity party is sitting on the 5 percent threshold meaning that a mere fraction of a percentage point could turn the whole race on its head.

Asked about Labour's poor polling, the party's leader Chris Hipkins said he would like support to be further ahead but "there is one poll that matters, and it is the poll that everybody gets to participate in, except for the people whose votes are going to be disqualified because of the dodgy law changes this government have pushed through."

World.title: Rise of GLP-1 unlocking new opportunities for New Zealand's premium food exports
World.content:
Audio player for " Morning rural news " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/2036071%2Frise-of-glp-1-unlocking-new-opportunities-for-new-zealand-s-premium-food-exports

The rise of GLP-1 weight loss drugs giving rise to more nutrition conscious consumers is good news for New Zealand farmers and growers.

The weight loss drugs, which mirror our natural hormone GLP-1 and regulate appetite, are seen to be disrupting the food sector, accelerating health-conscious trends seen post-Covid.

It means consumers are increasingly moving away from ultra processed foods as they look for more nutritional value from their foods.

Rabobank's new report - New Zealand's protein moment - found tight global beef and sheepmeat supply will mean positive prices in the near-term, but longer-term value will depend on market diversification, customer relationships and reliable delivery.

The report found GLP-1 weight-loss medications were accelerating the increased demand for protein, with US surveys suggesting nearly 1 in 8 adults has used a GLP-1 medication for weight loss in recent years.

Senior animal protein analyst Jen Corkran, who wrote the report, said while the strong prices helped open doors today, they were not a long-term strategy on their own.

"People using these medications generally eat less, but that does not mean demand for every food will fall at the same rate. Because weight loss can include the loss of lean body mass, protein is increasingly being positioned as important for preserving muscle," she said.

"The commercial signal is not simply 'more protein' or 'more meat'. It is about useful, high quality protein that delivers nutrition, convenience, eating quality and value for a smaller appetite."

Jen Corkran says currently New Zealand is experiencing great returns on red meat because there's a lack of supply.

Corkran said capturing lasting value would depend on proving claims behind nutrient-dense red meat products to increasingly deliberate consumers across diverse markets.

"It's being driven by a lack of global supply of red meat right now. The beef production is about 2 percent down on last year and there just isn't enough around the world so New Zealand is experiencing great returns because there's a lack of supply."

Corkran expected these conditions to continue for two to three years - noting rising input costs and volatility were also expected to remain.

She said this still provided a favourable window for farmers to grow the value of their products.

"This is a good season for farmers, processors and exporters to build the next one - to broaden their market and customer options, strengthen the evidence behind nutrition and provenance claims, and keep improving how product is delivered beyond the farmgate," she said.

"Tight supply may support farmgate prices for a time, but proven value is what is more likely to keep customers with us as the cycle turns."

RNZ/Carol Stiles

Premium fruit offerings also benefiting

Rockit Apples grows and sells miniature apples, promoting them as a healthy snack option.

Its chief executive Grant McBeath said the trend was helping grow demand for premium fruits like theirs.

He said consumers around the world appreciated its consistent quality, as well as health benefits and convenience.

"GLP-1 absolutely is a global phenomenon that is changing categories in supermarkets and health shops [...] it's absolutely driving growth in fruit and vegetables.

"We believe our product is ideally suited for those consumers that want a healthy, unprocessed snack - and that's where the tube format which is re-sealable, different pack format, different pricing options really remove the friction from consumers choosing a healthy snack versus something else."

Miniature apples from Rockit Apples. Zespri / supplied

And it's a similar story for kiwifruit.

Zespri chief marketing officer KokHwee Ng said the rise of GLP-1's is part of a broader trend where consumers are more selective about nutrition.

Speaking from Singapore, she said consumers are also increasingly looking for science backed nutrition claims.

For example the European Commission recognised last year that eating two green kiwifruit a day contributed to normal bowel function by increasing stool frequency].

"We know that when consumers are looking at premium fruit, consumers are always seeking the basic of taste and quality [...] but we know that's kind of just the beginning.

"To the conversation on GLP-1 they're becoming more selective and intentional about their nutritional consumption so value in terms of seeking more nutrient rich food in their diet and the composition of this food starts to matter a lot more to consumers."

World.title: Scott Watson's appeal being heard in Supreme Court
World.content:
Scott Watson's appeal of his double-murder conviction is being heard in the Supreme Court.

Watson was sentenced to life imprisonment for murdering Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in the Marlborough Sounds and has now been behind bars for 27 years.

The Blenheim friends, aged 21 and 17, were last seen stepping off a water taxi onto a stranger's yacht in Endeavour Inlet the early hours of 1 January, 1998, after a New Year's Eve party at Furneaux Lodge.

Their bodies have never been found.

Watson was found guilty of the murders in 1999 after an 11-week jury trial involving about 500 witnesses.

He appealed his convictions after the trial but the application was dismissed. He made another two applications that were unsuccessful before a 2017 bid for a royal pardon was granted, with the case heard by the Court of Appeal in 2024.

It focused on the use of photo montages shown to witnesses ahead of the original trial and the reliability of forensic testing used to show two hairs found on Watson's boat that belonged to Hope.

Ben Smart and Olivia Hope NZ Police

Watson relied on new expert opinion challenging the reliability of the forensic evidence at trial about the two hairs found on a tiger-patterned blanket aboard his boat.

It also considered whether a photo montage used by police had predisposed witnesses to pick out Watson.

At the original trial, the Crown's case relied completely on the positive identification of Watson by water taxi driver Guy Wallace, who dropped off the young pair to a stranger's yacht in the early hours of New Year's Day.

The court's decision, released last September, found there was no miscarriage of justice in relation to the hair evidence or the identification of Watson by Wallace.

Watson then sought leave to appeal that decision.

The Supreme Court granted the appeal in part, approving only the question of whether the Court of Appeal had been correct to conclude no miscarriage of justice arose from the decision of the trial judge to admit visual identification evidence of Guy Wallace.

The appeal focuses on the use of photo montages shown to Wallace.

World.title: Quick hits: Renshaw floored by miracle grab as Bavuma's six stops traffic
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has been shocked by his own miracle grab, while Temba Bavuma's soaring six has stopped the Gqeberha traffic on a day when a soggy outfield threatened to ruin it all.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. A soggy outfield almost ruins it all

Things did not look good as the scheduled start of play approached on day two. Dark skies and pouring rain meant a delay was inevitable.

But within two hours, the rain had ceased, and another hour after that, the sun was beating down in Gqeberha.

The St George's ground staff had a lot on their plate on day two. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The St George's outfield, however, just wasn't playing ball. Three surface inspections came and went, with the umpires and ground staff determining the soggy turf too treacherous for play on each occasion.

The two areas of particular concern, both deep in the outfield, were simply refusing to drain.

It was Test cricket at its exasperating, excruciating worst, and the threat of an entirely lost day loomed on the horizon.

But five hours after the scheduled start of play, and more than three since the last downfall, the officials finally determined the field fit for purpose.

By the time the Australian bowlers were going through their warm-ups, it was a glorious day in the Eastern Cape.

2. Hazlewood the latest to succumb to sickness

But when the Australians finally got on the field for a 30-over evening session, they were without one of their most dangerous weapons.

Josh Hazlewood was battling sickness and nowhere to be seen at St George's Park, leaving just the — admittedly serviceable — trio of Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc and Scott Boland for the South African batters to contend with.

A day earlier umpire Chris Gaffaney was forced to withdraw from the Test with a bout of food poisoning, no doubt leaving those in attendance wondering if there might be a dish to avoid at the St George's canteen.

Hazlewood is expected to return on day three.

3. Carey poised for 200

Scott Boland picked up from where he left off as play finally got underway. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

It was typically outstanding stuff from Boland as day two belatedly began.

The Victorian had Temba Bavuma swinging and missing dramatically with the first ball of the afternoon. He only had to wait until his second set of the day to claim his third wicket of the match, luring Marques Ackerman into a drive and nicking off the debutant for six.

Meanwhile, behind the stumps, Alex Carey was nearing a major milestone.

And when Mitchell Starc had Matthew Breetzke edging through to the Australian wicketkeeper only moments later, Carey was one take away from becoming the fifth Australian gloveman to take 200 catches in Test cricket after Adam Gilchrist, Ian Healy, Rod Marsh and Brad Haddin.

Carey will hope to join that group on day three.

4. Bavuma interrupts traffic with massive six

It was an absolutely massive six, and it came from absolutely nowhere.

Bavuma had been so composed and diligent in steadying ship after the losses of Ackerman and Breetzke, and looked set to defend his way to stumps.

But the South Africa captain absolutely exploded in hooking Cummins over the backward square leg boundary.

Temba Bavuma's six interrupted the Gqeberha traffic. (Fox Cricket)

The ball sailed over the rope, out of the stadium and then rolled onto the road, where a security guard was forced to weave through the Gqeberha traffic to collect it.

5. Renshaw stunned by own miracle grab

With only a matter of minutes remaining in the day's play, Australia was pushing for the one final wicket that would put them well on top in the game.

Shadows were lengthening, light was fading quickly, and Marnus Labuschagne had just put down a relatively simple catch at leg slip.

Visibility clearly wasn't great but, somehow, Matt Renshaw produced something remarkable.

Renshaw took a remarkable catch late on day two. (Fox Cricket)

It was definitely Carey's catch, but the Australian wicketkeeper was rooted to the spot as Ryan Rickleton edged towards the men behind the wicket.

The ball looked destined to fly between the keeper and slip, but there he was, Renshaw, diving at full stretch and managing to get his right hand between ball and turf.

Matt Renshaw was blown away by his stunning catch. (Fox Cricket)

The Queenslander looked absolutely stunned to have taken the catch that had South Africa rocking at 5-97 at stumps.

World.title: FIFA given deadline to answer questions over failed World Cup sell-off
World.content:
Soccer's governing body in Europe UEFA has given FIFA until November 2 to release documents relating to Gianni Infantino's aborted attempts at a secretive investment plan for the World Cup and other governance issues.

The latest move in a power struggle between the two governing bodies came in the week after UEFA's European delegates were disappointed by what they perceived as a lack of clarity by FIFA president Infantino over the issues at a FIFA council meeting last week.

Infantino provided no documents about the $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) FIFA World Cup sell-off plan he launched and quickly dropped in July amid a fierce backlash led by Europe.

Among the 42 questions that UEFA is demanding an answer to are: Infantino's personal remuneration package, financial payments made to singer Marc Anthony, the handling of US striker Folarin Balogun's disciplinary case, business and political relationships involving Donald Trump and his family, and the operational independence of FIFA's judicial, electoral, and ethics committees.

UEFA asked US federal courts to authorise subpoenas compelling the production of documents and sworn testimony about the abandoned investment plan called FIFA Forward Enterprise.

FIFA lawyers have claimed UEFA is harassing Infantino.

UEFA expresses deep dissatisfaction

The formal letter, signed by UEFA general secretary Theodore Theodoridis on behalf of European FIFA council members, stated Infantino's apology for his actions and subsequent explanation failed to address their core concerns.

"These explanations have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions raised by Council members. Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been [provided]," the letter said.

"The withdrawal of FFE, the recognition of mistakes, and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the FIFA Council was not involved at the appropriate stage."

UEFA has demanded a response by November 2 — 16 days before the nomination deadline for the presidential election next March 18.

With the next FIFA council meeting scheduled for December 16 in Doha — after nominations close — UEFA insisted that answers cannot wait.

"These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the FIFA Council — nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them," the letter emphasised.

The earlier deadline would give federations time to assess FIFA's answers — or its failure to answer — while they can still nominate or endorse a challenger.

AP

World.title: Toll of war in Ukraine cited as Svitolina, Monfils announce end of marriage
World.content:
World number six Elina Svitolina says she and former tennis player Gael Monfils are ending their marriage, with the Ukrainian adding that the emotional toll of Russia's war in her homeland left her needing to rediscover herself.

The couple married in July 2021 and welcomed a daughter, Skai, in October 2022.

Announcing the separation in an Instagram post, Svitolina described the personal struggles she had faced since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the impact they had on her life away from the tennis court.

Loading Instagram content

"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," Svitolina wrote. "Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside.

"Last year, I told you I needed to step away from the court because I wasn't in the right emotional space. Today, I want to open up a little more. What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself.

"Gael saw all of it. He never let go of my hand. We fought through this together for a long time, with everything we had. But some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you."

Svitolina asked for kindness and privacy as the family navigates the separation, stressing there was no-one to blame.

"With time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage," the 32-year-old Australian Open semi-finalist said.

"It is the hardest truth I have ever had to face and the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love.

"Gael listened. He has respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget. Gael has loved me through my greatest joys and my darkest moments, and I have loved him with all my heart.

"Skai will always come first. Our marriage is ending, but our family is not. We will always be her parents, side by side, at every step of her life.

"There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape."

On the court, four-time grand slam semifinalist Svitolina recently secured her place at the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

Frenchman Monfils, 40, a former world number six and one of the most charismatic players of his generation, has retired from professional tennis, according to the International Tennis Integrity Agency.

He planned to retire at the end of 2026 and bid farewell at November's Paris Masters, but the ITIA now lists him as retired.

Reuters

World.title: One man down and on a flattening pitch, Boland and Starc continue to shine
World.content:
As the afternoon meandered on and the stubbornly soggy outfield of St George's Park threatened to waste another day of the second Test at Gqeberha, South Africa had good and bad fortune to ponder.

The good news was that upon the game's long-awaited resumption at 3:45pm local time, Australia would be without one member of its intimidating quartet of fast bowlers due to illness. The bad news, with no disrespect to the others, was that it wasn't Scott Boland.

Sure enough, within 10 minutes of the restart, the Victorian had struck again to remove debutant opener Marques Ackerman — Boland's third wicket in five typically compelling overs.

Boland puts Australia in the box seat Scott Boland continues to deliver for Australia as the tourists make the most of a rain-shortened day two of the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha.

Worse still for the Proteas, Mitchell Starc, who'd been a little out of sorts in his brief spell on day one, was hitting his straps too. Bowling with fluency and at speeds nudging towards 150km/h, the left-armer soon struck as well thanks to a lazy waft outside off stump from Matthew Breetzke and a smart catch from Alex Carey.

At that stage, South Africa was 4-40 and staring into the abyss.

What transpired in the hour that followed was heartening for South Africa, though perhaps not enough to shift the course of this truncated contest.

The pitch — whose lack of hessian coverings during the worst of the downpours was said to be predictive of imminent mayhem — seemed to flatten out and not behave so treacherously at all.

The batting, circumspect but not unadventurous, started to look less fragile as Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma got going with South Africa's recast number six, Ryan Rickelton. And the missing bowler, Josh Hazlewood — who Cricket Australia says will return on day three — was suddenly looking like a real hole in the bowling rotation.

Indeed, a bubbly 50-run partnership later, and with stumps not far away, Bavuma could have permitted himself some satisfaction that he and Rickelton had pulled things out of the fire so calmly. He might also have felt his side's bad luck was starting to turn when a sun-blind Marnus Labuschagne put down Rickelton at leg slip.

As ever, though, Boland had other ideas. Well, one idea, to be honest: hammer away on a patch of the pitch roughly the size of a Wisden cricketers' almanac and wait for the ball to seam either way.

The burly right-armer duly took Rickelton's outside edge and Matt Renshaw, at first slip, took a catch that could be charitably described as fortunate; it looked like Carey's, but the keeper didn't move a muscle; Renshaw did, on a significant delay, grasping it in one hand when the ball was past him and then slowly mouthing some easily-made-out words of relief: "Oh. My. God."

Thus, from a relatively promising position, the Proteas finished the day 5-97 from the 43 overs that have been possible so far. Boland, with 4-31 from 14 overs, was not simply the pick of the bowlers but a one-man show who single-handedly lifted the contest out of its torpor, his every delivery imbued with potential.

Now that he is ranked in the world's top 10 Test bowlers without commanding regular selection, it is often said that Boland is unlucky. Another way of looking at it is that, at 37 — an overripe age for a fast bowler of any kind, let alone one so vigorous and impactful — he simply knows his own virtues and limitations better than he did as a younger man, and can conserve and channel his energies in ways the regulars cannot.

It is also, surely, a minor triumph of man management. That Boland and, perhaps more so, Starc continue to glide to the crease in such prolonged spells and with such devastating impact is not a matter of luck. Today, again, Starc, who is also pushing 37, was a genuine menace: a 148km/h bouncer to Bavuma was as scary as anything he bowled in his 20s.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

We talk often of Starc's eye-popping strike rate of 45 — six better than Dennis Lillee and Mitchell Johnson, seven better than Glenn McGrath and Jeff Thomson, 12 better than Starc's old sparring partner Shane Warne — but it is now his longevity that is so unusual to the point of freakishness.

Playing in his 109th Test, Starc is bowling at a level that history suggests should be impossible. Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee, the express quicks of preceding decades, were done with Test cricket at 31 and 32 respectively; like Johnson, they'd strung together 70-something Tests between the inevitable injuries.

Touch wood, Starc will feasibly play 50 or 60 more Tests than that — a coda of similar length to Merv Hughes's entire Test career. The way Cricket Australia has balanced Starc's financial and physical preparation requirements for the last decade is an organisational triumph that should be studied. If only it, and Starc himself, were replicable.

As for South Africa, what they can replicate remains to be seen, but it's very unlikely, as in Durban, that promising 50-partnerships will get this one done.

World.title: Athletes out for gold at 'really important' Special Olympics Australia
World.content:
Tenpin bowler Charlotte Bailey knows what it is like to appear before an audience.

She has addressed United Nations events to advocate for the rights of people with a disability in the workplace.

"I loved speaking at the United Nations and sharing my story," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport.

"If my voice helps another person with a disability get a chance, then that makes me very happy."

Bailey, who lives with Down syndrome, has already accomplished more than most her age.

And now she is stepping up again to represent the ACT in tenpin bowling at the Special Olympics Australia 2026 National Games.

"Events like this are really important," Bailey said.

"People get to see what athletes with disabilities can do."

Charlotte Bailey has addressed the United Nations twice, to advocate for people with disabilities in the workforce. (Supplied)

Bailey started bowling competitively about five years ago, and despite never participating at this level before, she is ready for the challenge.

"At first, I just did it for fun, and then I started getting better, and my scores improved," Bailey said.

"I went to competitions and did well. That's when I thought that I could do this.

"I'm looking forward to competing, meeting other athletes and doing my best."

'It helps people focus on our abilities'

The Special Olympics Australia National Games are held every four years.

They bring together athletes from across the country with an intellectual disability and/or autism and began in 1986.

The focus is on courage, connection, community and the power of inclusion.

More than 850 athletes will take part in this year's events, which run until October 23, in Melbourne.

Athletes will compete across 13 sports at the Albert Park sporting precinct.

Loading Instagram content

Along with tenpin bowling, other sports include athletics, basketball 5v5, bocce, equestrian, football (soccer), golf, gymnastics, swimming, table tennis, tennis, netball and DanceSport, a form of competitive ballroom and Latin dancing.

Bailey said it is an important opportunity for people to see what the disabled community can do.

"They see our skills. They see our hard work. They see our determination," she said.

"It helps people focus on our abilities, not our disabilities."

Advocating for something bigger

Bailey believes the right support is necessary for anyone to achieve their goals.

Working at both the ACT Down Syndrome & Intellectual Disability Association and a local bistro, she knows the importance of feeling supported.

She said her employers are right behind her as she chases sporting success.

International Day of People with Disability Find out how you can get involved this year on the IDPwD website.

"They understand that sport is important to me; they encourage me to follow my goals," Bailey said.

"I am lucky. Many people don't get the opportunities I have had or have bosses that are as great as mine.

"When we have the right support, we can achieve our goals."

While competing at a national level doing something she loves is a huge personal milestone, Bailey never loses sight of the bigger picture.

With her work ethic, she hopes to show people with a disability that living the life they want is attainable.

"I've worked hard. I've spoken at the United Nations. I've represented people with disabilities," Bailey said.

"I played netball and bowl with Special Olympics; I have jobs that I love.

"I want other people with disabilities to know that they can dream big too."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Boland puts Australia in the box seat against South Africa after rain-shortened day
World.content:
Australia's fast bowlers have put it in a strong position after a heavily rain-affected second day of the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha.

South Africa's captain Temba Bavuma (41*) led a spirited rearguard but the late dismissal of Ryan Rickelton, brilliantly caught at first slip by Matthew Renshaw, meant Australia took the honours from the 30 overs of play managed.

South Africa closed play at 5-96, Scott Boland the pick of the Australian bowlers with figures of 4-31.

Forced to wait for many hours, first for the rain to clear and then for the outfield to sufficiently dry, the players finally took to the field for an extended evening session.

Scott Boland shone again on day two in Gqeberha. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Boland, also the stand out of day one's brief spell of play, picked up where he left off by promptly taking the wicket of debutant Marques Ackerman, who was caught behind for 6.

Matthew Breetzke put up a brief rearguard alongside Bavuma but fell playing away from his body to a rising Mitchell Starc delivery.

When Breetzke was caught behind for 4 the score was 4-40 and there were justifiable fears of a major South African collapse.

But the steady hands of Bavuma and Rickelton settled their side and then punched back, their partnership dragging the hosts back into the game.

There was time for one more twist though with Renshaw's incredible reflex catch, claimed in one-hand low and to his right, removing Rickelton for 31 in the closing overs of the day.

With better weather forecast for the final three days of this Test match there remains hope of a result on a pitch that should get progressively better for batting.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Aussie seamer Darcie Brown cut down by back injury
World.content:
Darcie Brown's bid to feature in the inaugural T20 Women's Champions Trophy in India has suffered a huge blow after she was ruled out of the upcoming WBBL season with a back injury.

The Adelaide Strikers' pace ace was diagnosed with a disc injury following her participation in the Australia A tour of India last month.

It was initially hoped a period of de-loading would allow Brown to recover in time for the WBBL season, which runs from October 29 to December 5.

But Cricket Australia confirmed on Monday the injury had not healed sufficiently to allow Brown to resume training.

The news is a big blow to Brown, who was dropped ahead of this year's T20 World Cup and was looking to win back her spot in time for the T20 Champions Trophy in India from February 14-28.

The back injury also ruled the 23-year-old out of Australia's recent 3-0 ODI clean sweep of Bangladesh.

Brown has played six Tests, 30 ODIs and 41 T20s for Australia, and will be a huge loss for the Strikers this WBBL season.

"Darcie is a quality player who will be missed on the field, but she remains a hugely important part of our squad," Strikers coach Luke Williams said.

"She brings outstanding experience, professionalism and leadership, and those qualities will continue to have a positive influence on our group throughout WBBL 12."

Australia are 1-0 up in their three-match T20 series against New Zealand after posting a tense two-wicket win at North Sydney Oval on Sunday.

Games two and three will be held at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally runs over friend with car
World.content:
St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally ran over his close friend with a car on a private property in Western Australia earlier this month.

The ABC was contacted by two separate sources who said the accident occurred at a party at a rural property in Yallingup, in the state's south-west.

The ABC has been told that the victim was hospitalised with broken bones.

But despite the severity of the injuries, the ABC understands emergency services were not called to the scene.

Do you know more? Contact Jessica Halloran at Halloran.Jessica@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page.

St Kilda confirmed the accident occurred and said in a statement: "The St Kilda Football Club is aware of an incident involving Charlie Banfield on a rural private property in Western Australia.

"Our thoughts are with Charlie and the injured individual, who we understand will make a swift and full recovery.

"The club has already spoken to Charlie about this incident and will continue to support him through the matter."

It is understood the pair are close friends and no legal action would be taken against Banfield, as it was being treated as an accident.

Fiona Stanley Hospital has confirmed the young man was hospitalised but has since been discharged.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had not received any reports regarding the incident, while St John Ambulance said it did not have a record of attending the area that night.

Charlie Banfield with his mother Amber and his father Drew ahead of him making his AFL debut in May. (Instagram: @stkildafc)

The 19-year-old midfielder grew up in WA and made his AFL debut this year.

The ABC contacted Banfield's mother, Amber, who did not wish to comment.

Amber Banfield spent six years on the board of the West Australian Football Commission, while his father, Drew Banfield, was a two-time premiership player for the West Coast Eagles.

The teenager was picked up by the Saints after the Eagles decided not to match their bid in last year's national draft.

Banfield was recruited from the Claremont Colts in the WAFL, winning the Mel Whinnen Medal as best on ground in the 2025 WAFL Colts Grand Final.

He was also vice-captain at his prestigious Perth private school, Scotch College.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

President Donald Trump announced this afternoon that Elon Musk’s SpaceX shares for children will be given through Trump Accounts. Musk said earlier today that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” sometime next year. Musk had thanked Trump Account booster Brad Gerstner for “helping enable this,” and Trump appeared to confirm the plan in a post on Truth Social.

Given the value of SpaceX’s stock on Friday, 72 million shares would be worth approximately $10.5 billion, according to CNBC. “This will be the first of many,” Musk said.

Tech.title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.

Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.

America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.

While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world.

The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.

Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.

New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

Tech.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.

Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.

When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more

To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.

“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.

I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.

CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.

The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds

So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.

Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.

Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.

Tech.title: I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance.

The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. I tested the (now discontinued) Ring Car Cam when my son was learning to drive, but he hated it and refused to turn it on; I wondered if the Miles could provide the same peace of mind without feeling as intrusive.

Miles Plug is a small device without a screen or battery that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port, This is the rear. It slotted into the port on my Toyota easily.

Billed as “a wearable for your car,” Miles is a tiny cellular and GPS-enabled device that connects to an app to deliver real-time location, alerts, and driving insights (speeding, hard braking, trip recaps). The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs.

Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. They worked at Wink in the early days and bring combined experience from Amazon (Ring and Blink), Ubiquiti’s smart home line, and other companies. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.”

You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product. — Matt McGovren

Miles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). All plans are paid upfront with no auto-renewal. Anyone in the family can download and use the app, with each driver getting their own profile and alerts. Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker).

While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years.

McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. The app lets you download your data, stop location collection, and delete your account and all its data.

The Miles is very small and works with most gas and hybrid cars made in 2008 or later.

I set up Miles in my 2014 Toyota Highlander I nicknamed Tanya and have been using it for a couple of days. Setup was simple, and the app is clean, uncluttered, and easy to follow. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. I plugged it into my OBD-II port, and it read my VIN and correctly identified my car.

It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). Arrived- and left-home alerts came through promptly, and the events tab flagged hard acceleration and a cluster of three hard-braking alerts when I was running a little late to collect my daughter from work.

Previous Next





1 / 4 This is a demo screen of a car in the Miles app.

I like the home card, which shows a vehicle health summary: engine OK, fuel 63%, battery 13.5V, and the odometer reading. I played with the Miles Mechanic chatbot and asked how my car is and what upcoming maintenance is due; it answered in plain English, telling me the cabin air filter is due at about 140,000 miles, and the oil change and tire rotation at 142,500.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The Control Center lets you see and manage your data.

I haven’t been testing it long enough to comment on battery drain, an issue with earlier products in this space. “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. “We use a little bit of data to wake up and sync, but [that] doesn’t have a material impact on the battery.” He advises removing it if you won’t be driving the car for a while.

Beyond car battery life, an obvious concern for prospective users is how long Miles the company will last. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. The service shut down in 2020. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does.

McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. Charging for membership upfront is meant to avoid that type of outcome. He says the company is “well capitalized” and offers a 60-day money-back guarantee to users.

The car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app. — Matt McGovren

Automatic also had several smart-home tie-ins, but at launch Miles doesn’t connect to your smart home. McGovren says they have an MCP server in beta that could deliver “all of this information … to your AI of choice, your home assistant of choice,” he says. “And now the car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.” He envisions a future where you own your car’s data and can connect it to any service you want, and be able to ask Alexa, Siri, or Google, “When’s my next oil change?” or “How much gas is in my car?”

Miles is pitched as a solution for monitoring your teen driver, including notifications of possible crashes and risky driving, without also having to monitor their phone. But it also feels like a good solution for anyone with an older car or who doesn’t want to rely on data-tracking apps from insurance companies or car manufacturers but wants easy access to their car’s data. I plan to test it more thoroughly, hopefully try out the MCP integration, and follow up with a full review.

Tech.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
Tech.content:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.

No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.

Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.

This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.

Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.
