Tech.title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
Tech.content:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily out perform a frontier model, Soleiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words: the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

Tech.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
Tech.content:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents, which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

Tech.title: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
Tech.content:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.

But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.

While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

Tech.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
Tech.content:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.

As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.

“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.

While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.

Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote.

Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.

Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway.

The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X.

Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters.

“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.

OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.

OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.”

Security researchers have raised similar complaints, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.

The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X.

The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview.

OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing.

The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

Tech.title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
Tech.content:
Tolan, the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.

The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media. (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)

Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.

Image Credits:Tolan on App Store

Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”

The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people, who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)

Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “very cringe,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”

Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google. (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)

However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.

The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

Tech.title: Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago
Tech.content:
Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.

IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”

Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi.

The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.

our launch video from 2015 – Luka later pivoted into @replika. we were building personal agents 11 years ago! https://t.co/OBQqCF1MeW pic.twitter.com/rIS3ljEZFq — Eugenia Kuyda (@ekuyda) October 7, 2026

On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.

The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.

Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”

With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.

“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.

App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.

“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”

The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.

Image Credits:Wabi

Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.

“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”

Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.

In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.

Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.

“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.

On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.

“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”

Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

Tech.title: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips
Tech.content:
In Brief

Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.

The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.

Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.

Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

Tech.title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch
Tech.content:
In Brief

Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.

Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.

Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round.

We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

Tech.title: OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
Tech.content:
The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia.

US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release.

Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.”

William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said.

Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan.

Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive, but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government.

Pernik said there was no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.”

After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it.

While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026.

Tech.title: Election Offices in at Least 32 States Have Received Suspicious Letters
Tech.content:
At 12:20 pm last Tuesday, an official in the Louisiana secretary of state’s office opened a mailed letter and white powder fell out. The office was immediately evacuated and the employee was rushed to the emergency room. The employee was not injured, and subsequent tests showed that the substance was not harmful. By Wednesday, the office was back open.

“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Trey Williams, a spokesperson for Louisiana’s secretary of state, tells WIRED.

But the incident was not isolated. A WIRED investigation has found that over the course of the following days, election offices in at least 31 other states were targeted with similar letters as they prepared for the midterms that are now just two weeks away. Many of the states have made public statements acknowledging the receipt of these letters, but WIRED’s accounting of all the incidents shows the full scale of this campaign for the first time.

The vast majority of letters were intercepted by the United States Postal Service before they reached their intended targets, state officials tell WIRED, but in Arizona, Delaware, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Louisiana the letters were not intercepted, leading to election offices being evacuated when white powder was discovered.

The states that confirmed receipt of a letter are: Alaska, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

Election officials in 10 states—Colorado, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Texas, Vermont, West Virginia—and DC tell WIRED they have not received any suspicious packages. The eight remaining state election offices did not respond.

The white powder contained in the letters that have been opened so far has been reported as not harmful, but election offices remain on high alert.

“We are deeply concerned by these incidents,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors wrote in a joint statement. “As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”

As news of the letters being sent emerged last week, federal agencies alerted other election offices in some states that a potentially dangerous package was on the way. The FBI notified authorities in Alaska on Friday that an envelope was expected to arrive the following day. At about 9 am Saturday morning, the USPS identified the suspicious package, the Juneau Independent reported.

Tech.title: Japan’s MMX Mission Wants to Bring Martian Moon Samples Back to Earth
Tech.content:
It’s difficult to imagine a more daunting journey than one to an alien moon named after the Greek god of fear—especially when three other attempts to make that journey have failed.

And yet, as Japan’s space agency, JAXA, and its collaborators gear up to send a spacecraft to Mars’ formidably named moon, “all the members are filled with a quiet sense of excitement,” says Kiyoshi Kuramoto, who leads the mission’s slew of international scientists.

This mission, called the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is set to launch from Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center in the wee hours of Tuesday in Japan (Monday afternoon in the US). After almost a year of travel, the spacecraft will reach Mars and its two moons: Phobos, meaning fear in Greek, and Deimos, meaning dread. MMX will observe the pair from afar and collect samples from Phobos in a bid to answer a looming scientific question: How, exactly, did the moons come to be?

Researchers have been attempting similar gambits for decades. Since the 1980s, Russia has sent three probes to Phobos, all of which failed. Still, researchers are anxious to achieve this mission impossible because the origin of Phobos and its sibling remains a mystery. Some of their attributes, such as the pattern of visible light they reflect, suggest they are asteroids captured into Mars’ orbit by its gravity. But the moons’ circular orbits in line with the Martian equator indicate that they could have formed from debris left over from a collision between a nascent Mars and a gigantic asteroid, Tom Statler, MMX program executive at NASA, said at a press briefing.

The new mission is designed to help settle the debate by surveying Mars and the moons in detail using a suite of scientific instruments. With MMX’s MEGANE instrument, for instance, researchers will determine the elemental makeup of Phobos by measuring the neutrino particles and gamma rays it emits. If Phobos ends up having more volatile elements such as hydrogen or potassium, it could lean closer to the captured-asteroid hypothesis, while fewer volatiles could support the impact idea.

Tech.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
Tech.content:
Dozens of WhatsApp web pages designed to answer people’s questions about Meta’s encrypted messaging app inadvertently exposed the company’s own instructions to its chatbot. These included some sections titled “WHAT NOT TO SAY” to users asking questions and explicit instructions not to provide people with legal advice.

A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own. The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority” about the issue. WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” says Dan Saltman, the CEO and founder of Redact.dev. He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels. Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says. It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed. “We train our support chatbots to be as helpful as possible,” Breckman says.

The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading: “HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.” They are no longer visible in the live pages’ code.

Tech.title: Nathan Fielder’s Surprise Call From Elizabeth Holmes: ‘I Trust You’
Tech.content:
In the end, I decided that this time it was better not to know. It was better just to trust. And after a second talk with Fielder a few weeks after our first conversation, I learned that Elizabeth Holmes might feel the same way.

The interview has been edited for clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: I have a lot of anxiety about recording interviews.

NATHAN FIELDER: Why? About losing the recording?

Yeah.

OK. You have a backup too.

I have two.

I would do the same thing.

Do you?

What?

Double-record things?

No, but if I had your job, I would.

OK. Before we get into it, I just want you to know that I know how important it is for you to preserve the experience of the film.

Yes. But you know, some people enjoy knowing what happens. I read this thing where they told people the end of a story, and then they had another group that didn’t know, and then the group that knew the ending said they enjoyed it more.

So it could just be a me thing. Maybe it is. But I love being surprised. I love the experience of just sort of not knowing.

When this interview comes out, the film will be just out in theaters. But it was a secret for three years, right?

Yeah.

My understanding is that only a few dozen people knew it was happening.

We kept it really small.

Secrecy has been a feature of your work before. What made you decide to keep it so under wraps? Why was that important to you?

I think, firstly, it was a concern on the subjects’ part. No one knew where they were at first. But while we were shooting there, paparazzi started surrounding the location and all that. So one of the understandings was, we needed to keep it secret because it could affect things with them, and we didn’t want to do anything where our involvement would be a news story or change things with them.

In addition to that, I think when stuff comes out about a thing, then the narrative is out there, and it may affect our ability to make the project. We didn’t know who we wanted to talk to or get on camera. We didn’t have a plan when we went in, so we were just like, “It’s best to operate in a place where no one knows it exists.” We thought it would be a net benefit.

Tech.title: Hands-On: I Tried Apple’s HomeView. Is This the Smart Home Experience I’ve Been Waiting For?
Tech.content:
I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is… functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView smart display will be different. I recently spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the $299 Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board as long as the company can pull off the promised integration with third-party apps.

Preorder now Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

Bypassing 3rd-party apps is huge: Everything goes through Apple Home

Yes, the HomeView has a clock view. Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomeView’s biggest and most compelling appeal is that you don’t need to download, install and set up an account with a third-party app for each and every smart home device you own.

More from CNET

With most smart home products, you’re lucky if they integrate with the voice assistant you normally use. Once set up, in the best circumstances, you need only to interact with their app when its connection or functionality breaks (and it will), and then you’ll need to dig into settings to find out why and fix it. Sounds awful, right?

If you’re the average person trying to connect and navigate different smart home devices for the first time, the setup prospect is daunting, as the 10-plus third-party smart home apps on my phone can attest. It’s hard to overstate how big a barrier to entry Apple has just removed by exiling third-party apps from this process.

In the case of the HomeView, I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

It should work with all the new Apple Home collection devices from LG and Schneider Electric, as well as Matter and Apple Home accessories. This isn’t an exhaustive list, and it remains to be seen whether this will carry over to Google and Amazon devices, such as Nest and Ring.

Face ID recognition and personalized profiles make a big difference

From the side, the HomeView gives off strong iMac G4 vibes. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Personalized profiles for a smart home hub are an underrated feature, and their current implementation is pretty poor. Echo devices let you set up multiple profiles for family members and even guests, but God forbid you have to navigate the Alexa app to set what a guest has access to or trust that the voice print actually works. Despite having plenty of voice records for my wife and me, our Echo never seems to be able to differentiate between us.

With the HomeView, you have Face ID integrated, and in the brief time I had, it worked quickly without any bugs. An Apple representative showed me how they envision the HomeView being used in a nightstand setup in a bedroom, an environment where you want privacy and don’t want a stranger having access to your entire smart home.

The HomeView registered the owner and the correct profile immediately and pulled up relevant information, such as a calendar, scheduled events, and preferred home screen and customization options. The same carried over to the other HomeView devices Apple had set up in its simulated home environment, with the exterior HomeView offering a security camera view while limiting access for guests, while granting them certain features like temperature control or Safari access.

It can register up to six people by face and set up personalized profiles for each. While Apple didn’t go into detail or confirm this, I imagine that these include child and family accounts where you can set up parental controls.

The 7-inch square Liquid Retina display works well for a kitchen setup

The HomeView can keep your coffee and grinder company on the counter.

I keep an Echo Show and an Apolosign smart calendar in my kitchen. One helps with recipes and timers, while the other lets my wife and me coordinate meetings, appointments and important events. Both take up too much space on our kitchen counters because we don’t like how they look wall-mounted (more on that below).

The HomeView comes with a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display. I heard several people in the demo areas complain that it was too small. On the contrary, I think the size and shape are actually perfect for a smart home screen, especially one in my narrow galley kitchen with limited countertop space.



The square screen makes it easier to view and scroll through recipes, and it’s also hands-free while you’re cooking, adjustable and tiltable to suit your needs. You can easily share recipes from your iPhone directly to the HomeView by tapping it or accessing it directly through Siri AI and Safari. The recipes are also optimized to show you step-by-step screens that guide you through the process for those of us who aren’t great at following directions. Timers are also easy to access and set.

The base also keeps the screen directly off your dirty countertops. Apple placed it next to a fancy-looking espresso setup in a demo kitchen, and it looked great without being overwhelming. By contrast, my Apolosign calendar looks like a giant eyesore and immediately draws the eye of everyone who walks in and shows them our full schedule.

Smaller footprint and better functionality in my kitchen? Sold.

Wall mounting looks remarkably good and not like you nailed a tablet to your wall

When you buy a HomeView, you can choose between one ready to mount on a wall or one with a speaker base. Ajay Kumar/CNET

I like the idea of a smart home hub on my wall, but I hate how it looks in practice. I briefly considered mounting our Android-powered smart calendar to our kitchen wall as a central hub for our devices. Not only was it unsightly, but it also looked like we’d just taken a tablet and nailed it to our wall, with an ugly, dangling power cable off the bottom.

Apple showed me several examples of mounted HomeViews in different settings, and they all looked great. In Apple’s case, they’re professionally installed with a hidden, wired power connection in the wall, which the company recommends if you’re planning to use the HomeView as your main smart home dashboard for temperature control or as a security screen by your entryway, for instance. But if you don’t want to cut into your wall, you can also use an external adapter and cable to a nearby wall outlet.

For a wired install, you basically have three options. You can use the Schneider Home Power PoE wired mount, which provides hardwired power and Ethernet for $130, or a regular Power Mount AC Wired for $80, with installation by a licensed electrician. The last option, if you want to self-install, is to use a Power Mount with a USB-C Wall connector and a separate 20-watt power adapter, for $60, though this leaves an external cable dangling.

I like the look of a seamless wall-mounted HomeView enough to consider a professional install, especially since I plan to use it as my always-on smart home dashboard.

Don’t underestimate the FaceTime panel for older family members

The HomeView can be used for FaceTime video calls.

I’m not a big video call person, but as my parents get older, they default to video calls. Those calls are often shaky and low-quality on the selfie cameras of whatever ancient device they’re using. Apple’s FaceTime demo for the HomeView makes its use case particularly clear. You can get your older relatives a HomeView, even set it up for them, and they can use Siri AI to video call you as needed without needing an iPhone or iPad.

I want to note that the audio on the tabletop version of the HomeView is significantly more impressive than I expected, with easily audible, room-filling sound for both video calls and music. Not the robust bass or clear lyrics I expected from a tabletop device. A full-size HomePod will deliver better sound quality, but it far outstrips an iPad for video calls or music.

It also has easy Find My integration. Apple representatives demonstrated the feature multiple times, showing how you can ask Siri AI to find a missing phone, remote or AirPods case. It worked without a hitch each time and, notably, without requiring you to reach for a phone.

I also watched as the Apple representative demonstrated how the HomeView autoframed and autofocused on the video caller, and it did a good job of avoiding focusing on me as I lurked over her shoulder. (Hey, it’s my job to test these things!) Again, this is the sort of small but important quality-of-life feature that makes the HomeView more usable than its older competitors.

The smart displays I’ve tested don’t work that well. Is the HomeView really different?

Preorder now Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

I’ve used a lot of smart home screens that have promised a seamless home hub experience, including the Amazon Echo Show 8, Google Nest Hub, and various Android-powered smart calendar options like Apolosign and Skylight Calendar. While all of them worked, none did so well enough that I thought setting them up and managing them was particularly easy. Demoing the HomeView was a much smoother experience than I was expecting. Naturally, there were some hiccups — Siri AI didn’t always cooperate or register voice commands, but that may have been due to the loud environment, and nothing ever goes perfectly in a demo.

But overall, I was impressed with what I saw, and I can easily see the HomeView working for my own smart home. If it can pull off the miracle of integrating my disparate third-party apps and hodgepodge of systems together in one seamless interface for just $299, well, that’s an easy sell for me.

Tech.title: MapQuest App Shows You Where License Plate Readers Are in Your Area
Tech.content:
The roads have eyes, and MapQuest can now show you where they are. The navigational app added a feature this week that lets you discover where Flock cameras and other automatic license plate readers are in your neighborhood and beyond.

In a post on Bluesky, MapQuest said its app shows locations of license plate readers from Flock and many other companies — Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada and more.

To activate the feature, open the MapQuest app, tap the Layers icon and turn on the Surveillance option. You will then see tiny eyeballs on the map that indicate where license plate readers are located. If you click on an eyeball, it will show what type of license plate reader it is — dome or fixed, for example — and the exact coordinates.

More from CNET

MapQuest has been riding a wave of relevance, years after being relegated to lower-tier status by the likes of Google, Apple and Waze. In August, MapQuest refused to change Lake Ontario to Lake America in its maps despite President Donald Trump’s executive order. It then muscled into Android Auto to give drivers an alternative to Google Maps on their dashboards.

But MapQuest isn’t the first app to reveal locations of license plate readers. The others include DeFlock, FlockHopper, Pelican and LPR Maps. Some of them rely on crowdsourcing — drivers notify the app when they believe they have spotted a license plate reader and where it is.



Displaying surveillance camera locations was among the top three requests among MapQuest users, general manager Doug Bergen told CNET.



“In the last month, we’ve been inundated with direct requests from our users,” Bergen said. “They want to know where cameras are and what kind they are. Adding that information gives them a clearer picture of the road ahead and more choice in what their map shows.”



Bergen said that camera location data comes from OpenStreetMap, a global map of the world built by volunteers.

The Roads Have Eyes! 👁️Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras. — MapQuest (@mapquest.com) 2026-10-15T22:48:59.486Z

Although license plate readers have been around for decades and there are more than 140,000 all over the US, the technology has become highly unpopular. Flock cameras can collect a huge trove of data from a car: its license plate, make, model and color, and its location. Civil liberties groups and others say that all this information — input into law enforcement databases across the country — helps to create a mass surveillance network that can track everyone, not just suspected criminals.

There have been instances of Flock data being misused, such as police officers stalking ex-spouses and girlfriends and people being wrongly pulled over and accused of stealing their cars.

License plate readers are also used for more mundane operations, such as electronic toll collection on roads and bridges, traffic violations, parking enforcement, vehicle repossessions and parking gate activation for access to restricted areas.

I’m surrounded by license plate readers

I tried the new MapQuest feature. Being more of a Google Maps person, I didn’t have the MapQuest app, so I installed it on my phone.

I opened the app, found the Surveillance layer and turned it on. I was greeted by a bunch of eyeballs on the map in my city and county. I clicked on several of them and saw their coordinates and what type they were — dome, fixed, pan/tilt and so on — but I didn’t see the names of the companies that own them.

But at least now I know which streets have eyes on me.

Tech.title: Japan Launches Mission to Mars’s Moons and Plans to Bring Samples Home
Tech.content:
An ambitious Mars mission launched successfully from the Tanegashima Space Center in Japan on Monday afternoon. Led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, with contributions from NASA, the Martian Moons eXploration mission could be the first to make it all the way to Mars and back.

Not only will the mission send a spacecraft to study the Martian moons, Deimos and Phobos, but JAXA and NASA also aim to return samples from Phobos’s surface. JAXA livestreamed the historic launch.

The MMX mission launched successfully, headed to Mars. JAXA/Screenshot by CNET

“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, said in an announcement.

More from CNET

By studying these Martian moons, scientists may learn more about how our own world came to be and why the solar system looks like it does today.

The mystery of Martian moons

Many scientists believe that Earth’s moon was created long ago after one or more fast-moving objects from space collided with our planet, causing pieces to break off. This debris was captured by our planet’s orbit. Gravity collected it together over time and turned it into the rounded moon we know today.

But it’s still a theory. Similar theories surround the origins of Deimos and Phobos. Scientists think Mars’ asteroid-size moons might have formed through collision, like we think our moon formed, or the Martian moons might be asteroids that were captured in Mars’ gravity.

MMX Mission poster. JAXA

By studying the moons close up and then bringing samples home, scientists think they will be able to figure out how Deimos and Phobos came to be.

“Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds,” Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in the announcement.

Essentially, if we have more data on other moons, we’ll have a better understanding of how celestial bodies formed when our solar system was young. Studying the moons will also advance our knowledge of Mars’ surface and how the planet’s environment transitioned over eons.

NASA’s contributions for the mission include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (Megane) spectrograph instrument to study Phobos’ surface, as well as the pneumatic sampler (p-sampler) technology demonstration, which will collect the Phobos sample. NASA will also lend communications and navigation support with the agency’s Deep Space Network.

A long way home

The mission will also test technology that could help humans travel to Mars one day. Getting a spacecraft to Mars and back, using robotics to reach and collect samples from the surface of Phobos, and relying on deep space communication the whole time should teach NASA and JAXA quite a bit about what it takes for a successful round trip to Mars.

If all goes well, the mission will take five years. JAXA has scheduled the MMX spacecraft for a Mars arrival in August 2027. The craft will depart in November 2030 and return to Earth in July 2031.

However, even if the MMX mission is a success, there’s no guarantee it will be the first mission to Mars and back. China’s Tianwen-3, tasked with returning samples from Mars to Earth, is scheduled for a 2028 launch, with a return date also set for 2031.

In 2020, NASA’s Osiris-Rex spacecraft grabbed samples from the asteroid Bennu and brought them to Earth in 2023.

Tech.title: Meta Blames Bot Traffic for No Kings Day Instagram Suspension
Tech.content:
Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Oct. 17.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.

Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate.

More from CNET

“It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account,” Stone wrote.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”

As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes. A representative for the No Kings Coalition did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.

Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events.

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.

Tech.title: Verizon Sets New iPhone Handoff Feature at $10, Double T-Mobile’s Price (and Still No AT&T Interest)
Tech.content:
Verizon has now played its hand in supporting Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27, which lets you easily switch between two iPhones using a single phone number. Just by unlocking the phone you want to use, your calls, texts, voicemails and Find My location automatically move over.

At launch, the feature is supported only by T-Mobile and Verizon in the US. Along with the rollout of the iPhone Duo, Verizon announced that it will charge $10 a month for the service, which will be supported “soon.” T-Mobile is charging $5 a month. AT&T is sitting this feature out for now.

iPhone Handoff is similar to what the Apple Watch has done with data for a few generations: taking off one watch and putting on another automatically switches all of your information, such as activity tracking, to the new one. For example, some people use one watch during the day — perhaps the rugged Apple Watch Ultra — and switch to a slimmer, older Apple Watch at night, allowing the first to charge for the morning.

But replicating that behavior to the iPhone requires coordination with cellular providers. Each phone’s eSIM needs to be configured for iPhone Handoff by a carrier, and service needs to switch cleanly on the network side.

Ironically, the Apple Watch gets left out of the iPhone Handoff transaction: Your watch remains paired with just one iPhone, communicating with it via Wi-Fi or cellular (if that’s an option). “If neither is available,” Apple writes, “calls, messages, notifications, certain health and fitness features, Siri AI or other app experiences relayed from your paired iPhone may not be available.”

In its press release about offering the iPhone 18 Pro, T-Mobile writes, “iPhone Handoff is available on any iPhone with iOS 27 via iPhone settings and ready to use from day one on the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iPhone Duo. T-Mobile is introducing the feature at $5/month.”

When I reached out to T-Mobile asking about the charge, a spokesperson wrote via email, “The $5/month charge reflects the added service that powers the experience on both devices.”

A Verizon representative did not have further details to share.

While iPhone Handoff appears to seamlessly switch your eSIM just by picking up the phone you want to use, it’s not yet clear what else is different with this process versus just transferring your eSIM manually using your iPhone’s settings menu.

Notably absent from Apple’s news was the other major US carrier, AT&T. I contacted a spokesperson there to learn more about the company’s plans for the feature, but it sounds like it’s not a priority.

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

In addition to T-Mobile and Verizon, iPhone Handoff is currently supported by Deutsche Telekom in Germany. The UK carrier EE will also support the feature later this year, according to Apple.

Tech.title: Your Phone Can Now Spot Smart Glasses Faster Than You Can
Tech.content:
Meta’s Ray-Bans and similar smart glasses send out Bluetooth signals while they’re powered on, and a new category of apps uses those signals to flag them nearby.

Apps such as Zuckoff take a different approach to the problem, scanning for the Bluetooth signal that smart glasses emit while powered on and alerting nearby app users before anyone in range of the built-in LED indicator realizes recording might be happening.

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Broad concerns over privacy have led to a technical battle. On one side, hardware modifiers are tweaking wearable cameras to make them even harder to spot, often by disabling LED indicators. On the other, developers and privacy-focused coders are launching counter tech to give you a heads-up when a hidden camera walks into the room.

One of those developers has already gained traction with a free Apple iOS app called Zuckoff, a digital detection tool to spot nearby Ray-Ban Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles or similar hardware.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Sniffing out smart glasses

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

What drove Szydlowski to actively develop a software detector was seeing social media videos of people wearing smart glasses who recorded pranks or harassed women with pickup lines. None of the targets seemed aware that their content would appear online, which made Szydlowski angry. “There was not even a blur involved to try to censor them, to give them some sort of feeling of privacy,” he said. “These days, everybody feels entitled to post everything.”

App developer Pawel Szydlowski said he developed his app, Zuckoff, to help address people’s privacy concerns about smart glasses. Pawel Szydlowski

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Smart glasses detected… now what?

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

Unlike with smartphones, where it’s easier to tell when someone is recording or taking photos, “smart glasses shift the burden of privacy entirely onto the person being photographed,” Ananthakrishnan said.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

Privacy-conscious smart glasses?

That surveillance anxiety may prompt some hardware makers to release alternative versions of smart glasses that entirely avoid potential privacy violations.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker. Scott Stein/CNET

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

The future of smart glasses detectors

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Zuckoff’s Szydlowski said it’s possible a company could shrink the kind of 5G technology to fit in smart glasses, making them less dependent on phones and Bluetooth, but that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. If Meta or Snap deliberately updated their hardware to hide from detection apps and disable smart glasses’ digital footprint, it would further undercut any claim of privacy accountability.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

Tech.title: iOS 27.2 Could Bring These Features to Your iPhone Soon
Tech.content:
More than a month after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the iOS 27.2 release candidate on Monday, Oct. 19. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, such as FaceTime and Apple Music.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 this Friday, Oct. 23, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 afterwards.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only to a device other than your primary one. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2.

Screenshot by CNET

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the iOS 27.2 RC. Apple usually releases RC versions of updates about one week before it releases that update to the general public, so Apple could release iOS 27.2 on, or shortly after, Monday, Oct. 26.

Siri AI in more languages

Siri AI is available on iOS 27 now. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

In iOS 27, Siri AI is available only in English. And the iOS 27.2 RC expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in FaceTime

In the iOS 27.2 RC, you can use your front and rear-facing cameras at the same time in FaceTime calls. This allows you to FaceTime with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Apple Music gets a new color scheme

The old Apple Music logo (left) next to the logo introduced in the iOS 27.2 beta. Screenshot by CNET

The iOS 27.2 RC brings a new look to the Apple Music app. The app icon is now black and white, as opposed to the reddish hue it had in previous iOS versions. Tapping into the app also reveals new blue menu items throughout, rather than the same reddish tone as the older app logo.

An antisnatching feature

According to 9to5Mac, code within an earlier iOS 27.2 beta shows a feature called AutoLock. This is reportedly an antitheft feature that can lock your device if it detects it’s been snatched out of your hand. For example, AutoLock could lock your iPhone if it detects a sharp acceleration, as if it were snatched out of your hands, or if your device has been unlocked for an extended period of time.

It’s important to note that this feature is not a user-facing option on your iPhone in this beta. Rather, 9to5Mac says it saw internal code related to the feature. That means this feature may not be available when Apple releases iOS 27.2.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the iOS 27.2 RC. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of which podcasts are new and which you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the release candidate of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids’ shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 RC is Multiview. Developers and beta testers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racetrack while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

The updated Health app is gone

The Apple Health app just got a refresh. Apple

Apple removed the redesigned Health app earlier in a previous beta version of iOS 27.2. Developers and beta testers could explore the refreshed app in early iOS 27.2 betas and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

The redesign was always expected to launch sometime later this year. So it’s not surprising that Apple removed this feature in the lead-up to iOS 27.2’s general release.

It’s also not unusual for Apple to include features in early beta versions of software, then remove or change them in later betas or upon the release of an iOS update.

Those are a few of the new features developers and beta testers can try now with the iOS 27.2 RC. There could be more betas before the OS is released to the public, which might be next week.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

Tech.title: Apple Sends Invites Out for ‘Pro and Tell’ Special Event on Oct. 28
Tech.content:
Apple is holding a surprise special event at 10 a.m. PT/1 p.m. ET on Oct. 28 in Los Angeles that the company has dubbed “Pro and Tell,” according to invitations sent out on Monday.

“Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of marketing, wrote on X.

Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i — Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026

Apple did not immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment. The company is historically tight-lipped about what products it shows at its events, so we don’t expect to see any other details until the event on Oct. 28.

More from CNET

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple could unveil a revamped MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display as well as a new OLED iPad mini at the event.

Apple’s Pro and Tell event comes just weeks after its Welcome Home event, where it unveiled a lineup of smart home products, and almost two months after Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, where it announced the iPhone Duo as well as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and the Apple Watch Series 12. So while we may not know for sure what products Apple will announce at its Pro and Tell event, we likely won’t see new iPhones, Apple Watches or HomePods.
